dervis-irab:71-82.t:
* Vocabulary:
(إِمْراً): al-imr is a grave, abhorrent thing. Abū ʿUbayda said: al-imr is a great calamity, and he recited:
قد لقي الأقران مني نكرا ... داهية دهيا وأمرا إمرا
(My peers have met from me something abhorrent: a dire calamity and a grievous affair.)
One says: amira al-amru, i.e. the matter became grave and worsened. This lexical root is remarkable: you say al-amr with fatḥa, meaning a demand that something be brought about, plural awāmir; al-amr also means affair, plural umūr; ulū al-amr are the people of leadership and the scholars; al-immar and al-immara are a man of weak judgement; and al-amīr is the one who commands. So its meanings change as its form changes.
(تُرْهِقْنِي): burden me. In al-Mukhtār: rahiqahu means it covered him, of the pattern ṭariba; and arhaqahu ʿusran means he burdened him with it.
(زَكِيَّةً): pure of sins, because he was young and had not reached the age of moral responsibility. In al-Qāmūs: zakā yazkū zakāʾan and zukuwwan, and zakiya yazkā zakan: the crop grew, and the man became upright and lived in ease; zakkāhu Allāh with doubling means Allah made him grow, purified him and set him right; [Translator's note: the text reads «وأخا زكاته», apparently a corruption — perhaps «وأدّى زكاته», "he paid his zakāt" — translated as uncertain] … and zakkā mālahu means he paid the zakāt on it; and zakkā nafsahu means he praised himself.
(نُكْراً): with ḍamma then sukūn, or with two ḍammas: an abhorrent thing. It is more intense than al-imr, because it involves killing, unlike holing the ship, which could be remedied and made good. It has also been said:
al-imr is more intense, because the loss of lives through the holing is graver than the killing of a single soul.
(يُضَيِّفُوهُما): one says ḍāfahu when one becomes his guest; its root meaning is inclining: one says ḍāfa al-sahmu ʿan al-gharaḍ (the arrow veered from the target). Aḍāfahu and ḍayyafahu mean he made him his guest; they are ḍuyūf, aḍyāf and ḍīfān. Figuratively: aḍāfa ilayhi amran means he assigned a matter to him and charged him with it; "So-and-so has had matters assigned to him"; "he is nothing but muḍāf", i.e. an adopted hanger-on; and "a muḍūfa (calamity) befell him". The poet said:
وكنت إذا جاري دعا لمضوفة ... أشمر حتى يبلغ الساق مئزري
(Whenever my neighbour called out for help in a calamity, I would hitch up my garment until my waist-wrapper reached my shin.)

* I'rab:
(فَانْطَلَقا حَتَّى إِذا رَكِبا فِي السَّفِينَةِ خَرَقَها): the fāʾ is resumptive, and the clause is resumptive, introduced to begin the three matters we alluded to, whose inner realities were hidden from Moses while their outward appearances seemed objectionable to him. Something omitted must be supplied, i.e. "So they set off walking, with their attendant Joshua son of Nun with them" — mention of the one followed sufficing for the follower — i.e. along the seashore, seeking a ship to carry them; they found a ship and boarded it; then al-Khiḍr took the axe and holed the ship by pulling out two of its planks from the part adjoining [Translator's note: the sentence is incomplete in the source], and Moses began objecting to him, saying, etc. (حتى) is a particle of limit and a genitive-governing preposition; (إذا) is a future adverb (ẓarf); the clause (ركبا في السفينة) is in the position of the genitive by the adverb's being put in construct with it; and the clause (خرقها) is the apodosis (jawāb) of (إذا); it is a past verb, a latent (mustatir) pronoun as fāʿil (agent), and a mafʿūl bihi (direct object).
(قالَ: أَخَرَقْتَها لِتُغْرِقَ أَهْلَها لَقَدْ جِئْتَ شَيْئاً إِمْراً): (قال) — i.e. Moses — (أخرقتها): the hamza is for the interrogative of disapproval; (لتغرق): the lām is for causation and (تغرق) is an imperfect verb, accusative (manṣūb) by an implied (muḍmara) an after the lām of causation; (أهلها) is the mafʿūl bihi. The secret of his forgetting himself will come under Rhetoric. The lām [of (لقد)] is the response to an omitted oath; (قد) is a particle of affirmation; (جئت) is a verb and its fāʿil; (شيئا) is the mafʿūl bihi; and (إمرا) is an adjective (ṣifa).
(قالَ: أَلَمْ أَقُلْ إِنَّكَ لَنْ تَسْتَطِيعَ مَعِيَ صَبْراً): the hamza is for the interrogative of affirmation (taqrīr); (لم) is a particle of negation, conversion [of tense] and jussive; (إنّ) and its noun, and the clause (لن تستطيع معي صبرا) is its khabar (predicate).
(قالَ لا تُؤاخِذْنِي بِما نَسِيتُ وَلا تُرْهِقْنِي مِنْ أَمْرِي عُسْراً): (لا) is prohibitive; (تؤاخذني) is an imperfect verb, jussive (majzūm) by (لا); the nūn is the nūn of protection (wiqāya); the fāʿil is latent, implied as "you"; and the yāʾ is the mafʿūl bihi. (من أمري) is a ḥāl (circumstantial), because it was originally an adjective of (عسرا); and «عبرا» [Translator's note: so in the source, a misprint for (عسرا)] is the second mafʿūl bihi of (ترهقني).
(فَانْطَلَقا حَتَّى إِذا لَقِيا غُلاماً فَقَتَلَهُ قالَ أَقَتَلْتَ نَفْساً زَكِيَّةً بِغَيْرِ نَفْسٍ لَقَدْ جِئْتَ شَيْئاً نُكْراً): (فانطلقا): the fāʾ is conjunctive and (انطلقا) is a verb and its fāʿil; (حتى) is a particle of limit and a preposition; (إذا) is a future adverb; the clause (لقيا) is put in construct with the adverb and is the protasis (sharṭ) of (إذا); and (غلاما) is the mafʿūl bihi. The fāʾ is a conjunction, and (قتله) is conjoined to (لقيا), so it falls within the scope of the protasis — unlike His saying «حَتَّى إِذا رَكِبا فِي السَّفِينَةِ خَرَقَها» without a fāʾ, where He made it the apodosis. The reason for this difference is that the holing of the ship did not come immediately after the boarding, whereas the killing came immediately after meeting the boy. And (قال) is the apodosis of (إذا). (أقتلت): the hamza is for the interrogative of disapproval; (نفسا) is the mafʿūl bihi and (زكية) an adjective; (بغير نفس): the preposition and its genitive noun are in the position of the accusative as a ḥāl from the agent or the object, i.e. "you killed him wrongfully" or "him being wronged" — or it is attached (mutaʿalliq) to (قتلت). The lām is the response to an omitted oath; (قد) is a particle of affirmation; (جئت) is a verb and its fāʿil; (شيئا) is the mafʿūl bihi; and (نكرا) is an adjective.
(قالَ أَلَمْ أَقُلْ لَكَ إِنَّكَ لَنْ تَسْتَطِيعَ مَعِيَ صَبْراً): the hamza is for the interrogative of affirmation; (لم) is a particle of negation, conversion and jussive; (إنّ) and its noun, and the clause (لن تستطيع معي صبرا) is its khabar. Here He added the word (لك) because the cause for reproach was greater and its ground stronger; it has also been said that (لك) was added for emphasis, as you say to someone you are rebuking: "It is to you I am speaking, and you I mean."
(قالَ إِنْ سَأَلْتُكَ عَنْ شَيْءٍ بَعْدَها فَلا تُصاحِبْنِي): (إن) is conditional; (سألتك) is a past verb, its fāʿil and its mafʿūl bihi, in the position of the jussive as the protasis (fiʿl al-sharṭ); (عن شيء) is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to (سألتك); (بعدها) is an adverb attached to an omitted adjective of (شيء); the fāʾ links the apodosis; (لا) is prohibitive; and (تصاحبني) is jussive by (لا), the yāʾ being the mafʿūl bihi.
(قَدْ بَلَغْتَ مِنْ لَدُنِّي عُذْراً): (قد) is a particle of affirmation; (بلغت) is a verb and its fāʿil; (من) is a preposition, and (لدن) is an adverb, indeclinable (mabnī) on sukūn, in the position of the genitive; the preposition and its genitive noun are attached to (بلغت) or to an omitted ḥāl; and (عذرا) is the mafʿūl bihi.
(فَانْطَلَقا حَتَّى إِذا أَتَيا أَهْلَ قَرْيَةٍ اسْتَطْعَما أَهْلَها): the fāʾ is conjunctive; (انطلقا) is a verb and its fāʿil; (حتى) is a particle of limit and a preposition; (إذا) is a future adverb containing the sense of condition; (أتيا) is a verb and its fāʿil; (أهل) is the mafʿūl bihi and (قرية) is muḍāf ilayhi (genitive construct). It is said the town was Antioch. The meaning of (استطعما أهلها) is that they asked them for food by way of hospitality. The clause (استطعما أهلها) has no grammatical position, because it is the apodosis of (إذا); Ibn Hishām preferred that it be an adjective of (قرية). (أهل) is repeated for emphasis, by way of putting the overt noun in place of the pronoun — its precedents have already been given — or for comprehensiveness, so that the asking for food and the refusal of hospitality include all its people.
(فَأَبَوْا أَنْ يُضَيِّفُوهُما): the fāʾ is conjunctive; (أبوا) is a verb and its fāʿil; and (أن) with what falls within its scope is the object of (أبوا).
(فَوَجَدا فِيها جِداراً يُرِيدُ أَنْ يَنْقَضَّ فَأَقامَهُ): the fāʾ is conjunctive; (وجدا) is a verb and its fāʿil; (فيها) is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to (وجدا); (جدارا) is the mafʿūl bihi; and the clause (يريد) is an adjective of (جدارا). On the meaning of attributing will to the wall there is an enjoyable discussion the reader will find under Rhetoric. (أن) with what falls within its scope is the object of (يريد). (فأقامه): the fāʾ is conjunctive, and (أقامه) is a verb, a latent fāʿil and a mafʿūl bihi, i.e. he raised it, repaired it and set it right.
(قالَ لَوْ شِئْتَ لَاتَّخَذْتَ عَلَيْهِ أَجْراً): (لو) is a non-jussive conditional particle; (شئت) is a verb and its fāʿil; the lām occurs in the apodosis of (لو); (اتخذت) is a verb and its fāʿil, and the clause has no grammatical position, being the apodosis of (لو); (عليه) is attached to an omitted ḥāl; and (أجرا) is the mafʿūl bihi.
(قالَ هذا فِراقُ بَيْنِي وَبَيْنِكَ): (هذا) is the mubtadaʾ (subject), pointing to the parting that follows from the repeated questioning; (فراق) is the khabar; (بيني) is muḍāf ilayhi. Putting (بين) in construct with something not plural was permissible because (بين) is repeated through conjunction with the wāw; (بينك) is conjoined to (بيني).
(سَأُنَبِّئُكَ بِتَأْوِيلِ ما لَمْ تَسْتَطِعْ عَلَيْهِ صَبْراً): the sīn is a particle of the future; (أنبئك) is a verb, a latent fāʿil and a mafʿūl bihi; (بتأويل): the bāʾ is a preposition that has entered upon the content of the second and third objects — the details will come under Benefits; (ما) is a relative noun in construct with (تأويل); (لم) is a particle of negation, conversion and jussive; (تستطع) is an imperfect, jussive by (لم); (صبرا) is the mafʿūl bihi; and (عليه) is attached to (صبرا). I.e. "I will inform you of the secret of what I did in the three matters."
(أَمَّا السَّفِينَةُ فَكانَتْ لِمَساكِينَ يَعْمَلُونَ فِي الْبَحْرِ): (أما) is a particle of condition and detailing; (السفينة) is the mubtadaʾ; the fāʾ is linking; (كانت): kāna with its latent noun, the tāʾ being the quiescent tāʾ of the feminine; (لمساكين) is the khabar of (كانت); and the clause is the khabar of (السفينة). The clause (يعملون في البحر) is an adjective of (مساكين), and (في البحر) is attached to «يعلمون» [Translator's note: so in the source, a misprint for (يعملون)].
(فَأَرَدْتُ أَنْ أَعِيبَها وَكانَ وَراءَهُمْ مَلِكٌ يَأْخُذُ كُلَّ سَفِينَةٍ غَصْباً): the fāʾ is conjunctive; (أردت) is a verb and its fāʿil; (أن أعيبها) is the interpreted maṣdar (verbal noun), the object of (أردت). The wāw is circumstantial; (كان) is a defective past verb; (وراءهم) is an adverb attached to an omitted fronted khabar — it means "in front of", and it may also mean "behind"; (ملك) is the postponed noun of (كان); the clause «يؤخذ» [Translator's note: so in the source; the Qur'anic word is (يأخذ)] is an adjective; (كل سفينة) is the mafʿūl bihi; and (غصبا) is a mafʿūl muṭlaq (absolute object) specifying the kind of taking; the maṣdar may also be in the position of the accusative as a ḥāl. In the speech there is a fronting and postponing whose wonderful secret will come under Rhetoric.
(وَأَمَّا الْغُلامُ فَكانَ أَبَواهُ مُؤْمِنَيْنِ فَخَشِينا أَنْ يُرْهِقَهُما طُغْياناً وَكُفْراً): the wāw is conjunctive; (أما) is a particle of condition and detailing; (الغلام) is the mubtadaʾ; (فكان): the fāʾ is linking, and (كان) with its noun and its khabar; (فخشينا): the fāʾ is conjunctive and (خشينا) is a verb and its fāʿil; (أن) with what falls within its scope is the object of (خشينا); (طغيانا) is the second mafʿūl bihi and (كفرا) is conjoined to (طغيانا); the apodosis clause is the khabar of (الغلام). He attributed the fear to himself because Allah had acquainted him with how the boy would end up had his term been extended and his lifespan lengthened — or because he was relating the words of Allah.
(فَأَرَدْنا أَنْ يُبْدِلَهُما رَبُّهُما خَيْراً مِنْهُ زَكاةً وَأَقْرَبَ رُحْماً): (فأردنا) is conjoined to (خشينا); (أردنا) is a verb and its fāʿil; (أن يبدلهما): (أن) with what falls within its scope is the object of «يبدلهما» [Translator's note: so in the source; the sense requires "the object of (أردنا)"]; (خيرا منه) is the second object; (زكاة) is a tamyīz (specification), i.e. righteousness and piety; (أقرب رحما) is conjoined to (خيرا منه زكاة), and (رحما) is also a tamyīz, i.e. mercy towards his parents.
Abū Ḥayyān said: "(رحما) is accusative as a mafʿūl lahu (object of purpose). Al-Zamakhsharī allowed it to be accusative as a maṣdar governed by (أراد), saying: because it means 'He had mercy on them both'; and Abū al-Baqāʾ allowed it to be accusative as a ḥāl. Both are forced." So reflect.
(وَأَمَّا الْجِدارُ فَكانَ لِغُلامَيْنِ يَتِيمَيْنِ فِي الْمَدِينَةِ): the clause is conjoined to what preceded and its i'rab is the same; (في المدينة) is a second adjective or a ḥāl.
(وَكانَ تَحْتَهُ كَنْزٌ لَهُما وَكانَ أَبُوهُما صالِحاً): the wāw is conjunctive; (كان) is a defective past verb; (تحته) is an adverb attached to an omitted fronted khabar; (كنز) is its postponed noun; (لهما) is an adjective; and (كان أبوهما صالحا) is kāna with its noun and its khabar.
(فَأَرادَ رَبُّكَ أَنْ يَبْلُغا أَشُدَّهُما وَيَسْتَخْرِجا كَنزَهُما رَحْمَةً مِنْ رَبِّكَ): (فأراد) is conjoined to what preceded; (ربك) is the fāʿil; (أن يبلغا) is the object of (أراد); (أشدهما) is the mafʿūl bihi — the explanation of al-ashudd has already been given; (يستخرجا) is conjoined to (يبلغا), the alif being the fāʿil; (كنزهما) is the mafʿūl bihi; and (رحمة من ربك) is a mafʿūl li-ajlihi (object of purpose). I.e. had I not set it up, it would have collapsed and fallen, and the treasure would have come out from beneath it before the two were able to guard the wealth, increase it and invest it, and it would have been lost and scattered.
(وَما فَعَلْتُهُ عَنْ أَمْرِي ذلِكَ تَأْوِيلُ ما لَمْ تَسْطِعْ عَلَيْهِ صَبْراً): the wāw is conjunctive; (ما) is negating; (فعلته) is a verb, its fāʿil and its mafʿūl bihi, the pronoun referring to the whole of what was mentioned; (عن أمري) is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to an omitted ḥāl, i.e. "issuing from my own command" — rather it was by Allah's command and His inspiring me; (ذلك) is the mubtadaʾ; (تأويل) is the khabar; (ما) is muḍāf ilayhi; (لم) is a particle of negation, conversion and jussive; (تسطع), i.e. (تستطع) with the tāʾ of the iftiʿāl pattern dropped, is jussive by (لم); (عليه) is attached to (صبرا); and (صبرا) is the mafʿūl bihi.

* Rhetoric:
The rhetorical devices contained in the foregoing verses could not be accommodated in this book if we attempted to bring out their subtleties and fathom their hidden depths, so let us go on to survey them, inclining to the language of reflection. The first of them:

1- His forgetting himself when he said: «أَخَرَقْتَها لِتُغْرِقَ أَهْلَها»
— while he was among those on board, and was the one most entitled to be absorbed in his own affair and the evil fate he was facing. What drove him to hasten to object was burning zeal and ardour for the truth, so he forgot himself and was occupied with others, in the very state in which everyone says "Myself, myself!" and cares for neither wealth nor child — the state of drowning, in which minds are dazed, reason departs and judgement is lost from the intelligent.

2- Tawriya (double entendre) in His saying «قالَ لا تُؤاخِذْنِي بِما نَسِيتُ»
He framed the speech as a request not to be taken to task for forgetting, giving the impression that he had forgotten, in order to set out his excuse for objecting. Some call this type maʿārīḍ al-kalām (allusive speech); maʿārīḍ is the plural of miʿrāḍ, which here means giving an impression other than what is intended, so as to avoid lying. It is a delightful one of their arts, perhaps the most beautiful of the types of tawriya mentioned earlier. Al-Mutanabbī used to incline to it in his poems, especially the Kāfūriyyāt. He said:
برغم شبيب فارق السيف كفه ... وكانا على العلات يصطحبان
كأن رقاب الناس قالت لسيفه ... رفيقك قيسي وأنت يمان
(Against Shabīb's will the sword left his hand, though the two had kept company through every hardship; it was as if people's necks said to his sword: "Your companion is a Qaysī, and you are a Yemeni.")
This Shabīb was a rebel who rose against Kāfūr al-Ikhshīdī, made for Damascus and besieged it. It is said that a woman threw a millstone on him and felled him, and those with him fled when he died. It is also said that he drank wine to excess, which brought on epilepsy in him, and at the hour of battle a seizure came upon him; his companions left him and went off, and the people of Damascus seized him and killed him. This Shabīb was of Qays, and there have always been enmities and wars between Qays and Yemen, the reports of which are well known; and the sword is called "Yamānī" by attribution to Yemen. Al-Mutanabbī's meaning in this verse is that when Shabīb was killed and the sword left his hand, it was as if the people said to his sword: "You are Yemeni and your owner is a Qaysī" — and that is why the sword shunned him and left him. This is a fine sophism.
Among the fine examples of allusive speech is the saying of Abū al-ʿAlāʾ al-Maʿarrī describing camels:
صلب العصا بضرب قد دمّاها ... تود أن الله قد أفناها
إذا أرادت رشدا أغواها ... محاله من رقه إياها
(Hard of staff, with a beating/journeying that has bloodied/sculpted them; they wish Allah had annihilated them/fed them fanāʾ; whenever they seek rushd (right guidance/a plant), he leads them astray/feeds them ghawā …)
For al-ḍarb is a homonym used for beating with a stick and for al-ḍarb fī al-arḍ, which is travelling through it. Likewise dammāhā is used for two things: one says dammāhu when one makes his blood flow, and dammāhu when one makes him like a dumya, which is a statue. Likewise the word al-fanāʾ is used for nightshade and for the removal of a thing when nothing of it remains: one says afnāhu when one removes it, and afnāhu when one feeds it the berries of al-fanāʾ, which is nightshade. Al-rushd and al-ghawā are two plants: one says aghwāhu when one leads him astray, and aghwāhu when one feeds him «النوى» [Translator's note: so in the source; the context requires al-ghawā, the plant]; and one says ṭalaba rushdan when one seeks that plant, and ṭalaba rushdan when one seeks guidance.
It is related in the reports of the Badr expedition that the Prophet ﷺ was travelling with his Companions heading for Badr when a man of the Arabs met them and said: "Of which people are you?" The Prophet said: "From water (min māʾ)." That man began to ponder, saying:
"From water, from water?" — to see which clan of the Arabs is called Māʾ. The Prophet went on his way; his aim was to conceal his affair. This is an exemplary sophism, because it is possible that some clan of the Arabs is called Māʾ, and possible that the meaning is that they were created from water — and the Prophet is far above lying.

3- Emphasising the two pronouns:
That is in His saying «قالَ أَلَمْ أَقُلْ لَكَ إِنَّكَ لَنْ تَسْتَطِيعَ مَعِيَ صَبْراً» in the story of killing the boy, unlike the story of the ship, where he said «أَلَمْ أَقُلْ إِنَّكَ لَنْ تَسْتَطِيعَ مَعِيَ صَبْراً». The difference between the two forms is that he emphasised the pronoun in the second and not the first: «أَلَمْ أَقُلْ إِنَّكَ», and in the second he said «أَلَمْ أَقُلْ لَكَ إِنَّكَ». This was brought to intensify the confrontation in reproach for rejecting the instruction time after time and for being branded with lack of patience. It is as when a person does what you forbade him, and you blame and rebuke him, then he does it a second time — do you not increase your blame and rebuke? So it was done here: in the reproach it was said first «أَلَمْ أَقُلْ إِنَّكَ», then it was said the second time:
«أَلَمْ أَقُلْ لَكَ إِنَّكَ». This is a point too subtle to be found at a hasty glance, and its beauty can only be fathomed after deep reflection. It is a device of great worth and profound depth, for pronouns have secrets that only the inspired and the creative grasp; they are not merely pronouns mentioned as they appear in grammar books. Splendid examples of it will come in this book of ours, showing the extent of the worth of the Clear [Book] and its exaltation above all rivals.

Emphasis by pronouns in poetry:
We shall now give you examples of emphasis by pronouns found in poetry that astonish the mind. Among the marvels we found delightful is the saying of Abū Tammām:
لا أنت أنت ولا الديار ديار ... خف الهوى وتولت الأوطار
(Neither are you you, nor are the abodes abodes; passion has grown light and desires have departed.)
His saying «لا أنت أنت ولا الديار ديار» is among the rare and charming, because he is he and the abodes are the abodes; what he means is that the motives that used to impel [Translator's note: the rest of this sentence in the source is garbled, evidently mixed with words from the later discussion: «على قبيل أنت منهم وأنت أنت ولو تأتى له ذلك الرأب صدع البيت، ومع ولا الديار في عينه من الحسن تلك الديار» — roughly "… and the abodes no longer have, in his eyes, the beauty those abodes had"]. Abū al-Ṭayyib tried to weave on Abū Tammām's pattern, but fell short and did not catch up with him, when he said:
قبيل أنت أنت وأنت منهم ... وجدك بشر الملك الهمام
(A tribe — you are you, and you are of them, and your grandfather is Bishr, the noble king.)
His saying «أنت أنت» is of the emphasising of the two pronouns referred to, and its benefit is exaggeration in praising him; but he spoiled for himself what he wanted, because the casting of the verse is devoid of beauty, and it contains a fronting and postponing that also spoiled it, for he should have said:
قبيل أنت منهم وأنت أنت — had that been possible for him, it would have mended the crack in the verse; yet even so it remains beneath Abū Tammām's sweet, graceful verse. This comes down to taste, which is the judge in this matter.
The author of al-Aghānī related that ʿAmr ibn Rabīʿa said to Ziyād ibn al-Habūla:
"O best of young men, give me back the camels you took from me." So he returned them to him, and among them was their stallion; the stallion pulled him towards the camels, and ʿAmr threw it down. Ziyād said to him: "If you, O Banū Shaybān, threw down men as you throw down camels, you would be you indeed (la-kuntum antum antum)." ʿAmr said to him: "You have given little and claimed much, and dragged upon yourself a long woe." His saying "you would be you indeed" means you would be the mighty, or the brave, or the people of valour and strength; but the second "antum" specifies them with this quality to the exclusion of others, as though he said "you would be the brave ones and no others". Had he praised them with anything at all by way of describing strength, might and bravery, it would not have reached the level of this word — I mean the second "antum".
4- Al-istiʿāra al-makniyya (implicit metaphor):
In His saying: «فَوَجَدا فِيها جِداراً يُرِيدُ أَنْ يَنْقَضَّ», "will" has been borrowed for being on the verge and drawing near; it may also be a majāz ʿaqlī (rational metonymy). This disagreement is consistent in every attribution to what is not rational, as in the saying of «عمرو بن أبي ربيعة» [Translator's note: so in the source; the poet is ʿUmar ibn Abī Rabīʿa]:
أبت الروادف والثدي لقمصها ... مس البطون وأن تمس ظهورا
(Her hips and breasts refused to let her shifts touch her belly or touch her back.)
We shall set out the discussion of this verse for you fully, so that you can be sure of the truth of this statement. Refusal (al-ibāʾ) is voluntary prevention; the hips and breasts, because of their size, are likened to someone from whom that can properly come. The speech may be taken to intend a simile, in which case it is a figure whose relation is resemblance, and so a consequential (tabaʿiyya) implicit metaphor; or it may not be taken to intend a simile, and be merely an expression of attributing refusal to them to indicate their size, in which case it is a majāz ʿaqlī. The speech also contains a disordered laff wa-nashr (involution and evolution), because touching the belly goes back to the breasts and touching the back to the hips. To bring out the verse's meaning fully, the second verse must be cited, which is:
وإذا الرياح مع العشي تناوحت ... نبّهن حاسدة وهجن غيورا
(And when the winds blow against each other in the evening, they rouse an envious woman and stir a jealous man.)
One says tanāwaḥa al-jabalān, i.e. the two mountains faced each other; so tanāwuḥ means facing, such that some winds come at her from in front and some from behind, so her hips and breasts show and the clothes cling to her waist, revealing its slenderness; so they rouse the envious woman against her and stir the jealous man because he dislikes that of the winds. Of this kind is the saying of al-Ḥasan ibn Hāniʾ Abū Nuwās:
فاستنطق العود قد طال السكوت به ... لا ينطق اللهو حتى ينطق العود
(So make the lute speak, for its silence has been long; amusement does not speak until the lute speaks.)
He likened the lute to a human being by way of implicit metaphor; it may also properly be a majāz ʿaqlī, as we explained to you earlier.
And the saying of Ḥassān ibn Thābit:
ان دهرا يلف شملي بجمل ... لزمان يهمّ بالإحسان
(A time that gathers me together with Jumal is indeed a time that intends kindness.)
Jumal is the name of his beloved; [Translator's note: the source has «ويروى بعدي», "and it is narrated 'baʿdī'", apparently referring to a variant reading of the verse]. He says: the time that gathers me together with my beloved is indeed a time that intends kindness — by way of implicit metaphor, the word "intend" (al-hamm) being the takhyīl (imaginative attribute). It is also possible that attributing intention to it is a majāz ʿaqlī, like attributing the gathering.

5- Fronting and postponing:
The outward form of the speech requires that His saying «فَأَرَدْتُ أَنْ أَعِيبَها» be placed after His saying:
«وَكانَ وَراءَهُمْ مَلِكٌ يَأْخُذُ كُلَّ سَفِينَةٍ غَصْباً», because the wish to damage it was caused by the fear of its being seized, so it ought to come after the cause. The answer is that He, Glorified is He, put the effect before the cause out of concern for it, and because fear of seizure was not the sole cause, but together with its belonging to the poor.
In this verse and the one after it there are other wonderful secrets as well, in the variation of the pronouns in them: in the first he attributed the act to his own pronoun alone, saying «فَأَرَدْتُ أَنْ أَعِيبَها», and in the second he attributed it to the plural pronoun, the one who magnifies himself, in His saying «فَأَرَدْنا أَنْ يُبْدِلَهُما رَبُّهُما» and «فَخَشِينا أَنْ يُرْهِقَهُما». Perhaps attributing the first to himself alone is out of courtesy towards Allah the Exalted, because what is meant is that there is a defect, so he showed courtesy by attributing the damaging to himself. As for attributing the second to the pronoun mentioned, it appears to be in the manner of the king's intimates who say "We ordered such-and-such" or "We arranged such-and-such", meaning only that the king ordered or arranged it. This is supported by His saying in the third: «فَأَرادَ رَبُّكَ أَنْ يَبْلُغا أَشُدَّهُما». So the pronouns did not come in a single pattern, and this is among the highest of styles and the richest in fertile meanings, which the ear does not reject but takes in.

* Benefits:
1- The verbs that take three objects are aʿlama, arā, anbaʾa, nabbaʾa, akhbara, khabbara and ḥaddatha. The basic ones among these verbs are aʿlama and arā, whose origin before the hamza of transfer entered on them was ʿalima and raʾā, which take two objects. As for the remaining five, none has a triliteral form used in the sense of knowledge except khabara; but in some of their uses they were assimilated to aʿlama, which takes three objects, because inbāʾ, tanbiʾa, ikhbār, takhbīr and taḥdīth mean informing (iʿlām). These five are also used transitive to one object directly, and to the content of the second and third, or the content of the third alone, through the bāʾ, as in "I told you of Zayd's going out" (ḥaddathtuka bi-khurūji Zaydin). On this is construed His saying «سَأُنَبِّئُكَ بِتَأْوِيلِ ما لَمْ تَسْتَطِعْ عَلَيْهِ صَبْراً». Further discussion of these verbs will come in its place, Allah willing.
2- Warāʾ:
It is a word used for "behind" and for "in front", and its meaning here is "in front of them". That (وراءهم) means "in front of them" is the view of Qatāda, Abū ʿUbayda, Ibn al-Sikkīt and al-Zajjāj. There is no disagreement among the lexicographers that warāʾ may mean "in front"; it has come in the Revelation and in poetry. Allah the Exalted said: «مِنْ وَرائِهِ جَهَنَّمُ», and He said «وَمِنْ وَرائِهِ عَذابٌ غَلِيظٌ», and He said «وَمِنْ وَرائِهِمْ بَرْزَخٌ». Labīd said:
أليس ورائي إن تراخت منيتي ... لزوم العصا يحنى عليها الأصابع
(Is there not ahead of me, if my death is delayed, clinging to a staff over which the fingers are bent?)
Sawwār ibn al-Muḍarrib al-Saʿdī said:
أيرجو بنو مروان سمعي وطاعتي ... وقومي تميم والفلاة ورائيا
(Do the Banū Marwān hope for my hearing and obedience, when my people are Tamīm and the desert lies before me?)
Another said:
أليس ورائي أن أدب على العصا ... فتأمن أعداء وتسأمني أهلي
(Is there not ahead of me that I creep along on a staff, so that enemies feel safe and my family grows weary of me?)
Al-Farrāʾ said: "It is not permissible to say of a man in front of you 'he is behind you' (warāʾaka); that is permissible only for times — nights, days and ages. You say 'Severe cold is behind you (warāʾaka)' and 'Severe cold is in front of you'; both are permissible because cold, when it overtakes you, comes to be behind you, and it is as if, when you reach it, it comes to be in front of you." He said: "This was permissible in the language only because whatever is before you and in front of you, once it is hidden from you, has come to be behind you." Most lexicographers hold that warāʾ is one of the aḍdād (words with opposite meanings).

dervis-irab:83-88.t:
* Vocabulary:
(ذِي الْقَرْنَيْنِ): the views about him are greatly confused. While the Qur'an commentators claim he is someone other than Alexander the Great of Macedon, they say he is the one who built Alexandria — although Alexander the Great is its builder. As for the meaning of Dhū al-Qarnayn ("the one with the two horns"), it is a title he was given because he travelled round the two "horns" of the world, i.e. its two sides, east and west; or because he had two qarns, i.e. two braids — the Arabs call a lock of hair a qarn, plural qurūn. Majnūn Laylā said to her husband on the morning after his wedding:
بعيشك هل ضممت إليك ليلى ... قبيل الفجر أو قبلت فاها
وهل رفّت عليك قرون ليلى ... رفيف الأقحوانة في شذاها
(By your life, did you hold Laylā to you just before dawn, or kiss her mouth? And did Laylā's braids flutter over you as the chamomile flutters in its fragrance?)
It is also said that there was something on his head resembling two horns. He may also have been given this title for his bravery, just as a brave man is called a ram because he butts his peers. There is disagreement about his time and place, which may be consulted in the lengthy works, since this inquiry does not fall within the scope of our book.
(حَمِئَةٍ): i.e. very black, from al-ḥamʾa, i.e. mud. In al-Miṣbāḥ: al-ḥamʾa, with sukūn on the mīm, is black mud; ḥamiʾat al-biʾr ḥamaʾan, of the pattern taʿiba, means the well came to contain ḥamʾa; and al-ʿayn al-ḥamiʾa is water running over black mud. It has also been read ʿaynin ḥāmiya, i.e. hot. It is related that Ibn ʿAbbās read (حمئة) while he was with Muʿāwiya; Muʿāwiya read ḥāmiya, and Ibn ʿAbbās said ḥamiʾa. Muʿāwiya said to ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar: "How do you read it?" He said: "As the Commander of the Believers reads it." Then he sent to Kaʿb al-Aḥbār: "How do you find the sun sets?" He said: "In water and mud" — agreeing with what Ibn ʿAbbās said. A man there recited the words of Tubbaʿ:
قد كان ذو القرنين جدي مسلما ... ملكا تدين له الملوك وتسجد
بلغ المغارب والمشارق يبتغي ... أسباب أمر من حكيم مرشد
فرأى مغار الشمس عند مآبها ... في عين ذي خلب وثأط حرمد
(Dhū al-Qarnayn, my forefather, was a Muslim, a king to whom kings submitted and bowed down. He reached the places of setting and rising, seeking the means of an affair from One Wise and Guiding. He saw where the sun sinks at its return, in a spring of khulub, thaʾṭ and ḥarmad.)
Al-khulub, with two ḍammas, is al-ḥamʾa, which is mud; al-thaʾṭ is ḥamʾa mixed with water, so that it becomes wetter and spoils; and al-ḥarmad is black mud. Tubbaʿ praised Dhū al-Qarnayn, then said that he reached the places where the sun sets and the places where it rises, seeking from Allah means that would bring him to his goal; and he saw the place of the sun's «غبار» [Translator's note: so in the source, "dust" — evidently a misprint for maghār, "sinking", as in the verse] at its maʾāb, i.e. its return. (في عين) is attached to (مغار) and is a ḥāl (circumstantial) from it. Abū ʿAlī al-Jubbāʾī interpreted this in a novel way, saying that it is by way of how things appear, just as whoever sees the western shore of a vast sea sees the sun setting in it, whereas in reality it sets into a darkness behind the earth because of its rotation, as the first principles of science establish.

* I'rab:
(وَيَسْئَلُونَكَ عَنْ ذِي الْقَرْنَيْنِ): the wāw is resumptive; (يسألونك) is an imperfect verb, its fāʿil (agent) and its mafʿūl bihi (direct object); and (عن ذي القرنين) is attached (mutaʿalliq) to (يسألونك).
(قُلْ سَأَتْلُوا عَلَيْكُمْ مِنْهُ ذِكْراً): the clause (سأتلو) is the maqūl al-qawl (object of saying); (عليكم) is attached to (أتلو); (منه) is attached to an omitted ḥāl, because it was an adjective of (ذكر) and was fronted before it; and (ذكرا) is the mafʿūl bihi.
(إِنَّا مَكَّنَّا لَهُ فِي الْأَرْضِ وَآتَيْناهُ مِنْ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ سَبَباً): (إنّ) and its noun, and the clause (مكنا) is its khabar (predicate); (له) is attached to (مكنا), and (في الأرض) is also attached to (مكنا); (آتيناه) is conjoined to (مكنا), being a verb, its fāʿil and its mafʿūl bihi; (من كل شيء) is attached to an omitted ḥāl, because it was an adjective of (سببا); and (سببا) is the second object of (آتيناه).
(فَأَتْبَعَ سَبَباً): the fāʾ is conjunctive; (أتبع) is a past verb whose fāʿil is latent (mustatir), implied as "he"; and (سببا) is the mafʿūl bihi. It has also been said that it takes two objects, one of which is omitted, implied as "he made one means follow another means" or "he made his affair follow a means". Yūnus and Abū Zayd said: atbaʿa with the disjunctive hamza expresses one who is earnest, hurrying and urgent in pursuit, while with the conjunctive hamza [ittabaʿa] it only implies following, without these qualities.
(حَتَّى إِذا بَلَغَ مَغْرِبَ الشَّمْسِ وَجَدَها تَغْرُبُ فِي عَيْنٍ حَمِئَةٍ): (حتى) is a particle of limit and a genitive-governing preposition; (إذا) is an adverb for future time; the clause (بلغ) is put in construct with the adverb; (مغرب الشمس) is the mafʿūl bihi; the clause (وجدها) has no grammatical position, because it is the apodosis (jawāb) of a non-jussive condition; (في عين) is attached to (تغرب); and (حمئة) is an adjective of (عين).
(وَوَجَدَ عِنْدَها قَوْماً قُلْنا يا ذَا الْقَرْنَيْنِ إِمَّا أَنْ تُعَذِّبَ وَإِمَّا أَنْ تَتَّخِذَ فِيهِمْ حُسْناً): (ووجد) is conjoined to (وجدها); (عندها) is an adverb attached to (وجد); (قوما) is the mafʿūl bihi; (قلنا) is a verb and its fāʿil; (ذا القرنين) is a vocative in construct (munādā muḍāf); (إما) is a particle of condition and detailing; (أن تعذب) is an interpreted maṣdar (verbal noun) in the position of the nominative as the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ (subject), i.e. "it is your punishing"; or nominative as a mubtadaʾ with the khabar omitted, i.e. "either your punishing takes place". Among the evidence for the nominative is the poet's saying:
فسيروا فإما حاجة تقضيانها منها ... وإما مقيل صالح وصديق
(So travel on: either a need you two will fulfil, or a good resting-place and a friend.) [Translator's note: the word «منها» in the first hemistich appears to be an intrusion in the source; it breaks the metre.]
Or it is in the position of the accusative as the mafʿūl bihi of an omitted verb, i.e. "either you carry out the punishment". (وإما أن تتخذ) is conjoined to (إما أن تعذب); (فيهم) is attached to (تتخذ) or is the second object of (تتخذ); and (حسنا) is the first mafʿūl bihi, i.e. a course possessing goodness.
(قالَ: أَمَّا مَنْ ظَلَمَ فَسَوْفَ نُعَذِّبُهُ): (أما) is a particle of condition and detailing; (من ظلم) is the mubtadaʾ, and the clause (ظلم) is the ṣila (relative clause); (فسوف): the fāʾ is linking and (سوف) is a particle of the future; (نعذبه) is an imperfect verb, a latent fāʿil and an object; and the clause is the khabar of (من).
(ثُمَّ يُرَدُّ إِلى رَبِّهِ فَيُعَذِّبُهُ عَذاباً نُكْراً): (ثم) is a conjunction of sequence with delay; (يرد) is a passive imperfect verb whose nāʾib fāʿil (deputy agent) is latent, implied as "he"; (إلى ربه) is attached to (يرد); (فيعذبه): the fāʾ is conjunctive, and (يعذبه) is a verb, its fāʿil and its mafʿūl bihi; (عذابا) is a mafʿūl muṭlaq (absolute object); and (نكرا) is an adjective.
(وَأَمَّا مَنْ آمَنَ وَعَمِلَ صالِحاً فَلَهُ جَزاءً الْحُسْنى): (وأما) is conjoined to the preceding (أما); (من) is the mubtadaʾ; (آمن) is the ṣila; (عمل صالحا) is a verb, a latent fāʿil and a mafʿūl bihi — or (صالحا) is an adjective of an omitted mafʿūl muṭlaq, i.e. "a righteous deed". (فله): the fāʾ is linking and (له) is a fronted khabar; (جزاء) is a tamyīz (specification). Abū Ḥayyān parsed it as a maṣdar in the position of a ḥāl, i.e. "being recompensed", as when you say "In the house, standing, is Zayd". It has also been said that it is accusative as a maṣdar, i.e. "he is recompensed with a recompense". (الحسنى) is the postponed mubtadaʾ, i.e. "he shall have the finest deed as a recompense". Al-Farrāʾ said: (جزاء) is accusative by way of explanation (tafsīr), i.e. with respect to the relation — the relation of the fronted khabar, which is the preposition and its genitive noun, to the postponed mubtadaʾ, which is (الحسنى) — the implied sense being "the finest deed belongs to him by way of recompense" [Translator's note: the source ends this phrase with «من جزاء الجزاء», apparently a corruption].
(وَسَنَقُولُ لَهُ مِنْ أَمْرِنا يُسْراً): (وسنقول) is an imperfect verb, nominative (marfūʿ), whose fāʿil is a latent pronoun implied as "we"; (له) is attached to (نقول); (من أمرنا) is attached to an omitted ḥāl, because it was an adjective of (يسرا) and was fronted before it; and (يسرا) is the mafʿūl bihi or a mafʿūl muṭlaq, i.e. we will not command him with what is hard and arduous, but with what is easy and manageable.

* Benefits:
A novel discussion concerning «في»:
Ibn Qutayba held that «في» [here] means «عند» ("at"), because it can occur in the sense of «في» and in the sense of «مع» ("with"). The poet said:
حتى إذا ألقت يدا في كافر
(Until, when it [the sun] laid a hand in kāfir [the night])
its meaning is "at kāfir". And the poet said:
وفي الشر نجاة حين لا ينجيك إحسان
(And in evil there is deliverance when kindness does not save you)
its meaning is "and with evil". And «في» in the verse may mean «على» ("on"), as in His saying, Exalted is He:
«وَلَأُصَلِّبَنَّكُمْ فِي جُذُوعِ النَّخْلِ», i.e. on the trunks of the palm-trees. ʿAntara said:
بطل كأن ثبابه في سرحة
(A hero — as if his clothes were in a lofty tree)
i.e. on a lofty tree. And just as «في» occurs in the place of «على», so the case is reversed, as in the poet's saying:
ولقد سريت على الزمان بمعشر
(I have travelled by night "on" time with a company)
i.e. in the darkness. [Translator's note: so in the source; the explanation «أي في الظلام» suggests the verse originally read «على الظلام», "on the darkness".]
Further, we say that the address follows the judgement of the senses, as the eye sees it, because whoever stands on the shore of the encircling ocean, or near a high mountain, sees the sun at setting as though it had sunk into the sea itself or behind the mountain. Allah the Exalted said: «حَتَّى تَوارَتْ بِالْحِجابِ», i.e. behind the mountain. Were it not that the wording came according to the outward judgement of the senses, Allah the Exalted would not have said: «وَجَدَ عِنْدَها قَوْماً», for it is known rationally that the people do not sit at the edge of the sun, nor are they near it. But since Dhū al-Qarnayn had penetrated far in traversing the earth until he reached the encircling ocean on the western side, it would seem to the beholder that the sun sets there. So the address came according to the outward judgement of the senses — and how often the senses deceive! This has discussions to be taken from their proper sources, and it is not among our conditions to discuss these topics, important as they are. History relates that Ibn al-Haytham had a book of great worth in seven volumes on this science, but it was lost along with what was lost of our Arab heritage.
The poets, moreover, have been witty in alluding to the deception of the senses. Abū al-ʿAlāʾ al-Maʿarrī said:
والنجم تستصغر الأبصار رؤيته ... والذنب للطرف لا للنجم في الصغر
(The eyes deem the star small when they see it, but the fault in its smallness lies with the eye, not the star.)
And al-Khafājī said:
ولا ينال كسوف الشمس طلعتها ... وإنما هو فيما يزعم البصر
(The eclipse of the sun does not touch its face; it is only in what the eye claims.)

dervis-irab:1-8.t:
* Vocabulary:
(عِوَجاً): It is stated in al-Qāmūs and other lexicons: ʿawija, with kasra on the wāw, yaʿwaju, with fatḥa, ʿawajan — said of a stick and the like: it bent; and of a person: his character became bad, so he is aʿwaj. Al-ʿiwaj, with kasra then fatḥa, is the noun from ʿawija, meaning twistedness and lack of straightness. These lexicons did not distinguish between the two (forms), but in al-Asās: "One says: in the stick there is ʿawaj, and in opinion there is ʿiwaj" — so it distinguished between them, and this is correct, as the verse proves.
Thus al-ʿiwaj, with kasra then fatḥa, is in abstract matters what al-ʿawaj, with two fatḥas, is in concrete things. Al-Shihāb said in his gloss on al-Bayḍāwī: "That is, the form with kasra is for what is perceived not by sight but by insight, and the form with fatḥa for what is perceived by sight." And he [Zamakhsharī] said in al-Kashshāf: "Al-ʿiwaj, with kasra then fatḥa, is in abstract matters what al-ʿawaj, with two fatḥas, is in concrete things."
More about it will come in the Rhetoric section.
(قَيِّماً): straight, balanced, with neither excess nor deficiency; or "upholding" the interests of the servants, in which case it describes the Book as perfecting (others) after describing it as perfect; or "guardian" over the earlier scriptures, confirming them and bearing witness to their soundness. In al-Qāmūs, al-Tāj and al-Lisān: al-qayyim ʿalā al-amr is the one in charge of it, like the qayyim of an endowment and others; the qayyim of a woman is her husband; amr qayyim means a straight matter; al-diyāna al-qayyima is the straight religion; and in the Revelation «ذلك دين القيمة», i.e. the religion of the straight community. It is made transitive with bāʾ and with ʿalā.
(باخِعٌ نَفْسَكَ): destroying and killing yourself. One says: bakhaʿa al-rajulu nafsahu yabkhaʿuhā, of the pattern nafaʿa, bakhʿan and bukhūʿan: he destroyed himself with grief. More explanation of it will come in the Rhetoric section.
(صَعِيداً): dust, or fragments that vanish in the wind, not the dry matter that settles.
(جُرُزاً): with two ḍammas. Al-juruz is land with no vegetation in it, so its beauty has faded and its adornment is gone. One says: sana juruz (a barren year) and sinūn ajrāz; jarazat al-jarādu al-arḍa: the locusts ate what was on the land; al-jarūz is a woman who eats a great deal. The rajaz poet said:
إن العجوز حية جروزا ... تأكل كل ليلة فقيزا
(The old woman is a voracious snake; every night she eats a qafīz [a measure of grain].)
And jarazahu al-zamān: time swept him away. Tubbaʿ said:
لا تسقني بيديك إن لم ألقها ... جرزا كأن أشاءها مجروز
(Do not give me drink with your hands if I do not leave it [the land] barren, as if its young palms had been cut down.)
Among the proverbs of the Arabs: "A hater will not be pleased except with a jarza (an extirpation)"; it is applied to enmity, meaning that the one who hates is not pleased except with the uprooting of the one he hates.

* I'rab:
(الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ الَّذِي أَنْزَلَ عَلى عَبْدِهِ الْكِتابَ وَلَمْ يَجْعَلْ لَهُ عِوَجاً): الحمد is the mubtadaʾ (subject); لله is attached to (mutaʿalliq) an omitted word, its implied form being "established (thābit) for Allah", which is the khabar (predicate); الذي is a naʿt (adjective); the clause أنزل is the ṣila (relative clause); على عبده is attached to أنزل; الكتاب is the mafʿūl bihi (direct object). The wāw may be a conjunction, so the clause is conjoined to أنزل and falls within the domain of the ṣila; or it may be parenthetical, so the clause is a parenthesis between the ḥāl (circumstantial), namely قيما, and the one it describes (ṣāḥib al-ḥāl), namely الكتاب; or it may be the wāw of circumstance, so the clause is a ḥāl from الكتاب, and قيما is then an overlapping ḥāl (ḥāl mutadākhila), as will come.
(قَيِّماً لِيُنْذِرَ بَأْساً شَدِيداً مِنْ لَدُنْهُ): The statements of the grammarians and exegetes on the i'rab of قيما are in great confusion. Our choice has fallen on its being a ḥāl from الكتاب, with the clause ولم يجعل being parenthetical. Abū al-Baqāʾ chose that it be a ḥāl from the hāʾ in له, the ḥāl being emphatic (muʾakkida). Al-Zamakhsharī chose that it be accusative by an implied verb, its implied form being "He made it qayyim"; we quote his words because of their importance: "If you ask: by what is قيما put in the accusative? I say: it is best that it be put in the accusative by an implied verb and not made a ḥāl from الكتاب, because His saying ولم يجعل is conjoined to أنزل, so it falls within the domain of the ṣila; so whoever makes it a ḥāl from الكتاب separates the ḥāl from its owner by part of the ṣila. Its implied form is: 'and did not make any crookedness in it — He made it straight', because when He negated crookedness of it, He affirmed straightness for it."
Ḥafṣ perceived this confusion in the i'rab of قيما, so he paused at the tanwīn of عوجا, changing it into an alif, with a light pause (sakta) without breaking the breath, to indicate that قيما is not connected to عوجا but is a description of the Book.
Abū Ḥayyān stated explicitly in al-Baḥr that a single word may be a substitute for a clause, as in the saying of Allah the Exalted «ولم يجعل له عوجا قيما»: قيما is a badal (substitute) for the clause ولم يجعل له عوجا, because it has the meaning of a single word, i.e. "He made it straight". There are other analyses which we have passed over because they do not go beyond this range.
لينذر: the lām is causal (for taʿlīl); ينذر is an imperfect verb in the accusative by an implied أن after the lām of causation; the preposition and its genitive noun (the interpreted maṣdar) are attached to أنزل. ينذر takes two objects; the first is omitted, its implied form being "the unbelievers"; بأسا is the second mafʿūl bihi; شديدا is a naʿt; من لدنه is a second naʿt, or is attached to لينذر.
(وَيُبَشِّرَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ الَّذِينَ يَعْمَلُونَ الصَّالِحاتِ أَنَّ لَهُمْ أَجْراً حَسَناً ماكِثِينَ فِيهِ أَبَداً): ويبشر is conjoined to لينذر; the fāʿil (agent) is latent (mustatir), its implied form being "huwa"; المؤمنين is the mafʿūl bihi; the clause يعملون الصالحات is the ṣila. As for أن and what is in its domain: it is said to be an interpreted maṣdar that is the second mafʿūl bihi of يبشر, on the view of those who hold that يبشر takes two objects; and it is said to be an interpreted maṣdar accusative by removal of the preposition (manṣūb bi-nazʿ al-khāfiḍ), the (implied) preposition with its genitive being attached to يبشر. لهم is the preposed khabar of anna and أجرا its postponed noun; ماكثين is a ḥāl from the hāʾ (pronoun) in لهم, i.e. abiding in it; فيه is attached to ماكثين; أبدا is an adverb also attached to ماكثين.
(وَيُنْذِرَ الَّذِينَ قالُوا اتَّخَذَ اللَّهُ وَلَداً): وينذر is conjoined to the first لينذر. الذين is the first object of ينذر; the second is omitted, namely the thing warned of, because it has been mentioned before — namely the "severe punishment" (al-baʾs) — so there is iḥtibāk (reciprocal ellipsis) in the speech. The clause قالوا is the ṣila; the clause اتخذ is the maqūl al-qawl (object of the saying); الله is the fāʿil and ولدا the mafʿūl bihi.
(ما لَهُمْ بِهِ مِنْ عِلْمٍ وَلا لِآبائِهِمْ): a resumptive clause, brought to establish their ignorance and that they say what they do not know. ما is negative; لهم is a preposed khabar; به is attached to علم; من is a redundant (zāʾida) preposition; علم is a postponed mubtadaʾ. ولا: the wāw is a conjunction and لا is negative; لآبائهم is conjoined to لهم.
(كَبُرَتْ كَلِمَةً تَخْرُجُ مِنْ أَفْواهِهِمْ إِنْ يَقُولُونَ إِلَّا كَذِباً): كبرت is a past verb for expressing blame (inshāʾ al-dhamm); the tāʾ is the sign of the feminine; the fāʿil is a latent pronoun referring to their fabricated statement, namely their saying "Allah has taken a son", i.e. their statement was grievous. كلمة is a tamyīz (specification). The speech is built on the pattern of wonder (taʿajjub), as if it were said: "How grievous it is as a word!" The clause تخرج is a naʿt of كلمة; من أفواههم is attached to تخرج. The fāʿil may also be a pronoun explained by an indefinite noun, namely كلمة, which is accusative as a tamyīz; the speech is then pure blame, and the specified object of blame (al-makhṣūṣ bi-al-dhamm) is omitted [Translator's note: printed «مخذوفا»], its implied form being "it", i.e. the word. Both views are sound and acceptable. إن is negative; يقولون is an imperfect verb in the nominative, the sign of its nominative being the retention of the nūn; the wāw is the fāʿil; إلا is a particle of restriction (ḥaṣr). كذبا has two views, the more evident of which is that it is a naʿt of an omitted maṣdar, i.e. "except a false saying"; it may also be a mafʿūl bihi, because it implies a clause — and on this basis runs the saying of Diʿbil:
ما أكثر الناس لا بل ما أقلهم ... الله يعلم اني لم أقل فندا
إني لأغمض عيني ثم أفتحها ... على كثير ولكن لا أرى أحدا
(How many people there are — no, rather, how few they are! Allah knows I have not spoken a falsehood: I shut my eyes, then open them on many, but I do not see anyone.)
(فَلَعَلَّكَ باخِعٌ نَفْسَكَ عَلى آثارِهِمْ إِنْ لَمْ يُؤْمِنُوا بِهذَا الْحَدِيثِ أَسَفاً): the fāʾ is resumptive; لعل is a particle of hope (tarajjī) that puts its noun in the accusative, one of the sisters of inna; the kāf is its noun and باخع its khabar; نفسك is a mafʿūl bihi; على آثارهم is attached to باخع — more explanation of it will come in the Rhetoric section. إن is conditional; لم يؤمنوا is the protasis (fiʿl al-sharṭ); بهذا is attached to يؤمنوا; الحديث is a badal from the demonstrative; أسفا is a mafʿūl li-ajlihi (object of purpose), or a maṣdar in the position of a ḥāl. The apodosis (jawāb al-sharṭ) is omitted, indicated by the expression of hope; its implied form is "then do not grieve, and let not your soul go out in regrets over them".
(إِنَّا جَعَلْنا ما عَلَى الْأَرْضِ زِينَةً لَها لِنَبْلُوَهُمْ أَيُّهُمْ أَحْسَنُ عَمَلًا): inna and its noun; the clause gives the reason (taʿlīl) for the prohibition intended by the expression of hope. The clause جعلنا is the khabar of إنا; ما is a relative noun, the first mafʿūl bihi of جعلنا if it means "to make into"; على الأرض is the ṣila of ما; زينة is the second mafʿūl bihi of جعلنا; and if it means "We created", then زينة is a ḥāl. It is strange that some parse it as a mafʿūl li-ajlihi, although adornment is not one of the mental maṣdars, however far we stretch the interpretation. لها is a naʿt of زينة. لنبلوهم: the lām is causal, and نبلوهم is in the accusative by an implied أن after the lām of causation; the preposition and its genitive are attached to جعلنا. أيهم: an interrogative noun, mubtadaʾ, and the hāʾ is the muḍāf ilayhi; أحسن is the khabar; عملا is a tamyīz; and the clause is in the position of an accusative, standing in place of the two objects of نبلو, because it has the meaning of "We know", and it is suspended (muʿallaq) from operating by the interrogative أي. أي may also be a relative meaning "the one who", parsed as a badal from the hāʾ in نبلوهم, the implied form being "that We may test the one who is best"; أحسن is then the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ, i.e. "he is best", and the clause is the ṣila of the relative. The ḍamma on أي is then the ḍamma of indeclinability (bināʾ), because its condition is present, namely that it is in construct and the head of its ṣila is omitted; or its ḍamma is a ḍamma of declension, on the view of some grammarians. The pronoun in نبلوهم refers to the inhabitants of the earth, as understood from the context of the speech, or to ما; but this is far-fetched because it requires interpreting ما as specific to rational beings.
(وَإِنَّا لَجاعِلُونَ ما عَلَيْها صَعِيداً جُرُزاً): the wāw is a conjunction; inna and its noun; the lām is the shifted lām (al-lām al-muzaḥlaqa); جاعلون is its khabar; ما is the second mafʿūl bihi of جاعلون [Translator's note: so in the source; it should be the first, since صعيدا is then called the second]; عليها is the ṣila; صعيدا is the second mafʿūl bihi of جاعلون; جرزا is a naʿt of صعيدا. The two words may also be considered as having a single meaning, like "the pomegranate is sweet-sour", i.e. tart (muzz), so that together they take the place of the second object; and perhaps this is preferable. Its verification will come in its place in this book.

* Rhetoric:
These verses contain various kinds of rhetorical devices, which we mention as follows:
1- Repetition (takrīr):
1- Repetition, which has been mentioned before, in the saying of Allah the Exalted «ولم يجعل له عوجا قيما»: the negation of crookedness means the affirmation of straightness, and He inclined to repetition only for a benefit without equal, namely emphasis and clarification. For many a straight thing is attested to be straight, and its straightness is agreed upon, yet the careful examiner may find in it the slightest crookedness; so when He affirmed straightness for it, He removed the suspicion of that slightest (crookedness) remaining, which escapes the first superficial glance.
2- Antithesis (muṭābaqa):
He, glory be to Him, set crookedness and straightness in antithesis, so the speech came out fine, with no room in it for a critic — as happened to Abū al-Ṭayyib (al-Mutanabbī), who neglected antithesis in one of his most splendid odes. He recited in the assembly of Sayf al-Dawla his words:
نظرت إلى الذين أرى ملوكا ... كأنك مستقيم في محال
فإن تفق الأنام وأنت منهم ... فإن المسك بعض دم الغزال
(I looked at those I see as kings — as if you were the one straight thing among absurdities. If you surpass mankind while being one of them, musk too is part of the gazelle's blood.)
It was said to him: "Muḥāl (absurdity) does not correspond antithetically to straightness, but the rhyme forced you to it. But suppose you had said 'as if you were straight amid crookedness (iʿwijāj)' — what would you have done in the second verse?" He said without hesitating: "For eggs (al-bayḍ) are part of the blood of chickens (al-dajāj)." This was admired as an instance of his improvisation.
We say: this is admired only for quickness of improvisation; otherwise, how far is his saying "musk too is part of the gazelle's blood" from his saying "musk is part of the blood of chickens"! [Translator's note: so in the source, which repeats «المسك» here where the improvised line had «البيض».]
Since we wish to be fair in criticism, we cite what one of al-Mutanabbī's opponents faulted him for, namely that he gave no weight to antithesis and that his habit was to omit it — despite our intense admiration for the poet of immortality and our preferring him above all the poets of Arabic, ancient and modern. The early critic said:
As for the lack of antithesis in the poetry of Abū al-Ṭayyib al-Mutanabbī, it is very frequent. Of it is his saying:
ولكل عين قرة في قربه ... حتى كأن مغيبه الأقذاء
(Every eye finds coolness (delight) in his nearness, so that his absence is like specks of dirt in the eye.)
The opposite of qurra (coolness) is sukhna (heat), and specks of dirt are not its opposite. Also his saying:
ولم يعظم لنقص كان فيه ... ولم يزل الأمير ولن يزالا
(He did not become great because of a deficiency in him; he has always been the prince and always will be.)
Greatness is the opposite of lowliness, and deficiency the opposite of perfection; had he said "he did not become perfect because of a deficiency in him", it would have been more unassailable.
Likewise his saying, despite its loftiness and brilliance:
لمن تطلب الدنيا إذا لم ترد بها ... سرور محب أو اساءة مجرم
(For whom do you seek the world, if you do not intend by it the joy of a lover or the harming of a criminal?)
The criminal is not the opposite of the lover, nor is joy the opposite of harm; the criminal is the opposite of the doer of good, the lover the opposite of the hater, and harm the opposite of doing good.
Likewise his saying:
وانه المشير عليك فيّ بضدّه ... فالحر ممتحن بأولاد الزنا
(Forbid the one who counsels you against me; for the free-born man is afflicted by the children of fornication.) [Translator's note: printed «وانه», read as the imperative «وانهَ» (forbid).]
And the free-born man (al-ḥurr) is the opposite of the base man (al-laʾīm).
3- Negating a thing by affirming it (nafy al-shayʾ bi-ījābihi):
This is in the saying of Allah the Exalted «وقالوا اتخذ الله ولدا ما لهم به من علم». This device has been mentioned before, and it has another name, namely "the reverse of the apparent" (ʿaks al-ẓāhir); it is among the rarities of the science of bayān. It is that you mention speech whose apparent sense indicates that it negates a quality of something described, whereas it negates the described thing altogether. For someone could say: Allah's taking a son is in itself impossible, so how is His saying «مالهم به من علم» admissible?
It resembles the objection in the saying of Allah the Exalted «وان تشركوا بالله ما لم ينزل به سلطانا»: all of this comes by way of sarcasm (tahakkum); otherwise there is no authority for polytheism that could be sent down. And the son is in itself impossible, and knowledge cannot properly relate to it; but it comes by way of sarcasm and mockery of them. Its counterpart, as has preceded, is his ﷺ saying: "His slips are not spread abroad" (lā tuthnā faltātuhu), i.e. his lapses are not broadcast — and there are no slips there to be spread. And the saying of the poet describing a desert:
لا تفزع الأرنب أهوالها ... ولا ترى الضبّ بها ينجحر
(Its terrors do not frighten the hare, and you do not see the lizard taking refuge in a burrow there.)
The apparent sense of this is that there was a lizard there but it was not taking refuge in a burrow [Translator's note: printed here «منجمر», evidently for «منجحر»]; but it is not so — rather the meaning is that there was no lizard there at all.
4- The eloquent representational simile (al-tashbīh al-tamthīlī al-balīgh) preserved from triteness:
This is in the saying of Allah the Exalted «فلعلك باخع نفسك على آثارهم ان لم يؤمنوا بهذا الحديث أسفا». Allah the Exalted likened him and them — when they turned away from him, did not believe in him, and persisted in arrogance, obstinacy and contention with false sophistry, and then what entered him as a result of that, of grief and sorrow at their turning away and pity for them because of the evil outcome [Translator's note: printed «المغاب»] to which their affairs were heading — He, glory be to Him, likened that to a man whose loved ones and dear ones have left him, so that he is falling apart with regrets over their traces and destroying himself with grief for them and longing at their parting. He brought this unique image to preserve His simile from triteness, for longing at the parting of loved ones and feeling grief is a common matter which the poets have treated in their poetry, speaking in their odes of their burning passions. This is a standard by which the eloquent is measured: in his simile he rises above the ordinary simile, with its embellishments and adornments, and pours his own splendour upon it. Al-Mutanabbī in particular was alert to this and preserved from triteness the simile he could not do without. We shall cite for you samples of his poetry so that you may know what heights this immortal poet reached.
Abū al-Ṭayyib depicted a love scene in which he was forced to liken himself to a speaking dead man and his beloved to a smiling full moon. Both these similes are well-worn; the poets have treated them so that they have become trite and lost their freshness. So he made dialogue a means of depicting a splendid scene in which the simile becomes sweet and appears completely new. He said:
نرى عظما بالبين والصد أعظم ... ونتهم الواشين والدمع منهم
ومن لبّه مع غيره كيف حاله ... ومن سره في جفنه كيف يكتم
ولما التقينا والنوى ورقيبنا ... غفولان عنا ظلت أبكي وتبسم
فلم أر بدرا ضاحكا قبل وجهها ... ولم تر قبلي ميتا يتكلم
(We think separation a great thing, but estrangement is greater; we accuse the slanderers, while the tears are among them. How is one whose mind is with another? And how can one whose secret is in his eyelid keep it hidden? When we met, with distance and our watcher both heedless of us, I kept weeping and she kept smiling; I never saw a laughing full moon before her face, and she never saw before me a dead man speaking.) [Translator's note: the printed text runs these lines together; they are set out here by verse.]
After establishing the effect of estrangement — that its distance neither draws near nor can be traversed, whereas separation may draw near and its distance may be traversed — he confessed that he is unable to hide the lingering remnant of his love; for if your mind is with someone else, how will you fare? And if your secret is in your eyelid, how can you hide it? He means that the tears reveal it. Then he depicted the scene, making his beauty playful, carried away by coquetry and made light-hearted by ease, so she is playful and carefree, smiling while he gnashes his teeth (yaḥriqu al-uram) and is seared by the fire of abandonment — as they say: "Woe to the grieving from the carefree." This is among the most splendid and sweetest poetry.
We return to the verse and say: Allah the Exalted wished to console His Prophet and to soothe the burning grief and anguish that had befallen him, so He presented the scene in the form of hope (tarajjī), even though what is meant by it is prohibition, i.e. do not destroy yourself and do not ruin yourself out of your distress at their not believing; and He brought this marvellous representational simile. Al-asaf is extreme sorrow.

* Benefits:
1- The accusative of the mafʿūl li-ajlihi (object of purpose):
The grammarians laid down five conditions for the mafʿūl li-ajlihi to be in the accusative:
1- That it be a maṣdar.
2- That it be mental (qalbī), one of the inner acts of the soul, such as glorifying, respect, reverence, contempt, apprehension, fear, boldness, desire, dread, modesty, impudence, compassion, knowledge, ignorance and the like; it is contrasted with the acts of the limbs, i.e. of the external senses and what is connected with them, such as reading, writing, standing up, sitting down, standing, sitting, walking, sleeping, waking and others. This is because the cause is what prompts the bringing about of the act, and what prompts a thing precedes it, which the acts of the limbs do not.
3- That it be a cause, because it is what motivates the act.
4- That it coincide in time with the act it explains; so one may not say "I prepared today the travel tomorrow" (taʾahhabtu al-yawma al-safara ghadan), because the time of preparing is not the time of travelling.
5- That it share the same agent as the act it explains; so one may not say "I came to you your love for me" (jiʾtuka maḥabbataka iyyāya), because the agent of coming is the speaker and the agent of love is the addressee.
Whenever one of these conditions is lacking, it must be put in the genitive with a particle of causation such as lām, min, bāʾ and fī. Here are examples for each missing condition:
1- «والأرض وضعها للأنام»: الأنام is the cause of the placing, but it is not a maṣdar; therefore it is put in the genitive with lām.
2- «ولا تقتلوا أولادكم من إملاق»: إملاق is the cause of the killing, but it is not a mental maṣdar; therefore it is put in the genitive with min.
3- قتلته صبرا ("I killed him in confinement"): صبرا is a maṣdar but it is not a cause, so it cannot be put in the accusative as a mafʿūl li-ajlihi, and it cannot be put in the genitive with lām, because the lām conveys causation.
4- The saying of Imruʾ al-Qays:
فجئت وقد نضت لنوم ثيابها ... لدى الستر إلا لبسة المتفضل
(I came when she had taken off her clothes for sleep by the curtain, except for the garment of one in undress.)
Sleep, though it is the cause of taking off the clothes, the time of taking them off precedes the time of sleep [Translator's note: printed «وفت» for «وقت»]; therefore it is put in the genitive with lām. Moreover, sleep is not a mental maṣdar either, so citing it as evidence only for non-coincidence of time is lax.
5- The saying of Abū Ṣakhr al-Hudhalī:
وإني لتعروني لذكراك هزة ... كما انتفض العصفور بلّله القطر
(A tremor seizes me at the remembrance of you, as a sparrow shakes itself when the rain has wetted it.)
Remembrance is the cause of the tremor; the agent of "seizing" is the tremor while the agent of remembrance is the speaker; therefore it is put in the genitive with lām.
We return to the verse: His saying «زينة لها» is the cause of the making, but it is not mental, because it is among the works of the hand. Therefore we found it strange that some parse it as a mafʿūl li-ajlihi, unless a verb of willing is implied, i.e. "willing adornment"; but this strained interpretation is not permissible, and there is an alternative in parsing it as a second object of جعلنا, as has preceded, or as a ḥāl.

Substituting a single word for a clause:
We said in the I'rab that Abū Ḥayyān chose to parse قيما as a badal from the clause لم يجعل لها عوجا [Translator's note: so in the source, «لها»; the verse has «له»], because it has the meaning of a single word. I say: the grammarians have explicitly stated that a clause may substitute for a single word as a complete substitute (badal kull), as in the saying of al-Farazdaq:
إلى الله أشكو بالمدينة حاجة ... وبالشام أخرى كيف يلتقيان
(To Allah I complain of a need in Medina and another in Syria — how can the two meet?)
He substituted the clause كيف يلتقيان for حاجة and أخرى, which are single words; this is valid only because the pronoun refers back to a single word. So is the reverse permissible? The meaning of the verse is: to Allah I complain of these two states — the impossibility of their meeting; so "impossibility" is a maṣdar in construct with its agent, and it is a badal from "these two". Al-Damāmīnī said: it is possible that كيف يلتقيان is a resumptive clause by which he draws attention to the cause of the complaint, namely the unlikelihood of these two needs coming together. Al-Shām is a land named after Shām son of Noah — for it is with the dotted shīn in Syriac — or because its land has patches (shāmāt) of white, red and black; on this view it is not pronounced with a hamza; and it may be masculine. So in al-Qāmūs.

dervis-irab:89-98.t:
* Vocabulary:
(بَيْنَ السَّدَّيْنِ): between the two mountains. It is related that Dhū al-Qarnayn blocked what lay between them. The mountain is called a sadd (barrier) because it is, broadly, a barrier — in al-Qāmūs: al-sadd is a mountain and a barrier — or because it adjoined the barrier, so it is a figure based on the relation of adjacency. The second view is the one suited to what precedes it; the details are in the lengthy works.
(يَأْجُوجَ وَمَأْجُوجَ): two foreign names, as shown by their being diptotes for being proper names and foreign. It has also been said that they are Arabic, and there is disagreement about their derivation: some say from ajīj al-nār, i.e. the blazing and fierce burning of fire; some say from al-awja, which is mixing, or intense heat; and some say from al-awj, which is swift running. On this view they are diptotes for being proper names and feminine. Both are from ajja al-ẓalīm, said of the male ostrich when it hurries, or from ajjat al-nār, when the fire blazes. The views about what they really are are many and may be consulted in the lengthy works.
(خَرْجاً): a payment of money; or kharāj, with the khāʾ taking any of the three vowels — it has been read so — from which comes "al-kharāj bi-l-ḍamān" (the yield goes with the liability). Later, what the ruler takes came to be called kharāj, and the jizya is called kharāj, so one says: he paid the kharāj of his land. Figuratively: kharaja fulān fī al-ʿilm wa-l-ṣināʿa khurūjan means he excelled in learning or craft; kharrajahu fulān fa-takharraja means So-and-so trained him and he became trained; and he is a khirrīj (graduate) of the school. Zuhayr said, describing horses:
وخرّجها صوارخ كل يوم ... فقد جعلت عرائكها تلين
(He trained them with battle-cries every day, so that their stubbornness began to soften.)
i.e. he disciplined them as a learner is trained.
(رَدْماً): a strong, firmly secured barrier. Al-radm is greater than al-sadd; it is from their expression "thawb murdam" (a patched garment). From it is the saying of ʿAntara:
هل غادر الشعراء من متردم ... أم هل عرفت الدار بعد توهم
(Have the poets left any place in need of patching? Or did you recognise the abode after uncertainty?)
Al-mutaraddam is the place that needs patching and mending because of the weakness and wear that has befallen it. Al-taraddum is also like al-tarannum, i.e. modulating the voice with a sad tone. The meaning of ʿAntara's saying is: the first left nothing for the last, i.e. poets preceded me who left me nothing needing a patch for me to patch and nothing needing mending for me to mend.
(زُبَرَ الْحَدِيدِ): plural of zubra, like ghurfa, i.e. a piece.
(الصَّدَفَيْنِ): with two fatḥas, also with two ḍammas, and with ḍamma on the first and sukūn on the second; it has been read in all three ways. It is the dual of ṣadaf with two fatḥas, ṣuduf with two ḍammas, and ṣudaf with ḍamma on the first and fatḥa on the second, and the reverse: the end of a mountain or its forelock. They were so called because they face each other.
(قِطْراً): with kasra then sukūn: copper melted onto heated iron.
(يَظْهَرُوهُ): to climb onto its top (ẓahr), because of its height and smoothness.
(نَقْباً): a breach, [impossible] because of its hardness and thickness.
(دَكَّاءَ): with the long vowel: level ground, from their expression nāqa dakkāʾ, i.e. a she-camel without a hump, levelled by pounding. It has been read dakkan, the maṣdar of dakka.

* I'rab:
(ثُمَّ أَتْبَعَ سَبَباً): conjoined to its counterparts; its i'rab has been given.
(حَتَّى إِذا بَلَغَ مَطْلِعَ الشَّمْسِ وَجَدَها تَطْلُعُ عَلى قَوْمٍ لَمْ نَجْعَلْ لَهُمْ مِنْ دُونِها سِتْراً): (حتى) is a particle of limit and a genitive-governing preposition; (إذا) is a future adverb (ẓarf); the clause (بلغ) is put in construct with the adverb; (مطلع), with kasra on the lām, is the place of rising — discussion of it will come under Benefits; the clause (وجدها) has no grammatical position, because it is the apodosis (jawāb) of a non-jussive condition; the clause (تطلع) is the second object of (وجدها); (على قوم) is attached (mutaʿalliq) to (تطلع); the clause (لم نجعل) is an adjective of (قوم); (لهم) is in the position of the accusative as the second object of (نجعل); (من دونها) is a ḥāl (circumstantial); and (سترا) is the first object of (نجعل). For their land has no buildings in it, only underground tunnels: when the sun rises they enter them, and when the day is advanced they go out to their livelihoods. It has also been said that what is meant by covering is clothing, so they are always naked.
(كَذلِكَ وَقَدْ أَحَطْنا بِما لَدَيْهِ خُبْراً): (كذلك) is the khabar (predicate) of an omitted mubtadaʾ (subject), i.e. "the matter is thus"; (وقد): the wāw is conjunctive or circumstantial, and (قد) is a particle of affirmation; (أحطنا) is a verb and its fāʿil (agent); (بما) is attached to (أحطنا); (لديه) is the ṣila (relative clause) of the relative; and (خبرا) is a tamyīz (specification) or a mafʿūl bihi (direct object), as was given before.
(ثُمَّ أَتْبَعَ سَبَباً): its i'rab has been given.
(حَتَّى إِذا بَلَغَ بَيْنَ السَّدَّيْنِ وَجَدَ مِنْ دُونِهِما قَوْماً لا يَكادُونَ يَفْقَهُونَ قَوْلًا): (بين السدين): (بين) is accusative as a mafʿūl bihi, the thing reached, just as it is genitive by construct in His saying «هذا فِراقُ بَيْنِي وَبَيْنِكَ» and nominative in His saying «لقد تقطع بينكم», because it is one of the adverbs used both as nouns and as adverbs — the details will come under Benefits. The clause (وجد) has no grammatical position, because it is the apodosis of (إذا); (من دونهما) is the second object of (وجد) and (قوما) is the first object of (وجد); the clause (لا يكادون) is an adjective of (قوما); the wāw is the noun of (يكاد) and the clause (يفقهون) is its khabar; and (قولا) is the mafʿūl bihi.
(قالُوا يا ذَا الْقَرْنَيْنِ إِنَّ يَأْجُوجَ وَمَأْجُوجَ مُفْسِدُونَ فِي الْأَرْضِ): (يا) is the vocative particle and (ذا القرنين) is a vocative in construct (munādā muḍāf); (إنّ) and its noun; (مأجوج) is conjoined to (يأجوج); (مفسدون) is the khabar of (إنّ); and (في الأرض) is attached to (مفسدون).
(فَهَلْ نَجْعَلُ لَكَ خَرْجاً عَلى أَنْ تَجْعَلَ بَيْنَنا وَبَيْنَهُمْ سَدًّا): the fāʾ is conjunctive; (هل) is an interrogative particle; (نجعل) is an imperfect verb with a latent (mustatir) fāʿil; (لك) is the second object of (نجعل) and (خرجا) is the first object of (نجعل); (على) with what it governs is attached to an omitted adjective of (خرجا), i.e. "resting on this condition", so (على) here has its basic sense, i.e. superiority (istiʿlāʾ); the adverb (بيننا) is attached to the omitted second object of (تجعل); (بينهم) is conjoined to (بيننا); and (سدا) is the first object of (تجعل).
(قالَ ما مَكَّنِّي فِيهِ رَبِّي خَيْرٌ): (ما) is a relative noun in the position of the nominative as the mubtadaʾ; the clause (مكني) is the ṣila; (فيه) is attached to (مكني); (ربي) is the fāʿil of (مكني); and (خير) is the khabar of the mubtadaʾ.
(فَأَعِينُونِي بِقُوَّةٍ أَجْعَلْ بَيْنَكُمْ وَبَيْنَهُمْ رَدْماً): the fāʾ is the fāʾ al-faṣīḥa (the fāʾ implying an omitted condition); (أعينوني) is an imperative verb, its fāʿil and its mafʿūl bihi; (بقوة) is attached to (أعينوني); (أجعل) is an imperfect verb, jussive (majzūm) because it is the response to the request; the adverb (بينكم) is the second object of (أجعل), and (بينهم) is conjoined to it; and (ردما) is the first object of (أجعل). The meaning of (أعينوني بقوة) is: with workers and craftsmen skilled in building, and with tools — its explanation will follow.
(آتُونِي زُبَرَ الْحَدِيدِ حَتَّى إِذا ساوى بَيْنَ الصَّدَفَيْنِ): (آتوني) is an imperative verb, its fāʿil and its first mafʿūl bihi; (زبر الحديد) is the second mafʿūl bihi; (حتى) is a particle of limit and a preposition; (إذا) is a future adverb; and (ساوى) is a past verb whose fāʿil is latent, implied as "he". Something omitted must be supplied for the limit, i.e. "so they brought him what he asked for, and he built, and put charcoal and firewood between the two cliffs, until he had blocked what lay between the two mountains up to their tops". The adverb is attached to (ساوى).
(قالَ انْفُخُوا حَتَّى إِذا جَعَلَهُ ناراً قالَ آتُونِي أُفْرِغْ عَلَيْهِ قِطْراً): the clause (انفخوا) is the maqūl al-qawl (object of saying); the clause (قال) has no grammatical position, because it is the apodosis of (إذا); (حتى) marks the limit of the blowing; the clause (جعله نارا) is put in construct with the adverb, and (نارا) is the second object of (جعل); the clause (آتوني) is the maqūl al-qawl; (أفرغ) is an imperfect, jussive because it is the response to the request, its fāʿil being "I"; (عليه) is attached to (أفرغ); and (قطرا) is the mafʿūl bihi of (أفرغ). The implied sense is "Bring me molten copper; I will pour molten copper on it", the first being omitted because the second indicates it. The matter belongs to the chapter of tanāzuʿ (two governors contending for one word): the second was given governance; had the first been given governance, they would have said "Bring me, I will pour it on it, molten copper", since the implied sense would be "Bring me molten copper, I will pour it on it". Similar is His saying, Exalted is He: «هاؤُمُ اقْرَؤُا كِتابِيَهْ» — the second was given governance; had the first been given governance He would have said «هاؤُمُ اقْرَؤُا كِتابِيَهْ» [Translator's note: so in the source, repeating the verse unchanged; the intended form is presumably «اقرؤوه», "read it"]. Discussion of it will come in its time.
(فَمَا اسْطاعُوا أَنْ يَظْهَرُوهُ وَمَا اسْتَطاعُوا لَهُ نَقْباً): the fāʾ conjoins to something omitted, i.e. "then the people of Gog came, after he had finished building and levelling it, trying to climb over it or breach it, but they could not". (اسطاعوا) is a verb and its fāʿil; (أن) and what follows it is an interpreted maṣdar (verbal noun) in the position of the accusative as the object of (اسطاعوا); (وما استطاعوا) is conjoined to (فما اسطاعوا); (له) is attached to (نقبا); and (نقبا) is the mafʿūl bihi.
(قالَ هذا رَحْمَةٌ مِنْ رَبِّي فَإِذا جاءَ وَعْدُ رَبِّي جَعَلَهُ دَكَّاءَ وَكانَ وَعْدُ رَبِّي حَقًّا): the clause (هذا…) is the maqūl al-qawl; (هذا) is the mubtadaʾ and (رحمة) the khabar, the reference being to the barrier, because it prevents their coming out; (من ربي) is an adjective of (رحمة); (فإذا): the fāʾ is resumptive and (إذا) is a future adverb; the clause (جاء وعد ربي) is put in construct with the adverb; the clause (جعله) has no grammatical position; (دكاء) is the second object of (جعل); (وكان): the wāw is conjunctive or circumstantial; (كان وعد ربي) is kāna and its noun; and (حقا) is its khabar.

* Benefits:
1- Nouns of time and place indicate the time and place of the action.
They are formed from the bare triliteral on the pattern mafʿal, with fatḥa on the ʿayn, and on the pattern mafʿil, with kasra on it. The pattern mafʿal with fatḥa on the ʿayn is for the bare triliteral taken from a yafʿulu with ḍamma on the ʿayn, or yafʿalu with fatḥa on the ʿayn in the imperfect, or from a verb with a weak final radical in general. The first is like maktab, maḥḍar, and maḥall from ḥalla bi-l-makān; the second like malʿab and mazraʿ; and the third like malhā, mathwā and mawqā. Some words are anomalous in coming with kasra even though they are built from verbs with ḍamma on the ʿayn in the imperfect.
