They are eleven: al-maṭliʿ; al-mansik, for the place of nusuk, i.e. worship; al-majzir, for the place of slaughtering camels, i.e. sacrificing them — one says jazartu al-jazūr ajzuruhā, with ḍamma, when I slaughter and skin it; al-manbit, for the place where plants grow; al-mashriq and al-maghrib, for the place of rising and setting; al-mafriq, for the middle of the head, because it is where the hair is parted, and likewise mafriq al-ṭarīq, for the place where another road branches off; al-maskin, the place of dwelling; al-masqiṭ, the place of falling — one says "this is my masqiṭ raʾsī", i.e. where I was born and my head fell; al-mirfaq, the place of ease; and al-masjid, which is the name of the building, not meaning the place of prostration. They gave these words kasra, whereas the rule for them is fatḥa.
The pattern mafʿil with kasra on the ʿayn is for the bare triliteral taken from a sound yafʿilu with kasra on the ʿayn, or from a mithāl verb with initial wāw. The first is like majlis, maḥbis, maḍrib, mabīt and maḍīf; the second like mawrid and mawʿid.
The feminine tāʾ may enter nouns of place, as in al-mazalla, with fatḥa or kasra on the zāy — with fatḥa from the pattern fariḥa and with kasra from the pattern ḍaraba — which is a noun of place from zalla, when he slipped; al-maẓinna, for the place where something is supposed and its usual haunt, with fatḥa on the ẓāʾ [Translator's note: so in the source; the usual form is maẓinna with kasra on the ẓāʾ], because it is from ẓanna yaẓunnu with ḍamma; al-maqbara, for the place of the grave; al-maʿbara, for the place on the shore prepared for crossing; al-mashraqa, with the rāʾ taking any of the three vowels; al-madraja, the road, from daraja yadruju durūjan, when he walked; al-mawqaʿa, with fatḥa or kasra on the qāf, the place on which something falls; and al-mashraba, with fatḥa or ḍamma on the rāʾ, i.e. the place of drinking — it is also used for an upper room, because they used to drink in it, and it is also soft land with lasting vegetation. When something is abundant in a place, mafʿala with fatḥa is used, so the noun of place is built from nouns, as in arḍ masbaʿa, i.e. full of beasts of prey; madhʾaba, full of wolves; maʾsada, full of lions; mabṭakha, full of melons; maqthaʾa, full of cucumbers; maḥyāh, full of snakes; mafʿāh, full of vipers; and madraja, full of durrāj — with ḍamma on the dāl and doubling of the rāʾ — a beautiful bird with coloured plumage, used for both male and female.
As for their pattern from verbs of more than three letters, it is on the pattern of the imperfect, with ḍamma on the mīm, which replaces the imperfect prefix, and fatḥa on the letter before the last, as in mujtamaʿ, muntadā, muntaẓar and mustashfā. They thus resemble the passive participle and the mīmī maṣdar, and they are distinguished from one another by feel and by contextual indicators.

2- The adverb (ẓarf):
The adverb is of two kinds: declinable (mutaṣarrif) and non-declinable (ghayr mutaṣarrif).
The declinable is that which is used both as an adverb and otherwise, so it leaves adverbial status for a state unlike it, such as being used as a mubtadaʾ, a khabar, a fāʿil, a mafʿūl bihi or the like — like shahr, yawm, sana and layl. The non-declinable adverb is that which keeps to the accusative as an adverb and is only used as an accusative adverb, like qaṭṭu, ʿawḍu, baynā, baynamā, idhā, ayyāna, annā, dhā ṣabāḥ and dhāt layla; among them are compound adverbs like ṣabāḥa masāʾa and layla layla; and among them is that which keeps to the accusative as an adverb or to the genitive with min, such as qabl, baʿd, the six directions, ladā, ladun, ʿinda, matā, ayna, hunā, thamma, ḥaythu and al-āna. The details are in the lengthy works.

3- Istaṭāʿa and isṭāʿa:
They said: the origin of isṭāʿa is istaṭāʿa, the tāʾ having been dropped for lightness, and the connecting hamza was given fatḥa and made disjunctive; this is the view of al-Farrāʾ. In istaṭāʿa there are dialectal forms: asṭāʿa yusṭīʿu, with fatḥa on the hamza in the past and ḍamma on the imperfect prefix — it is from aṭāʿa yuṭīʿu, originally yuṭwiʿu, with the fatḥa shifted from the wāw to the ṭāʾ in aṭwaʿa as a phonological modification, by analogy with the past, so it became aṭāʿa; then the sīn entered as a kind of compensation for the middle radical. This is the school of Sībawayh. The second form is istaṭāʿa yastaṭīʿu, with kasra on the hamza in the past, which is connecting, and fatḥa on the imperfect prefix; it is istafʿala, like istaqāma and istaʿāna.

dervis-irab:9-12.t:
* Vocabulary:
(الْكَهْفِ): a cave in a mountain. It is said to be any cave; and it is said to be a spacious cavity in a mountain, and if it is not spacious it is a ghār. The plural is kuhūf. In al-Qāmūs: "Al-kahf is like a house hollowed out in a mountain; when it is small it is a ghār; (it means) a refuge; the plural is kuhūf." In al-Asās: "They took refuge in a kahf and in kuhūf, which are ghīrān (caves); takahhafa al-jabal: caves formed in the mountain. Figuratively: so-and-so is the kahf of his people, i.e. their refuge; and you say: those are their strongholds and their kuhūf."
(الرَّقِيمِ): In al-Qāmūs: al-raqīm is the book, the written thing (al-marqūm). Raqama yarqumu, of the pattern naṣara, al-kitāba: he made the writing clear and marked it with dots, vowels and so on; raqama al-thawb: he striped the garment; (raqama) the camel: he branded it; (raqama) the bread: he decorated it. And they say: "So-and-so writes (yarqumu) on water", of one who is skilful in affairs. It is said to be a tablet on which the names of the People of the Cave and their story were written, which they then placed at the entrance of the cave; the tablet was of lead, or, it is said, of stone. From Ibn ʿAbbās: al-raqīm is the name of the valley in which the Companions of the Cave were; it is also said to be the name of the village they left, or the name of the mountain in which the Companions of the Cave were, or the name of their dog. Umayya ibn Abī al-Ṣalt said:
وليس بها إلا الرقيم مجاورا ... وصيدهم والقوم في الكهف همد
(There is none there but al-Raqīm, keeping close to their threshold, while the people lie still in the cave.)
Al-waṣīd is the courtyard of a house, its door and its threshold, and the verse allows (any of) them; hummad is the plural of hāmid, i.e. sleeping. He says: there is nothing in that desert but the dog, keeping close to the courtyard of their cave, and the people, sleeping in the cave.
Al-Zajjāj said: when the youths fled from their families fearing for their religion, (their families) missed them and told the king their story; he ordered a tablet of lead, and their names were written on it, and he put it in his treasury and said: "It will have significance." That tablet is al-raqīm.
And he said in his Amālī: Know that there are five views on al-raqīm. The first is this one related from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah have mercy on him, that it is a tablet on which their names were written. The second is that al-raqīm is the inkwell; this is related from Mujāhid, who said it is in the language of the Romans (Rūm) — Ibn Durayd reported this and said: "I do not know how sound it is." The third is that al-raqīm is the village, related from Kaʿb. The fourth is that al-raqīm is the valley. The fifth is what is related from al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Qatāda, who said: al-raqīm is the book; the lexicographers incline to this and say it is faʿīl in the sense of mafʿūl — one says raqamtu al-kitāba, i.e. I wrote it, so it is marqūm and raqīm — as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: «كتاب مرقوم».

* I'rab:
(أَمْ حَسِبْتَ أَنَّ أَصْحابَ الْكَهْفِ وَالرَّقِيمِ كانُوا مِنْ آياتِنا عَجَباً): أم is the disconnected (munqaṭiʿa) am, which has been mentioned before. It is usually interpreted as بل together with the hamza, and it is interpreted as بل alone and as the hamza alone; i.e. did you think that the story of the People of the Cave is a wonder of its kind? Rather, do not think it is the most wondrous of the signs; there are signs more wondrous than it. حسبت is a verb and its fāʿil (agent); أن with what is in its domain stands in place of the two objects of حسبت; أن and its noun; الرقيم is conjoined to الكهف; the clause كانوا is the khabar (predicate) of أن; من آياتنا is a ḥāl (circumstantial); عجبا is the khabar of كانوا. The interrogative here is for disapproval and negation; what is meant is not to negate wonder of the story of the People of the Cave — it is a wonder, as we mentioned — but to negate that it is the most wondrous of the signs. Then He began narrating their story, saying:
(إِذْ أَوَى الْفِتْيَةُ إِلَى الْكَهْفِ): the past-time adverb is attached to (mutaʿalliq) an omitted اذكر ("remember"); the clause أوى is in the position of a genitive as the muḍāf ilayhi of the adverb; الفتية is the fāʿil of أوى; إلى الكهف is attached to أوى — fearing for themselves from the unbelievers, because they were believers. Their story is widely related in all the lengthy works, and the contemporary writer of fiction Tawfīq al-Ḥakīm composed the play "Ahl al-Kahf" (The People of the Cave); refer to it, for it is one of the most enjoyable of stories.
(فَقالُوا رَبَّنا آتِنا مِنْ لَدُنْكَ رَحْمَةً وَهَيِّئْ لَنا مِنْ أَمْرِنا رَشَداً): فقالوا is conjoined to أوى; ربنا is vocative (munādā); آتنا is a verb of supplication, indeclinable (mabnī) on the dropping of the weak letter; the fāʿil is latent (mustatir), its implied form being "anta"; نا is the mafʿūl bihi (direct object); من لدنك is a ḥāl, because it was a naʿt (adjective) of رحمة and was preposed before it; رحمة is a mafʿūl bihi; هيئ is conjoined to آتنا; لنا is attached to هيئ; من أمرنا is a ḥāl; رشدا is a mafʿūl bihi.
(فَضَرَبْنا عَلَى آذانِهِمْ فِي الْكَهْفِ سِنِينَ عَدَداً): the fāʾ is a conjunction; ضربنا is a verb and its fāʿil; على آذانهم is attached to ضربنا. The object of ضربنا is omitted, its implied form being "a veil preventing them from hearing". في الكهف is a ḥāl; سنين is an adverb of time for ضربنا; عددا is a naʿt of سنين, or a mafʿūl muṭlaq (absolute object) of an omitted verb. For it is either a maṣdar, in which case both views are permissible, or faʿal in the sense of mafʿūl, in which case only the naʿt is permissible.
(ثُمَّ بَعَثْناهُمْ لِنَعْلَمَ أَيُّ الْحِزْبَيْنِ أَحْصى لِما لَبِثُوا أَمَداً): ثم is a conjunction for delay (tarākhī); بعثناهم is a verb, its fāʿil and its mafʿūl bihi. لنعلم: the lām may be causal (for taʿlīl) or of consequence (lām al-ʿāqiba); in either case نعلم is an imperfect verb in the accusative by an implied أن after it. The meaning of the knowledge of their reckoning — when Allah already knows it — will come in the Rhetoric section. أي is an interrogative noun, the mubtadaʾ (subject); for this reason نعلم is suspended (muʿallaq) from operating. الحزبين is the muḍāf ilayhi. أحصى is a past verb whose fāʿil refers to "which of the two parties". لما لبثوا: the lām is a preposition, ما is maṣdariyya, لبثوا is a verb and its fāʿil, and ما with what follows is an interpreted maṣdar in the genitive by the lām; the preposition and its genitive are attached to أحصى. أمدا is the mafʿūl bihi. The grammarians disagreed whether أحصى may be an elative (ism tafḍīl) or not; those who allow it parse أحصى as the khabar of أي, and أمدا as a tamyīz (specification), or as the object of an omitted verb, i.e. "he reckoned a span". Discussion of these views will come in the Benefits section.

* Rhetoric:
In these verses there are kinds of rhetoric that astonish the mind and lift the veil from the marvellous eloquence of the Qur'an. Here is the detail:
1- The explicit metaphor (al-istiʿāra al-taṣrīḥiyya):
In the saying of Allah the Exalted «فضربنا على آذانهم»: He used, as a metaphor for the persistence of sleep, the preventing veil over their ears. He singled out the ears because by striking over them it (sleep) comes about. Rhetorical images only take shape by resting on aesthetic and psychological foundations close to modern research. The aestheticians have mentioned that the sensations which can most fully be described as beautiful are visual sensations, so much so that Descartes defined beauty by saying: "It is what pleases the eye; for the eye is the sense of light, and man's need for light goes back to his need for life, since certain elements that supply the body with life, energy, movement, enjoyment and joy depend on it." What the Qur'an relied on of visual images will come. Nor does the matter stop at the sense of sight; rather, it is the sense of hearing that brought into being the loftiest arts: poetry, music and eloquence. Al-Rummānī said in his book al-Nukat fī Iʿjāz al-Qur'an: "And the perception of hearing (is involved) in the saying of Allah the Exalted «فضربنا على آذانهم في الكهف سنين عددا»; its literal meaning is: We prevented them from perceiving with their ears, without deafness." So it is as if the metaphor aimed at this auditory depiction and at highlighting the loss of the sense of hearing rather than the other senses, and without indicating permanent deafness. The completion of this awesome image — the image of striking upon the ears — will come in the saying of Allah the Exalted in Sūrat Yā Sīn «يا ويلنا من بعثنا من مرقدنا».
2- Al-taʿlīq [Translator's note: here apparently in the sense of linking an act to a purpose stated as divine knowledge]:
This is in His saying «ثم بعثناهم لنعلم أي الحزبين أحصى لما لبثوا أمدا». What is meant is not that Allah should come to know something that is already within the scope of His knowledge; rather He meant what the knowledge relates to, namely the matter becoming manifest to them, so that they might increase in faith and in taking heed, and so that this might be one of the hidden kindnesses to the believers of their time; or so that the connection of Our knowledge might come about as a present connection [Translator's note: printed «نعلقا» for «تعلقا»], i.e. We know that the matter is occurring now, after We knew before that it would occur in the future. As for what is meant by the two parties that disagreed, al-Farrāʾ said: two groups of Muslims in the time of the Companions of the Cave disagreed about the length of their stay. It is said that the two parties are the Companions of the Cave themselves, because they disagreed among themselves about the length of time they remained asleep. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbās that the two parties are the kings who ruled the city one king after another, and the Companions of the Cave — and other views besides, which there is no room to cite.

* Benefits:
1- We have judged it preferable that «أحصى» in the saying of Allah the Exalted «لنعلم أي الحزبين أحصى لما لبثوا أمدا» be a past verb, because forming the elative from verbs other than the bare triliteral is not regular; as for such expressions as "more contagious (aʿdā) than mange" and "more bankrupt than Ibn al-Mudhāq" [Translator's note: so in the source; the proverb is usually given as «أفلس من ابن المذلّق»], they are anomalous, and analogy on the anomalous outside the Qur'an is impermissible, so how much more so in it! Moreover, the i'rab of أمدا is only sound if «أحصى» is a past verb; if we make it an elative, we need to imply a verb, because the elative does not govern (an object). However, some grammarians made the formation of the elative from the verb augmented with hamza (afʿala) regular; so on their view you say from the verb akrama: "So-and-so is more generous (akram) than so-and-so". These grammarians claimed that Sībawayh held this, and explained it by saying that forming it from that verb does not change the structure of the word; it is only replacing one hamza with another. Al-Zajjāj and al-Tibrīzī chose that أحصى is an elative, while Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī and al-Zamakhsharī chose that it is a past verb, and we have followed this.
2- What al-Mubarrad says about أي:
Al-Mubarrad said in his discussion of أيّ: "Do you not see that its meaning is 'this or that?' [Translator's note: printed «أذا أم ذا»]. And Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said «لنعلم أي الحزبين أحصى لما لبثوا أمدا», because its meaning is 'this one or this one?'; and Allah the Exalted said «فلينظر أيها أزكى طعاما», according to what I have explained to you. And you say: 'Know which of them struck Zayd' (aʿlam ayyuhum ḍaraba Zaydan), and 'Know which of them Zayd struck' (aʿlam ayyahum ḍaraba Zaydun), putting أي in the accusative by ضرب because Zayd is the fāʿil; this (form of أي) is determined only by what comes after it. Likewise what is in construct with one of these interrogative nouns, e.g. 'I knew whose servant is in the house' (ghulāmu ayyihim fī al-dār), and 'I recognised whose servant is in the house' (ghulāmu man fī al-dār) [Translator's note: printed «في في الدار»], and 'I knew whose servant you struck' (ghulāma man ḍarabta), where you put it in the accusative by ضربت. This is how the chapter runs." The gist of what al-Mubarrad wanted to say in this useful glimpse is that the interrogative particles, when they are nouns, are shielded from (the government of) what precedes them.
Ibn Hishām said in al-Mughnī that it is an error — meaning its being an elative — because the condition for the accusative tamyīz after afʿal is that it be the agent in meaning, as in "Zayd is greater in wealth" (Zaydun aktharu mālan), as opposed to "Zayd's wealth is the greatest wealth" (mālu Zaydin aktharu mālin); in the first example the agent of the "greatness" in meaning is the wealth, not Zayd. And he [Ibn Mālik] said in al-Khulāṣa:
والفاعل المعنى انصبن بأفعلا ... مفضلا كأنت أعلى منزلا
(Put the agent in meaning in the accusative after afʿal used as elative, as in "you are higher in rank".)

dervis-irab:13-15.t:
* I'rab:
(نَحْنُ نَقُصُّ عَلَيْكَ نَبَأَهُمْ بِالْحَقِّ): نحن is the mubtadaʾ (subject) and the clause نقص is the khabar (predicate); عليك is attached to (mutaʿalliq) نقص; نبأهم is the mafʿūl bihi (direct object); بالحق is a ḥāl (circumstantial) from the fāʿil (agent) of نقص or from its object, namely the story; the bāʾ is for accompaniment (mulābasa).
(إِنَّهُمْ فِتْيَةٌ آمَنُوا بِرَبِّهِمْ وَزِدْناهُمْ هُدىً): the clause is resumptive, brought to narrate their story. Inna, its noun and its khabar; the clause آمنوا بربهم is a khabar [Translator's note: so in the source; it is usually taken as a naʿt of فتية]. زدناهم is a verb, its fāʿil and the first mafʿūl bihi; هدى is the second mafʿūl bihi, or a tamyīz (specification).
(وَرَبَطْنا عَلى قُلُوبِهِمْ إِذْ قامُوا فَقالُوا رَبُّنا رَبُّ السَّماواتِ وَالْأَرْضِ): وربطنا is conjoined to زدناهم; على قلوبهم is attached to ربطنا; إذ is an adverb of past time attached to ربطنا; the clause قاموا is the muḍāf ilayhi of the adverb; فقالوا is conjoined to قاموا; ربنا is the mubtadaʾ and رب السموات والأرض its khabar.
(لَنْ نَدْعُوَا مِنْ دُونِهِ إِلهاً لَقَدْ قُلْنا إِذاً شَطَطاً): لن is a particle of negation, accusative and futurity; ندعو is in the accusative by لن; من دونه is a ḥāl, because it was a naʿt (adjective) of إلها and was preposed before it. لقد: the lām is the answer to an omitted oath and قد is a particle of affirmation (taḥqīq); قلنا is a verb and its fāʿil; إذن is a particle of answer and requital, inoperative (muhmal); شططا is a mafʿūl muṭlaq (absolute object), i.e. "a saying of extravagance", so it is a naʿt of the omitted maṣdar with an implied muḍāf. It may also be a mafʿūl bihi, because shaṭaṭ contains the meaning of a clause. Sībawayh said, in these exact words: "It is put in the accusative as a ḥāl from the pronoun of the maṣdar of قلنا." Shaṭaṭ is excess in injustice and going far in it, from shaṭṭa, "to be far"; so Sībawayh's view has a large measure of soundness. They said this while standing before the tyrant king Decius (Daqyānūs).
(هؤُلاءِ قَوْمُنَا اتَّخَذُوا مِنْ دُونِهِ آلِهَةً): هؤلاء is the mubtadaʾ; قومنا is a badal (substitute) from the demonstrative or an ʿaṭf bayān (explicative apposition); the clause اتخذوا is the khabar; من دونه is a ḥāl; آلهة is the mafʿūl bihi. The meaning of the statement here is disapproval. هؤلاء may also be parsed as mubtadaʾ with قومنا as the khabar, and the clause اتخذوا in the position of an accusative as a ḥāl.
(لَوْلا يَأْتُونَ عَلَيْهِمْ بِسُلْطانٍ بَيِّنٍ فَمَنْ أَظْلَمُ مِمَّنِ افْتَرى عَلَى اللَّهِ كَذِباً): لولا is a particle of urging (taḥḍīḍ); يأتون is an imperfect verb and its fāʿil, and the clause is resumptive; عليهم, i.e. upon their worship (of them), is attached to an omitted ḥāl; بسلطان is attached to يأتون; بيّن is a naʿt. فمن أظلم: the fāʾ is resumptive; من is an interrogative noun meaning negation and disapproval, the mubtadaʾ; أظلم is its khabar; ممن is attached to أظلم; the clause افترى is the ṣila (relative clause); على الله is attached to افترى; كذبا is the mafʿūl bihi.

* Rhetoric:
In the saying of Allah the Exalted «وربطنا على قلوبهم» there is a dependent explicit metaphor (istiʿāra taṣrīḥiyya tabaʿiyya), resembling «فضربنا على آذانهم», because rabṭ is tying with a rope, and what is meant is: We strengthened their hearts with patience in abandoning their homelands, fleeing with their religion to the caves and grottoes and taking their ground as a bed, and We emboldened them to speak the truth and proclaim it before the tyrant Decius.

dervis-irab:16-18.t:
* Vocabulary:
(مِرفَقاً): with kasra on the mīm and fatḥa on the fāʾ (mirfaq), and the reverse (marfiq); it has been read both ways. It means what you make use of, such as the morning and evening meal, i.e. what you benefit from. He [al-Zamakhsharī] said in Asās al-Balāgha: "Irtafaqtu bihi: I benefited from it; I have no mirfaq or marfiq in it; and there is no marfiq in it of the conveniences of the house (marāfiq al-dār), such as the place of ablution and the kitchen." It is said that with kasra on the mīm it is for the hand (the elbow), and with fatḥa for affairs, and each may be used in place of the other; al-Azharī reported this from Thaʿlab. Some said: they are two dialectal forms for what one makes use of, while the limb is only with kasra on the mīm. In al-Qāmūs, al-Tāj and others: "Al-mirfaq, with kasra on the mīm and fatḥa on the fāʾ, and al-marfiq, with fatḥa on the mīm and kasra on the fāʾ, is the joint between the forearm and the upper arm, and what you make use of; they are two dialectal forms."
(تزاور): i.e. inclines. Its origin is tatazāwar, lightened by assimilating the tāʾ into the zāy or dropping it — it has been read both ways — and it has also been read tazwarru and tazwārru. All of them are from al-zawr, which is inclining; from it is zārahu, "he visited him", when he inclined towards him; and al-zūr is deviation from the truth.
(تَقْرِضُهُمْ): it cuts them off and passes them by, so that it does not touch them at all; taken from the sense of severance and cutting. Dhū al-Rumma said:
إلى ظعن يقرضن أجواز مشرف ... شمالا وعن أيمانهن الفوارس
(Towards women in howdahs who were leaving the middle stretches of Mushrif on their left, with al-Fawāris on their right.)
And before it:
نظرت بجرعاء السبية نظرة ... ضحى وسواد العين في الماء شامس
(I cast a glance at Jarʿāʾ al-Sabiyya in the forenoon, while the pupil of the eye was restive in water [tears].)
Jarʿāʾ al-Sabiyya is the name of a place; "the pupil of the eye…" is a circumstantial clause, i.e. the tears were constantly moving and agitated, from shamasa al-faras, when a horse bolts and is ill-tempered. Al-ẓuʿun is the plural of ẓaʿīna, which is a woman in a howdah; yaqriḍna means they cut across; ajwāz is the plural of jawz, which is the passage and the road, i.e. they leave it to one side of them; and al-Fawāris is the name of a place, not the plural of fāris (horseman).
Al-Fārisī said: the meaning of taqriḍuhum is that it gives them something of its light like a loan (qarḍ), which is then taken back after a while, and it also passes away quickly.
(فَجْوَةٍ): a wide space; from al-fajāʾ, which is a wide gap between the thighs: one says rajul afjā and imraʾa fajwāʾ. The plural is fijāʾ, like qaṣʿa and qiṣāʿ. In al-Qāmūs: "Al-fajwa is the gap between two things, the courtyard of a house, and a wide stretch of land; the plural is fajawāt and fijāʾ."
(الوصيد): its explanation has preceded, and we add to it what the author of al-Qāmūs said: al-waṣīd is the threshold, the courtyard of a house, the cave; others said: and also the door. And he recited:
بأرض فضاء لا يسد وصيدها ... علي ومعروفي بها غير منكر
(In an open land whose door is not shut against me, and my kindness there is not disowned.)
The verse is by Zuhayr. He says: I alighted in a land empty of buildings; there is no building in it having a waṣīd, i.e. a door, that would be shut on me and keep guests away from me, as with town-dwellers. So the negation of the shutting is a metonymy (kināya) for the negation of the door altogether; it is thus of the type "negating a thing by affirming it". And my kindness there is known; no one among people disowns it.

* I'rab:
(وَإِذِ اعْتَزَلْتُمُوهُمْ وَما يَعْبُدُونَ إِلَّا اللَّهَ): an address from some of them to others when they resolved to flee with their religion. إذ is accusative by an implied (verb), its implied form being "some of them said to others"; the clause اعتزلتموهم is in the position of a genitive as the muḍāf ilayhi of the adverb; it is a verb, its fāʿil (agent) and its mafʿūl bihi (direct object). وما يعبدون: the wāw is a conjunction and ما is conjoined to the hāʾ, i.e. you have withdrawn from them and withdrawn from what they worship; ما is a relative, or maṣdariyya, in which case "and their worship" is implied. إلا is a particle of exception, and الله is a connected excepted (mustathnā muttaṣil) on the assumption that they were polytheists (who also worshipped Allah), and disconnected (munqaṭiʿ) on the assumption that they were devoted purely to the worship of idols. It has also been said that the wāw is parenthetical, ما is negative, and the clause is parenthetical — a statement from Allah about the youths that they did not worship other than Allah; and there is nothing to prevent this. Al-Farrāʾ said it (فأووا) is the answer of إذ, as you say "since you have done (such), then do such-and-such"; this is a weak view, because it means that إذ conveys a conditional sense, whereas it is well known that it conveys it only when joined with ما (i.e. إذما).
(فَأْوُوا إِلَى الْكَهْفِ): the fāʾ is the fāʾ al-faṣīḥa (implying an omitted condition), i.e. if you want salvation with your religion, then take refuge. أووا is an imperative verb, indeclinable (mabnī) on the dropping of the nūn; the wāw is the fāʿil; إلى الكهف is attached to it.
(يَنْشُرْ لَكُمْ رَبُّكُمْ مِنْ رَحْمَتِهِ وَيُهَيِّئْ لَكُمْ مِنْ أَمْرِكُمْ مِرفَقاً): ينشر is an imperfect verb in the jussive (majzūm) because it occurs as the answer to the request (imperative); لكم is attached to ينشر; ربكم is the fāʿil of ينشر; من رحمته is a naʿt (adjective) of the omitted object of ينشر, i.e. "He will spread out for you success from His mercy". يهيئ is conjoined to ينشر; لكم is attached to يهيئ; من أمركم is a ḥāl (circumstantial) because it was a naʿt of مرفقا; مرفقا is the mafʿūl bihi.
(وَتَرَى الشَّمْسَ إِذا طَلَعَتْ تَتَزاوَرُ عَنْ كَهْفِهِمْ ذاتَ الْيَمِينِ): in the speech there is concision (ījāz) by the omission of several clauses. The implied form of the speech is: so they took refuge in the cave as they had decided among themselves, and they felt tired, so they slept and sank deep into sleep; and Allah answered their prayer when they said «ربنا آتنا من لدنك رحمة وهيىء لنا من أمرنا رشدا». The wāw is resumptive; ترى is an imperfect verb whose fāʿil is "anta"; الشمس is the mafʿūl bihi; إذا is an adverb of future time attached to تزاور, which is the answer; تزاور is an imperfect verb whose fāʿil is latent (mustatir), its implied form being "hiya", and the clause has no grammatical position; عن كهفهم is attached to تزاور; ذات اليمين is an adverb attached to تزاور.
(وَإِذا غَرَبَتْ تَقْرِضُهُمْ ذاتَ الشِّمالِ): conjoined to the preceding clause, and identical to it in its i'rab.
(وَهُمْ فِي فَجْوَةٍ مِنْهُ ذلِكَ مِنْ آياتِ اللَّهِ): the wāw is the wāw of circumstance; هم is the mubtadaʾ (subject); في فجوة is the khabar (predicate); منه is a naʿt of فجوة; ذلك is a mubtadaʾ and من آيات الله its khabar.
(مَنْ يَهْدِ اللَّهُ فَهُوَ الْمُهْتَدِ وَمَنْ يُضْلِلْ فَلَنْ تَجِدَ لَهُ وَلِيًّا مُرْشِداً): من is conditional, in the position of an accusative as a preposed object; يهد is the protasis (fiʿl al-sharṭ), jussive, the sign of its jussive being the dropping of the weak letter. The fāʾ connects the apodosis (jawāb al-sharṭ) because it is a nominal clause; هو is the mubtadaʾ and المهتدي its khabar; the yāʾ has been dropped in the script of the Muṣḥaf. ومن يضلل فلن تجد له وليا مرشدا is conjoined to what precedes, and the clause is parallel to the previous one.
(وَتَحْسَبُهُمْ أَيْقاظاً وَهُمْ رُقُودٌ): the wāw is resumptive; تحسبهم is an imperfect verb with a latent fāʿil and the first mafʿūl bihi; أيقاظا is the second mafʿūl bihi. وهم: the wāw is circumstantial, هم is the mubtadaʾ and رقود the khabar, and the clause is in the position of an accusative as a ḥāl.
(وَنُقَلِّبُهُمْ ذاتَ الْيَمِينِ وَذاتَ الشِّمالِ وَكَلْبُهُمْ باسِطٌ ذِراعَيْهِ بِالْوَصِيدِ): ونقلبهم: the wāw is a conjunction, and نقلبهم is a verb with a latent fāʿil and a mafʿūl bihi; ذات اليمين is an adverb attached to نقلبهم; ذات الشمال is conjoined to ذات اليمين. وكلبهم: the wāw is circumstantial, كلبهم is the mubtadaʾ and باسط the khabar; ذراعيه is a mafʿūl bihi; بالوصيد is attached to باسط.
(لَوِ اطَّلَعْتَ عَلَيْهِمْ لَوَلَّيْتَ مِنْهُمْ فِراراً وَلَمُلِئْتَ مِنْهُمْ رُعْباً): لو is conditional; اطلعت is a verb and its fāʿil; عليهم is attached to اطلعت. لوليت: the lām occurs in the answer of لو, and وليت is a verb and its fāʿil; منهم is attached to فرارا; فرارا is a mafʿūl muṭlaq (absolute object) [Translator's note: the source repeats «مطلق»] from the meaning of the preceding verb, because it is synonymous with it; it may also be parsed as a maṣdar in the position of a ḥāl, i.e. "fleeing". ولملئت is conjoined to لوليت; منهم is attached to رعبا; رعبا is a tamyīz (specification). Abū Ḥayyān preferred that it be a second object of ملئت.

* Rhetoric:
In the saying of Allah the Exalted «وتحسبهم أيقاظا وهم رقود» there is a simile (tashbīh) and antithesis (ṭibāq). The antithesis is evident between أيقاظ (awake) and رقود (asleep). As for the simile, it is one of the types of simile in which the particle (of comparison) is a verb of doubt or certainty: you say "I reckoned Zayd, in his boldness, the lion, and ʿAmr, in his generosity, the rain-cloud"; the upshot of that is the likening of Zayd to the lion and ʿAmr to the rain-cloud. In the verse, its upshot is the likening of the People of the Cave, in their state of sleep, to those awake in some of their qualities, because it is said that their eyes were open while they slept.

* Benefits:
Al-Kisāʾī cited His saying «وكلبهم باسط ذراعيه بالوصيد» as evidence that the active participle governs as the verb does even when it has a past meaning. The Basrans rejected this and said: al-Kisāʾī and those who followed him have no proof in (claiming) that the active participle here has a past meaning while it governs ذراعيه in the accusative; rather it is meant as a narration of a past state (ḥikāyat al-ḥāl al-māḍiya), i.e. one conceives the posture that occurred in past time as occurring at the time of speaking, and the meaning is "he stretches out his forelegs", so the imperfect can properly take its place — as is proven by the wāw in وكلبهم being the wāw of circumstance. That is why He, glory be to Him, said ونقلبهم with the imperfect, which indicates the present, and did not say وقلبناهم with the past.

dervis-irab:99-106.t:
* Vocabulary:
(يَمُوجُ): mingles [surging like waves].
(الصُّورِ): the horn that is blown into, and the trumpet.

* I'rab:
(وَتَرَكْنا بَعْضَهُمْ يَوْمَئِذٍ يَمُوجُ فِي بَعْضٍ): (وتركنا) is a verb and its fāʿil (agent); (بعضهم) is the mafʿūl bihi (direct object); (يومئذ) is an adverb (ẓarf) in construct with its like, attached (mutaʿalliq) to (يموج); and the clause (يموج في بعض) is the second mafʿūl bihi. The tanwīn in (إذ) compensates for a clause, as has been given before. Some have made (ترك) transitive to one object, in which case the clause (يموج) is in the position of the accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial).
(وَنُفِخَ فِي الصُّورِ فَجَمَعْناهُمْ جَمْعاً): (ونفخ) is a passive past verb with a latent (mustatir) nāʾib fāʿil (deputy agent); (في الصور) is attached to (نفخ); (فجمعناهم): the fāʾ is conjunctive, and (جمعناهم) is a verb, its fāʿil and its mafʿūl bihi; and (جمعا) is a mafʿūl muṭlaq (absolute object).
(وَعَرَضْنا جَهَنَّمَ يَوْمَئِذٍ لِلْكافِرِينَ عَرْضاً): (وعرضنا) is conjoined to what preceded; (جهنم) is the mafʿūl bihi; (يومئذ) is an adverb in construct with its like, attached to (عرضنا); (للكافرين) is also attached to (عرضنا); and (عرضا) is a mafʿūl muṭlaq.
(الَّذِينَ كانَتْ أَعْيُنُهُمْ فِي غِطاءٍ عَنْ ذِكْرِي وَكانُوا لا يَسْتَطِيعُونَ سَمْعاً): (الذين) is an adjective of (الكافرين) or a badal (substitute) from them; the clause (كانت) is the ṣila (relative clause); (أعينهم) is the noun of (كانت); (في غطاء) is the khabar (predicate) of (كانت); (عن ذكري) is an adjective of (غطاء); (كانوا) is kāna and its noun; and the clause (لا يستطيعون سمعا) is its khabar.
(أَفَحَسِبَ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا أَنْ يَتَّخِذُوا عِبادِي مِنْ دُونِي أَوْلِياءَ): the hamza is for the interrogative of disapproval and rebuke; (الذين) is the fāʿil; the clause (كفروا) is the ṣila; (أن) with what falls within its scope stands in place of the two objects of (حسب); (من دوني) is the second object of (يتخذوا); and (أولياء) is the first mafʿūl bihi.
(إِنَّا أَعْتَدْنا جَهَنَّمَ لِلْكافِرِينَ نُزُلًا): (إنا) is inna and its noun; the clause (أعتدنا) is the khabar; (جهنم) is the mafʿūl bihi; (للكافرين) is a ḥāl, because it was an adjective of (نزلا); and (نزلا) is a ḥāl, i.e. prepared for them like the nuzul (hospitality) prepared for a guest.
(قُلْ هَلْ نُنَبِّئُكُمْ بِالْأَخْسَرِينَ أَعْمالًا): the clause (هل ننبئكم) is the maqūl al-qawl (object of saying); in (بالأخسرين) the bāʾ has entered upon the content of the second and third objects; and (أعمالا) is a tamyīz (specification). The tamyīz was put in the plural — though singular is its norm — to match the thing specified, and to signal that their loss came from many directions, not from one direction.
(الَّذِينَ ضَلَّ سَعْيُهُمْ فِي الْحَياةِ الدُّنْيا وَهُمْ يَحْسَبُونَ أَنَّهُمْ يُحْسِنُونَ صُنْعاً): (الذين) is an adjective of (الأخسرين) or a badal; it is preferable that it be the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ (subject), as though in answer to someone asking "And who are the greatest losers in deeds?" The clause (ضل) is the ṣila; (سعيهم) is the fāʿil; (في الحياة) is attached to (ضل); the wāw is circumstantial; (هم) is the mubtadaʾ and the clause (يحسبون) is the khabar; (أنّ) with what falls within its scope stands in place of the two objects of (يحسبون); the clause (يحسنون) is the khabar of (أنهم); and (صنعا) is the object — it may also be parsed as a tamyīz. The clause (وهم يحسبون) is a ḥāl from the agent of (ضل).
(أُولئِكَ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا بِآياتِ رَبِّهِمْ وَلِقائِهِ فَحَبِطَتْ أَعْمالُهُمْ): (أولئك) is a demonstrative, the mubtadaʾ; (الذين) is its khabar; the clause (كفروا) is the ṣila; (بآيات ربهم) is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to (كفروا); (لقائه) is conjoined to (آيات); (فحبطت) is conjoined to (كفروا); and (أعمالهم) is the fāʿil of (حبطت).
(فَلا نُقِيمُ لَهُمْ يَوْمَ الْقِيامَةِ وَزْناً): (فلا نقيم) is conjoined to what preceded, its fāʿil latent, implied as "we"; (لهم) is attached to (نقيم); (يوم القيامة) is also attached to (نقيم); and (وزنا) is the mafʿūl bihi, i.e. they will have no weight or worth with Us.
(ذلِكَ جَزاؤُهُمْ جَهَنَّمُ بِما كَفَرُوا وَاتَّخَذُوا آياتِي وَرُسُلِي هُزُواً): (ذلك) is the mubtadaʾ; (جزاؤهم) is the khabar; and (جهنم) is a badal or ʿaṭf bayān (explicative apposition) of (جزاؤهم). (ذلك) may also be parsed as the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ, i.e. "the matter is that", with (جزاؤهم جهنم) a mubtadaʾ and khabar, so that each of the two clauses is a clause in its own right. (ذلك) may also be parsed as the mubtadaʾ, (جزاؤهم) a second mubtadaʾ and (جهنم) the khabar of (جزاؤهم), the clause being the khabar of the first mubtadaʾ, (ذلك). These options are equally weighted. (بما كفروا) may be attached to the omitted khabar of (ذلك) in one of its options, or to an omitted ḥāl, i.e. because of their disbelief, (ما) being maṣdariyya (forming a maṣdar). (اتخذوا) is conjoined to (كفروا); (آياتي) is the first mafʿūl bihi; (رسلي) is conjoined to (آياتي); and (هزوا) is the second mafʿūl bihi.

* Rhetoric:
1- Al-istiʿāra al-makniyya (implicit metaphor):
In His saying, Exalted is He, «وَتَرَكْنا بَعْضَهُمْ يَوْمَئِذٍ يَمُوجُ فِي بَعْضٍ» there is a metaphor of the sensible for the sensible, according to our classification of the types of metaphor. The basic sense of mawj is the movement of water, and it was borrowed for the movement of Gog and Magog, because the thing borrowed and the thing it is borrowed for share movement. It is a consequential (tabaʿiyya) implicit metaphor — «أوهم الخلق يموجون» [Translator's note: so in the source; perhaps "or [the pronoun refers to] the created beings surging"].

2- Jinās al-taṣḥīf (paronomasia by dotting):
In His saying, Exalted is He, «وَهُمْ يَحْسَبُونَ أَنَّهُمْ يُحْسِنُونَ صُنْعاً» there is jinās al-taṣḥīf, in which the dots alone distinguish the two words, along the lines of al-Buḥturī's saying:
ولم يكن المغتر بالله إذ سرى ... ليعجز والمعتز بالله طالبه
(The one deluded about Allah (al-mughtarr bi-llāh), when he fled by night, could not escape while al-Muʿtazz bi-llāh was pursuing him.)

Jinās and its divisions:
Jinās is also called tajnīs, mujānasa and tajānus — all words derived from jins (kind). Its technical definition is the resemblance of two words in sound and their difference in meaning. Its benefit is that it inclines the hearer to listen attentively, for the correspondence of words produces an inclination and attentiveness to them; and because when the word mentioned has been taken in one meaning and then comes again intending another meaning, the soul feels a longing for it.
The following are the divisions of jinās, in brief:
1- Compound jinās (al-murakkab): where [one of the elements] is composed of two parts. It is of two kinds:
a- Where its two elements resemble each other in sound but not in writing, as in the saying of al-ʿImād al-Iṣfahānī, who was riding with al-Qāḍī al-Fāḍil in the Sultan's procession when dust rose:
أما الغبار فإنه ... مما أثارته السنابك
والجوّ منه مظلم ... لكن أنار به السنابك
يا دهر لي عبد الرحي ... م فلست أخشى مسّ نابك
(As for the dust, it is what the hooves (al-sanābik) raised; the air is dark with it, but "your splendour" (sanā bik) lit it up. O Time, I have ʿAbd al-Raḥīm, so I do not fear the touch of your fang (massa nābik).)
It is told that when al-Muʿtamid ibn ʿAbbād was in the prison of Aghmāt and his state had long continued so, his slave-girl said to him: "We have been humbled here (la-qad hunnā hunā)." So he composed on her words:
قالت لقد هنّا هنا ... مولاي أين جاهنا
قلت لها: إلهنا ... صيرنا إلى هنا
(She said: "We have been humbled here, my master — where is our standing?" I said to her: "Our God has brought us to here.")
b- Where its two elements resemble each other in sound and in writing. Among its examples:
عضنا الدهر بنابه ... ليت ما حل بنابه
(Time has bitten us with its fang (bi-nābih); would that what has befallen us befell it (binā bih).)
And of Abū al-Fatḥ al-Bustī:
إذا لم يكن ملك ذا هبه ... فدعه فدولته ذاهبه
(If a king is not one of gifts (dhā hibah), leave him, for his reign is passing (dhāhibah).)
2- Patched jinās (al-mulaffaq):
Its definition is that each of the two elements is composed of two words, as in someone's saying:
رعى الله دهرا بكم قد مضى ... بلغت الأماني به في أمان
وأيام أنس تولت لنا ... بأحلام عان بأحلى معان
(May Allah protect a time with you that has passed, in which I attained my wishes in safety, and days of intimacy that turned away from us, with the dreams of a captive (bi-aḥlāmi ʿānin), with the sweetest meanings (bi-aḥlā maʿānin).)
3- Semantic jinās (al-maʿnawī):
It is mere laborious artifice, though it may come out well. It is where the speaker conceals the two elements of the jinās and mentions words synonymous with one of them, so that what is expressed points to what is concealed. The finest we have heard of it is the saying of Abū Bakr ibn ʿAbdūn, who had taken a morning draught of wine and left some of it until night, and it turned into vinegar:
ألا في سبيل الله كأس مدامة ... أتتنا بطعم عهده غير ثابت
حكت بنت بسطام بن قيس صبيحة ... وأضحت كجسم الشنفري بعد ثابت
(Alas, in the cause of Allah, a cup of wine that came to us with a taste whose covenant was not constant: in the morning it resembled the daughter of Bisṭām ibn Qays, and it became like the body of al-Shanfarā after Thābit.)
So two concealed jināses are sound in it, in the first and second halves of the verse, because the daughter of Bisṭām ibn Qays was named al-Ṣahbāʾ, and al-Shanfarā's [uncle's] name was Thābit [Translator's note: the source says «والشنفري اسمه ثابت», "al-Shanfarā's name was Thābit"; Thābit ibn Jābir is the name of Taʾabbaṭa Sharran, his maternal uncle, as the following lines show], and he described his own body as khall (emaciated) in his elegy on his maternal uncle Taʾabbaṭa Sharran, where he said:
فاسقنيها يا سواد بن عمرو ... إن جسمي بعد خالي لخل
(So give it to me to drink, O Sawād ibn ʿAmr; my body, after my uncle, is indeed wasted (khall).)
Al-khall is the emaciated one. The concealed jinās [in the first half] is the daughter of Bisṭām, who is al-Ṣahbāʾ; and the one in the second half is the body of al-Shanfarā after Thābit, which is khall. The meaning is that the wine resembled its namesake, the daughter of Bisṭām, in the morning, and resembled the body of al-Shanfarā in the evening, i.e. it was ṣahbāʾ (red wine) and became khall (vinegar). Thus from the allusive wording two concealed jināses appeared: al-ṣahbāʾ, which is wine, and al-Ṣahbāʾ, the daughter of Bisṭām; and khall, the emaciated, and khall, that with which bread is eaten (vinegar).
4- Jinās al-muṭarraf:
Where one of its two elements exceeds the other by a letter at its beginning, as in the saying of ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Muʿtazz:
زارني والدجى أحمّ الحواشي ... والثريا في الغرب كالعقود
وكأن الهلال طوق عروس ... بات يجلى على غلائل سود
ليلة الوصل ساعدينا بطول ... طول الله فيك غيظ الحسود
(He visited me when the darkness was black at its edges and the Pleiades in the west were like necklaces, and the crescent like a bride's collar displayed over black garments (sūd). O night of union, help us with length — may Allah lengthen in you the rage of the envious (al-ḥasūd).)
His word al-ḥasūd exceeds sūd by a letter [Translator's note: so in the source; it exceeds it by two letters, al-ḥa-].
5- Distorted jinās (al-muḥarraf):
Where its two elements agree in the number and order of letters and differ only in the vowelling of the letters; it is so called because the form of one deviates from the form of the other. Abū al-ʿAlāʾ said:
والحسن يظهر في شيئين رونقه ... بيت من الشعر أو بيت من الشعر
(Beauty shows its splendour in two things: a verse of poetry (al-shiʿr) or a tent of hair (al-shaʿar).)
6- Verbal jinās (al-lafẓī):
Where its two elements are alike in sound and one of them differs from the other in writing. Abū Tammām said:
يمدون من أيد عواص عواصم ... تصول بأسياف قواض قواضب
(They stretch out hands that are rebellious and protecting, assailing with swords that are decisive and cutting.)
[Translator's note: the source uses this same verse again below as the example of jinās al-mudhayyal, which it fits.]
And al-Buḥturī said:
من كل ساجي الطرف أغيد أجيد ... ومهفهف الكشحين أحوى أحور
(Every one of languid glance, supple and long-necked, slender-waisted, dark-lipped and dark-eyed.)
7- Absolute jinās (al-muṭlaq):
Where its two elements differ in vowels and letters, so that it resembles a derived word whose meaning goes back to a single root, though it is not so. It is beautiful and unforced. Among it is the saying of Abū Firās:
سكرت من لحظه لا من مدامته ... ومال بالنوم عن عيني تمايله
فما السلاف دهتني بل سوالفه ... ولا الشمول ازدهتني بل شمايله
ألوى بعزمي أصداغا لوين له ... وغال صبري بما تحوي غلايله
(I became drunk from his glance, not his wine; his swaying drove sleep from my eyes. It was not the wine (al-sulāf) that struck me but his side-locks (sawālifuh), nor the chilled wine (al-shamūl) that bewitched me but his qualities (shamāyiluh). Temple-locks that curled for him twisted away my resolve, and what his garments (ghalāyiluh) contain destroyed (ghāla) my patience.)
Abū Firās was fond of this kind of jinās, and he said:
عذيري من طوالع في عذاري ... ومن برد الشباب المستعار
وثوب كنت ألبسه أنيق ... أجرّر ذيله بين الجواري
وما زادت على العشرين سني ... فما عذر المشيب إلى عذاري
(Who will excuse me for [white hairs] rising on my cheeks (ʿidhārī), and for the borrowed cloak of youth, an elegant garment I used to wear, trailing its hem among the maidens? My age has not exceeded twenty, so what excuse (ʿudhr) has grey hair for coming to my cheeks?)
Among it is the Prophetic hadith: «الظلم ظلمات يوم القيامة» (Injustice will be darknesses on the Day of Resurrection).
8- Tailed jinās (al-mudhayyal):
Where one of its two elements exceeds the other by one or more letters at its end, so that it is like a tail attached to a garment. Among it is the saying of Abū Tammām:
يمدون من أيد عواص عواصم ... تصول بأسياف قواض قواضب
And of Ḥassān ibn Thābit:
وكنا متى يغز النبي قبيلة ... نصل جانبيها بالقنا والقنابل
(Whenever the Prophet raided a tribe, we would assail its two flanks with spears (al-qanā) and troops of horse (al-qanābil).)
9- Adjoined jinās (al-lāḥiq):
Where one letter in one of its two elements is replaced by another not of the same point of articulation, whether the replacement is at the beginning, middle or end. Al-Buḥturī said:
عجب الناس لاغترابي وفي الأطراف تلقى منازل الأشراف
وقعودي عن التقلب والأرض لمثلي رحيبة الأكناف
ليس عن ثروة بلغت مداها ... غير أني امرؤ كفاني كفافي
(People wondered at my living abroad — yet in the outlying lands (al-aṭrāf) the abodes of the nobles (al-ashrāf) are found — and at my refraining from roaming, though the earth is wide of sides (al-aknāf) for one like me. It is not from wealth that has reached its limit, but I am a man whose sufficiency suffices me (kafānī kafāfī).)
And of Abū Firās al-Ḥamdānī:
تعس الحريص وقلّ ما يأتي به ... عوضا عن الإلحاح والإلحاف
إن الغني هو الغني بنفسه ... ولو انه عاري المناكب حافي
ما كلّ ما فوق البسيطة كافيا ... فإذا قنعت فكل شيء كافي
(Wretched is the greedy man, and little is what he gains in return for importuning (al-ilḥāḥ) and pestering (al-ilḥāf). The rich man is the one rich in himself, even if he be bare-shouldered and barefoot (ḥāfī). Not all that is on the earth suffices; but when you are content, everything suffices (kāfī).)
10- Jinās al-muṣaḥḥaf (by dotting):
It has already been given in the discussion of the verse. Abū Firās has masterpieces in it; listen to this piece:
ما كنت مذ كنت إلا طوع خلاني ... ليست مؤاخذة الاخوان من شاني
يجني الخليل فأستحلي جنايته ... حتى أدل على عفوي واحساني
إذا خليلي لم تكثر إساءته ... فأين موقع إحساني وغفراني
يجني عليّ وأحنو صافحا أبدا ... لا شيء أحسن من حان على جاني
(Ever since I have been, I have only been obedient to my friends; taking brothers to task is not my way (shānī). The friend wrongs me and I find his wrong sweet, so that I may show my pardon and kindness. If my friend's offences are not many, where then is the place for my kindness and forgiveness? He wrongs me and I always lean towards him forgiving; nothing is finer than one tender (ḥānin) towards a wrongdoer (jānī).)
11- Complete jinās (al-tāmm):
Where the two words agree in the kinds of letters, their number, their vowelling and their order. It is of two kinds:
a- Homogeneous complete jinās (al-mutamāthil): where the two words are of one type, like two nouns, two verbs or two particles, as in His saying, Exalted is He: «وَيَوْمَ تَقُومُ السَّاعَةُ يُقْسِمُ الْمُجْرِمُونَ ما لَبِثُوا غَيْرَ ساعَةٍ».
And the saying of Abū Tammām:
السيف أصدق أنباء من الكتب ... في حدّه الحد بين الجد واللعب
(The sword is truer in its tidings than books; in its edge (ḥadd) is the boundary (ḥadd) between earnest and play.)
He made a jinās between the edge of the sword and the boundary separating two things, both being nouns. The poets showed great ingenuity in it, especially in the ages of decline, as in the saying of al-Malik al-Ṣāliḥ Dāwūd:
عيون من السحر المبين تبين ... لها عند تحريك الجفون سكون
تصول ببيض وهي سود فرندها ... ذبول فتور والجفون جفون
إذا أبصرت قلبا خليا من الهوى ... تقول له: كن مغرما فيكون
(Eyes that show plain magic, which have stillness when the lids move; they assail with white blades though they are black, their damascening is languid drooping, and the eyelids (al-jufūn) are scabbards (jufūn). When they see a heart free of love, they say to it: "Be enamoured!" — and it is.)
b- If they are of two types, like a noun and a verb, a noun and a particle, or a verb and a particle, it is called comprehensive jinās (al-mustawfā), as in the saying of Abū al-Faḍl al-Mīkālī:
يا من يضيع عمره في اللهو أمسك ... واعلم بأنك ذاهب كذهاب أمسك
(O you who waste your life in amusement, hold back (amsik), and know that you are passing away as your yesterday (amsuk) passed.)
He made a jinās between amsik, an imperative verb, and amsuk, the day before your day.

Abū Tammām and tajnīs:
Abū Tammām went to excess in using tajnīs; the following is a selection of it.
He said:
فأصبحت غرر الأيام مشرقة ... بالنصر تضحك عن أيامك الغرر
(The blazes (ghurar) of the days became radiant with victory, smiling at your noblest (ghurar) days.)
The first ghurar is a metaphor from the blazes on a face, and the second ghurar is taken from ghurrat al-shayʾ, its noblest part. And he said in his ode on the conquest of Amorium:
عداك حر الثغور المستضامة عن ... برد الثغور وعن سلسالها الخصب
(The heat of the wronged frontier-posts (al-thughūr) has kept you from the coolness of front teeth (al-thughūr) and their abundant sweet water.)
Al-thughūr is the plural of thaghr, which is a single front tooth, and it is also the town on the border of the enemy. Then he said in it:
كم أحرزت قضب الهندي مصلتة ... تهتز من قضب تهتز في كثب
بيض إذا انتفيت من حجبها رجعت ... أحق بالبيض أبدانا من الحجب
(How many swaying stems (quḍub) on sand-hills have the drawn Indian blades (quḍub) won! White ones (bīḍ) which, when unsheathed from their coverings, returned with bodies more deserving of the white ones (bīḍ) than the veils.)
Al-quḍub are swords, and al-quḍub are statures by way of metaphor; likewise al-bīḍ are swords and al-bīḍ are women. This is among the rare feats of Abū Tammām that no one can match.
Abū Tammām used tajnīs abundantly in his poetry; some of it he made strikingly novel and fine, and some came out heavy and jarring, as in his saying:
قرّت بقرّان عين الدين واشتترت ... بالأشترين عيون الشرك فاصطلما
(The eye of the religion was gladdened (qarrat) at Qarrān, and the eyes of polytheism were slit (ishtatarat) at al-Ashtarān, and it was cut off at the root.)
He made a jinās between qarrat, from qarrat al-ʿayn, i.e. the eye was cooled with joy, and Qarrān, a place name; and ishtatarat, i.e. was split, and al-Ashtarān, also a place name; and iṣṭulima means was cut off from its root.
Uglier than that is his saying:
فاسلم سلمت من الآفات ما سلمت ... سلام سلمى ومهما أورق السلم
(Be safe — may you be safe from afflictions as long as the rocks (silām) of Salmā remain safe, and as long as the salam tree puts forth leaves.)

Al-Buḥturī's jinās:
As for al-Buḥturī, he did not sink to the depths to which Abū Tammām sank, and he produced tajnīs only when it was beautiful, natural and unforced, as in his saying:
إذا العين راحت وهي عين على الهوى ... فليس بسرّ ما تسر الأضالع
(When the eye (al-ʿayn) has become a spy (ʿayn) upon love, what the ribs conceal is no secret.)
Al-ʿayn is the spy, and al-ʿayn [the eye] is well known.
And how beautiful is the saying of Abū al-ʿAlāʾ al-Maʿarrī:
لم يبق غيرك إنسانا يلاذ به ... فلا برحت لعين الدهر إنسانا
(No human (insān) remains but you in whom refuge is sought; so may you never cease to be the pupil (insān) of the eye of Time.)
Abū Tammām has a tajnīs repeated within a single verse; he said:
ليالينا بالرقمتين وأهلنا ... سقى العهد منك العهد والعهد والعهد
(Our nights at al-Raqmatān, and our people — may the ʿahd water the ʿahd of you, and the ʿahd, and the ʿahd.)
The first ʿahd, the one watered, is the time; the second ʿahd is loyalty, from their expression "So-and-so has no ʿahd"; the third ʿahd is a charge, from their expression "So-and-so made a charge (ʿahida) to So-and-so" and "I charged him (ʿahidtu ilayhi)", i.e. he charged me with his charge; and the fourth ʿahd is rain, plural ʿihād. Ibn Rashīq said: "Some people found this tajnīs heavy, and they were right to."

* Benefits:
1- The verbs of transformation (afʿāl al-taṣyīr) are those that indicate change and transition from one state to another. They put two objects in the accusative, originally a mubtadaʾ and a khabar — so the grammarians said. Some objected to this, saying that the two words governed by these verbs differ both in concept and in external reality, so it cannot be claimed that they are a mubtadaʾ and khabar, since that requires their being one in external reality. This becomes clear to you when you say "I made the poor man rich and the non-existent existent": obviously the predication of one of them of the other is impossible. The reply is that something like "the poor man is rich" is sound, i.e. the one who was poor in the past has acquired wealth; and likewise "the non-existent is existent", since the descriptive title is not required to exist always — its existence at some time suffices. Al-Shihābī al-Qāsimī said: It is possible to answer the objection thus: if what is meant is that the two words governed by the verbs of transformation are never other than differing in concept and in external reality, that is refuted by His saying, Exalted is He, «وَتَرَكْنا بَعْضَهُمْ يَوْمَئِذٍ يَمُوجُ فِي بَعْضٍ», for (ترك) here is one of the verbs of transformation, yet one of its two objects is predicable of the other and one with it in external reality, since "surging" is predicable of some of them and one with them in external reality. And if what is meant is that its two governed words may sometimes be so, that is granted and does no harm, because the verbs of this chapter need not enter upon a mubtadaʾ and khabar; they may enter upon other than these.
2- Know that the tamyīz may be singular and may be plural. When it occurs after a number, such as twenty, thirty and the like, the tamyīz can only be singular, as in your saying:
"I have twenty garments and thirty turbans", because the number has indicated the quantity and we have no remaining need except to clarify the kind of that amount, and that is achieved with the singular, which is lighter. But when it explains something other than a number, as in "This one is more spirited than you in slave" and "better than you in deed", both singular and plural are permissible, since he may have one slave or several slaves. When you say "He is more spirited than you in slaves" or "better than you in deeds", by the plural form you indicate two meanings: the kind, and that they are many. Allah the Exalted said:
«قُلْ هَلْ نُنَبِّئُكُمْ بِالْأَخْسَرِينَ أَعْمالًا» — from this is understood the kind, and that [their loss] came from many directions, not from one direction; whereas if you use the singular, only the kind is understood.

dervis-irab:19-20.t:
* Vocabulary:
(بِوَرِقِكُمْ): al-wariq, with fatḥa on the wāw and kasra on the rāʾ, is silver, whether minted or not. From it is the ḥadīth: "ʿArfaja's nose was struck off on the day of al-Kulāb, so he took a nose of silver (wariq), but it putrefied, so the Messenger of Allah ﷺ ordered him to take a nose of gold." Al-Kulāb, with ḍamma, is the name of a watering place where the battle took place, as in al-Ṣiḥāḥ. (The poet) said:
أعطيتني ورقا لم تعطني ورقا ... قل لي بلا ورق ما ينفع الورق؟
(You gave me leaves (waraq) — you did not give me silver (wariq); tell me, without silver, what use are leaves?)
(أَزْكى): purer, better. In al-Qāmūs: zakā yazkū zakāʾan and zukuwwan, said of crops: they grew [Translator's note: printed «فما» for «نما»]; and of land: it was good; and al-zakī is what is growing, good and wholesome.

* I'rab:
(وَكَذلِكَ بَعَثْناهُمْ لِيَتَسائَلُوا بَيْنَهُمْ): the kāf is a naʿt (adjective) of an omitted maṣdar, i.e. just as We put them to sleep this long sleep, so We raised them. بعثناهم is a verb, its fāʿil (agent) and its mafʿūl bihi (direct object). ليتساءلوا: the lām is causal (for taʿlīl), and يتساءلوا is an imperfect verb in the accusative by an implied أن after the lām of causation; the adverb (بينهم) is attached to (mutaʿalliq) an omitted ḥāl (circumstantial).
(قالَ قائِلٌ مِنْهُمْ كَمْ لَبِثْتُمْ قالُوا لَبِثْنا يَوْماً أَوْ بَعْضَ يَوْمٍ): قال قائل is a verb and its fāʿil; كم is an interrogative noun in the position of an accusative as an adverb; its accusative specifier (tamyīz) is omitted, its implied form being "how many days", as is proven by the answer to it. منهم is a naʿt of قائل. قالوا is a verb and its fāʿil; the clause لبثنا is the maqūl al-qawl (object of the saying); يوما is an adverb attached to لبثنا; أو is a conjunction; بعض يوم is conjoined to يوما. أو here expresses doubt on their part.
(قالُوا رَبُّكُمْ أَعْلَمُ بِما لَبِثْتُمْ): قالوا is a verb and its fāʿil; ربكم is the mubtadaʾ (subject) and أعلم its khabar (predicate); بما is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to أعلم; لبثتم is the ṣila (relative clause) of ما. How beautiful is their entrusting the knowledge of the length of their stay to Allah, and the good manners this entrusting contains! For they became doubtful about their situation after they came back to themselves [Translator's note: printed «راعوا إلى أنفسهم»] and looked at the length of their hair and nails.
(فَابْعَثُوا أَحَدَكُمْ بِوَرِقِكُمْ هذِهِ إِلَى الْمَدِينَةِ فَلْيَنْظُرْ أَيُّها أَزْكى طَعاماً): the fāʾ coordinates with something omitted, i.e. so leave off the questioning and take up what is more important and more useful for us in this situation of ours [Translator's note: printed «موفقنا» for «موقفنا»] — so send. أحدكم is the mafʿūl bihi; بورقكم is attached to ابعثوا, or to an omitted ḥāl from أحدكم, the bāʾ being for accompaniment (mulābasa), i.e. having it with him and accompanied by it; هذه is a naʿt of ورقكم; إلى المدينة is attached to ابعثوا. فلينظر: the fāʾ is a conjunction, the lām is the lām of command, and ينظر is an imperfect verb in the jussive (majzūm) by the lām of command. أيها may be interrogative or relative — this has preceded in His saying «أيهم أحسن عملا», so refresh your memory of it. It is a mubtadaʾ whose khabar is أزكى; طعاما is a tamyīz (specification) transferred from the muḍāf ilayhi, i.e. which of the city's foods is purest, most lawful, cheapest and best.
(فَلْيَأْتِكُمْ بِرِزْقٍ مِنْهُ وَلْيَتَلَطَّفْ وَلا يُشْعِرَنَّ بِكُمْ أَحَداً): the fāʾ is a conjunction, the lām is the lām of command, and يأت is jussive by the lām of command; the fāʿil is latent (mustatir), its implied form being "huwa"; the kāf is the mafʿūl bihi; برزق is attached to يأتكم; منه is a naʿt of رزق; وليتلطف is conjoined to فليأتكم. ولا: the wāw is a conjunction and لا is prohibitive; يشعرن is an imperfect verb, indeclinable (mabnī) on fatḥa because it is joined to the heavy nūn of emphasis, and it is in the position of a jussive by the prohibitive لا; the fāʿil is latent, its implied form being "huwa"; بكم is attached to يشعرن; أحدا is the mafʿūl bihi.
(إِنَّهُمْ إِنْ يَظْهَرُوا عَلَيْكُمْ يَرْجُمُوكُمْ أَوْ يُعِيدُوكُمْ فِي مِلَّتِهِمْ): inna and its noun; إن is conditional; يظهروا is the protasis (fiʿl al-sharṭ) and the wāw is the fāʿil; عليكم is attached to يظهروا; يرجموكم is the apodosis (jawāb al-sharṭ); أو يعيدوكم is conjoined to يرجموكم; في ملتهم is attached to يعيدوكم, i.e. they will return you to their creed which you followed before Allah guided you; or "return" here means "becoming", on the assumption that they had not been of their creed. The choice of the word «في» over the word «إلى» indicates settledness (in it).
(وَلَنْ تُفْلِحُوا إِذاً أَبَداً): the wāw is a conjunction; لن is a particle of negation, accusative and futurity; تفلحوا is an imperfect verb in the accusative by لن, and the wāw is the fāʿil; إذن is a particle of answer and requital, inoperative (muhmal); أبدا is an adverb attached to تفلحوا.

dervis-irab:107-110.t:
* Vocabulary:
(الْفِرْدَوْسِ): a garden of vines in particular; it has also been said: rather one most of which is vines. It has also been said: every enclosed place is a firdaws, plural farādīs. Al-Mubarrad said:
"Al-firdaws, according to what I have heard from the Arabs, is dense, intertwined trees, mostly grapevines." Al-Zajjāj reported that it means valleys that grow various kinds of plants. There is disagreement about it: some say it is Arabic, some foreign; some say it is Greek (Rūmī), some Persian, some Syriac. In al-Qāmūs and al-Tāj: "al-firdaws, with kasra: valleys that grow various kinds of plants; and a garden that gathers everything found in gardens, in which there are vines — it may be treated as feminine — Arabic, or Greek borrowed, or Syriac; and a meadow below al-Yamāma belonging to the Banū Yarbūʿ; and a water belonging to the Banū Tamīm near Kufa; and the fortress of Firdaws in Qazvin" — until he says: "and al-fardasa is wideness, and ṣadr mufardas is a wide chest; or [Translator's note: so in the source, «أو ومنه»] from it comes al-firdaws." Its commentator said: his saying "or from it comes al-firdaws" means its derivation, as Ibn al-Qaṭṭāʿ reported; and this supports its being Arabic. It is also indicated by the saying of Ḥassān:
وان ثواب الله كل موحد ... جنان من الفردوس فيها يخلد
(The reward of Allah for every monotheist is gardens of Paradise (al-firdaws), in which he will dwell for ever.)
(حِوَلًا): al-ḥiwal is changing place. One says ḥāla min makānihi ḥiwalan, like your saying "her love returned to me ʿiwadan", meaning there is nothing beyond it. Al-ḥiwal, with kasra on the ḥāʾ and fatḥa on the wāw, is a maṣdar (verbal noun) meaning changing; one says ḥāla ʿan makānihi ḥiwalan, so it is a maṣdar like al-ʿiwaj and al-ṣighar.
(المداد): the name of the ink with which an inkwell is replenished, and of the oil with which a lamp is replenished; and one says: manure is the replenishment (midād) of the earth.

* I'rab:
(إِنَّ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَعَمِلُوا الصَّالِحاتِ كانَتْ لَهُمْ جَنَّاتُ الْفِرْدَوْسِ نُزُلًا): (إنّ) and its noun; the clause (آمنوا) is the ṣila (relative clause); the clause (وعملوا الصالحات) is conjoined to the ṣila; the clause (كانت) is the khabar (predicate) of (إنّ); (لهم) is a ḥāl (circumstantial) from (نزلا), because it was an adjective and was fronted before it; (جنات الفردوس) is the noun of (كانت); and (نزلا) is its khabar. (لهم) may also be the khabar and (نزلا) a ḥāl.
(خالِدِينَ فِيها لا يَبْغُونَ عَنْها حِوَلًا): (خالدين) is a ḥāl from the pronoun in (لهم); (فيها) is attached (mutaʿalliq) to (خالدين); the clause (لا يبغون) is circumstantial; (عنها) is attached to (حولا); and (حولا) is the object of (يبغون).
(قُلْ لَوْ كانَ الْبَحْرُ مِداداً لِكَلِماتِ رَبِّي لَنَفِدَ الْبَحْرُ قَبْلَ أَنْ تَنْفَدَ كَلِماتُ رَبِّي وَلَوْ جِئْنا بِمِثْلِهِ مَدَداً): (لو) is conditional; (كان البحر) is kāna and its noun; (مدادا) is its khabar; (لكلمات) is an adjective of (مداد); the lām occurs in the apodosis of (لو); the clause (نفد البحر) is the apodosis (jawāb) of a non-jussive condition, with no grammatical position. «وقيل ظرف متعلق بنفد» [Translator's note: so in the source, "and it was said: an adverb attached to (نفد)"; the word (قبل) appears to have dropped out — i.e. "(قبل) is an adverb attached to (نفد)"]. (أن تنفد) is the maṣdar, in construct with (قبل); and (كلمات ربي) is the fāʿil (agent). The wāw conjoins what follows it to an implied clause indicated by what precedes it, i.e. "the sea would be exhausted before His words were exhausted if He did not bring the like of it as a supplement" [Translator's note: so in the source]. (لو) is conditional; (جئنا) is the protasis (fiʿl al-sharṭ); and the apodosis of (لو) is omitted, implied as "it would be exhausted and they [His words] would not be finished" [Translator's note: the source reads «ولم تفرع», presumably a misprint for «ولم تفرغ», "and would not be finished"]. (بمثله) is attached to (جئنا); and (مددا) is a tamyīz (specification), as in your saying "I have the like of him as a man". Further discussion of the apodosis of (لو) will come under Benefits.
(قُلْ إِنَّما أَنَا بَشَرٌ مِثْلُكُمْ): (إنما) is the restraining (kāffa) and restrained (makfūfa) particle; (أنا) is the mubtadaʾ (subject); (بشر) is the khabar; and (مثلكم) is an adjective.
(يُوحى إِلَيَّ أَنَّما إِلهُكُمْ إِلهٌ واحِدٌ): the clause (يوحى) is an adjective of (بشر); (إليّ) is attached to (يوحى); (أنما) is the restraining and restrained particle, but it has not lost its maṣdar-forming function, so it and what follows it are in the position of the nominative as the nāʾib fāʿil (deputy agent); (إلهكم) is the mubtadaʾ, (إله) the khabar, and (واحد) an adjective.
(فَمَنْ كانَ يَرْجُوا لِقاءَ رَبِّهِ فَلْيَعْمَلْ عَمَلًا صالِحاً وَلا يُشْرِكْ بِعِبادَةِ رَبِّهِ أَحَداً): the fāʾ is resumptive; (من) is a jussive conditional noun in the position of the nominative as the mubtadaʾ; (كان) is a defective past verb whose noun refers to (من); the clause (يرجو) is its khabar; and (لقاء ربه) is the mafʿūl bihi (direct object). (فليعمل): the fāʾ links the apodosis, the lām is the lām of command, and (يعمل) is an imperfect verb, jussive (majzūm) by the lām of command; (عملا) is a mafʿūl muṭlaq (absolute object) or a mafʿūl bihi, and (صالحا) is an adjective. (ولا يشرك): (لا) is prohibitive, and (يشرك) is an imperfect verb, jussive by the prohibitive (لا); (بعبادة ربه) is attached to (يشرك); and (أحدا) is the object of (يشرك).

* Benefits:
The apodosis of law:
More discussions of (لو) will come in this book, for it is one of the particles about which much is said, so we have distributed it over the verses. We now speak about the apodosis of (لو), and say: its apodosis is either past in meaning, as in "What an excellent servant Ṣuhayb is! Had he not feared Allah, he would not have disobeyed Him", or past in form. The latter is either affirmative — in which case its being joined with the lām, as in «لو نشاء لجعلناه حطاما», is more frequent than its omission, as in «لو نشاء جعلناه أجاجا». This lām is called the lām of deferral (al-taswīf), because it indicates the delay of the apodosis after the condition and its coming later, just as dropping it indicates haste, i.e. the apodosis occurs right after the condition without delay. That is why it entered in «لو نشاء لجعلناه حطاما» and was dropped in the likes of «لو نشاء جعلناه أجاجا», i.e. at once, in the rain-clouds, without delay. The benefit in delaying the making of it into chaff and bringing forward the making of it bitter is the intensification of the punishment, i.e. when the crop has stood firm on its stalks and hopes have grown strong in it, We make it chaff. Or it is because the crop, its growth, and its drying out after freshness until it becomes chaff, are things one might imagine to be the doing of the farmers — which is why Allah the Exalted said: «أَأَنْتُمْ تَزْرَعُونَهُ أَمْ نَحْنُ الزَّارِعُونَ» — or [imagine] that it comes from watering, and its drying out from lack of watering, the heat of the sun or the passing of whirlwinds. So He, Glorified is He, informed that He is the true doer of that, and that He is able to make it chaff in its state of growth if He willed; whereas sending down water from the sky is something no one imagines anyone other than Allah the Exalted has power over. This is among the choicest of subtle points, so know it and ponder it.
Or the apodosis of (لو) is negated with (ما): usually it is free of the lām, and less often joined with it. The first is like «ولو شاء ربك ما فعلوه», and the second like the poet's saying:
ولو نعطى الخيار لما افترقنا ... ولكن لا خيار مع الليالي
(Had we been given the choice, we would not have parted; but there is no choice with the nights.)
He put the lām on the negating (ما), and the lām does not enter on any negator other than it. It has also been said that (لو) may be answered by a nominal clause joined with the lām, as in «ولو انهم آمنوا واتقوا لمثوبة من عند الله خير», the lām in (لمثوبة) being the apodosis of (لو), since between the past verb and the noun there is a resemblance in this respect. Al-Zamakhsharī said: its apodosis was made a nominal clause only to indicate the continuity of the content of the recompense. Abū Ḥayyān rejected this in al-Baḥr, saying: the lām in (لمثوبة) is the lām of the mubtadaʾ, not the one that occurs in the apodosis of (لو) — and this is one of al-Zamakhsharī's two possibilities; it was given before in al-Baqara — i.e. so the clause is resumptive, or the response to an implied oath. Ibn Hishām said in al-Mughnī: "It is better that the lām of (لمثوبة) be the lām of the response to an implied oath, as shown by the clause's being nominal; as for the view that it is the lām of the apodosis of (لو) and that the nominal clause was borrowed in place of the verbal one, it is forced." And I say: the forcedness in supplying an oath is greater than in making the apodosis a nominal clause.

dervis-irab:21-26.t:
* Vocabulary:
(أَعْثَرْنا عَلَيْهِمْ): We made their people and the believers come upon them. In al-Asās: "ʿathara ʿalā kadhā: he came upon it; aʿtharahu ʿalā kadhā: he made him come upon it; aʿtharahu ʿalā aṣḥābihi: he led him to them. Of one who has got himself into trouble one says: 'he fell into an ʿāthūr'; and so-and-so seeks pitfalls (ʿawāthīr) for his companion — its origin is a pit dug for the lion and others, which stumbles on it and falls into it."
(رَجْماً بِالْغَيْبِ): throwing out hidden information and bringing it forth. In al-Miṣbāḥ: al-rajam, with two fatḥas, is stones; rajamtuhu rajman, of the pattern qatala, I struck him with rajam, i.e. small stones; and rajamtuhu bi-al-qawl: I pelted him with obscenity [Translator's note: printed «رمبته» for «رميته»]. Allah the Exalted said: «رجما بالغيب», i.e. conjecture without evidence or proof — like the saying of Zuhayr ibn Abī Sulmā describing war:
وما الحرب إلا ما علمتم وذقتم ... وما هو عنها بالحديث المرجم
(War is nothing but what you have known and tasted; and what is said of it is no conjectural tale.)
— i.e. conjectured. More discussion of this expression will come in the Rhetoric section.
(تُمارِ): to dispute. In al-Qāmūs: "mārā mirāʾan and mumārātan: he disputed, contended and persisted in contention; tamārayā: they disputed with each other; imtarā fī al-shayʾ: he doubted it; al-mirya, with kasra on the mīm, and al-murya, with ḍamma: disputation — one says: there is no mirya in that, i.e. no dispute or doubt."

* I'rab:
(وَكَذلِكَ أَعْثَرْنا عَلَيْهِمْ لِيَعْلَمُوا أَنَّ وَعْدَ اللَّهِ حَقٌّ وَأَنَّ السَّاعَةَ لا رَيْبَ فِيها): the kāf is a naʿt (adjective) of an omitted maṣdar, i.e. and just as We put them to sleep and raised them, We made their people and the believers come upon them. أعثرنا is a verb and its fāʿil (agent); the mafʿūl bihi (direct object) is omitted, as we supplied it in the Vocabulary section; عليهم is attached to (mutaʿalliq) أعثرنا. ليعلموا: the lām is causal (for taʿlīl) and يعلموا is an imperfect verb in the accusative by an implied أن after the lām of causation; أن with what is in its domain stands in place of the two objects of يعلموا; أن and its noun, and حق is its khabar (predicate). وأن الساعة is conjoined; anna and its noun; لا is the lā of generic negation, ريب is its noun and فيها its khabar; the clause of لا with its noun and khabar is in the position of a nominative as the khabar of أن. What is meant by the promise of Allah is the resurrection, because whoever was able to put them to sleep this long sleep and raise them after it is able to bring them to life after death.
(إِذْ يَتَنازَعُونَ بَيْنَهُمْ أَمْرَهُمْ): the adverb is attached to أعثرنا, i.e. We made their people come upon them when they were contending and disagreeing about the reality of the resurrection: some of them said that the spirits are resurrected without the bodies, and some said that the bodies are resurrected together with the spirits. The clause يتنازعون is in the position of a genitive as the muḍāf ilayhi of the adverb; بينهم is an adverb of place attached to يتنازعون; أمرهم is accusative by removal of the preposition (manṣūb bi-nazʿ al-khāfiḍ), i.e. "about their affair". It is also said that tanāzaʿū takes an object when it means "pulling at one another", in which case there is a metaphor in the speech.
(فَقالُوا ابْنُوا عَلَيْهِمْ بُنْياناً): the fāʾ is a conjunction; قالوا is a verb and its fāʿil; the clause ابنوا is the maqūl al-qawl (object of the saying); it is an imperative verb and its fāʿil; عليهم is attached to ابنوا; بنيانا is the mafʿūl bihi. I.e. they said that when Allah took the Companions of the Cave in death. Most reports hold that they died a real death when Tamlīkhā, the bearer of the silver coins, had told their story, and those who had been assailed by doubt about the resurrection of bodies returned to certainty. I.e. build a building over them, out of jealous care for their resting place and to preserve it. The clause ابنوا عليهم بنيانا is the object of their saying.
(رَبُّهُمْ أَعْلَمُ بِهِمْ): the clause is either the completion of what they said — they said it entrusting the knowledge to Allah, glory be to Him — or, it is said, it is the words of Allah, glory be to Him, rejecting the saying of those who contended about them, i.e. leave the contention you are engaged in, for I know them better than you. The speech is a mubtadaʾ (subject) and khabar; بهم is attached to أعلم.
(قالَ الَّذِينَ غَلَبُوا عَلى أَمْرِهِمْ لَنَتَّخِذَنَّ عَلَيْهِمْ مَسْجِداً): قال الذين is a verb and its fāʿil; the clause غلبوا is the ṣila (relative clause) of the relative; على أمرهم is attached to غلبوا. They were the believers, who had the say at that time. لنتخذن: the lām is the lām that prepares for the oath (al-lām al-muwaṭṭiʾa li-al-qasam); نتخذن is an imperfect verb indeclinable (mabnī) on fatḥa, and its fāʿil is latent (mustatir) [Translator's note: printed «مستر»], its implied form being "naḥnu"; عليهم is a ḥāl (circumstantial); مسجدا is the mafʿūl bihi.
(سَيَقُولُونَ ثَلاثَةٌ رابِعُهُمْ كَلْبُهُمْ وَيَقُولُونَ خَمْسَةٌ سادِسُهُمْ كَلْبُهُمْ رَجْماً بِالْغَيْبِ): the sīn is for the future, indicating that the dispute about them took place in the time of the Prophet ﷺ, i.e. in the distant future relative to their story. يقولون is an imperfect verb and its fāʿil; the pronoun refers to those of the People of the Book and the believers who delved into their story in the time of the Prophet. Abū Ḥayyān said: "He brought the sīn of the future because there is, as it were, folding and incorporation (ṭayy wa-idmāj) in the speech; the implied form is: when you have answered their question and narrated to them the story of the People of the Cave, ask them about their number, for when you ask them they will say. And He did not bring the sīn in what follows because it is conjoined to the future and so falls within futurity, or because the future meaning is intended, for which it is suitable."
ثلاثة is the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ, i.e. "they are three persons". We supplied "persons" only because رابعهم is an active participle in construct with the pronoun, and the meaning is that it "fourthed" them, i.e. made them four and brought them to this number; if one supplied "three men", it would be impossible for three men to become four, since the two kinds differ. رابعهم is a mubtadaʾ and كلبهم a khabar; the clause ثلاثة is the maqūl al-qawl, and the clause رابعهم كلبهم is in the position of an accusative as a ḥāl, i.e. their dog making them four by joining them. ويقولون خمسة سادسهم كلبهم is conjoined to the previous clause and identical in its i'rab. رجما is accusative as a maṣdar, governed by an omitted verb, i.e. "they cast (yarjumūna) a casting", the meaning being: they throw out hidden, conjectured information; or as a ḥāl, meaning "casting (conjectures)". بالغيب is attached to رجما.
(وَيَقُولُونَ: سَبْعَةٌ وَثامِنُهُمْ كَلْبُهُمْ): the wāw is a conjunction; يقولون is a verb and its fāʿil; سبعة is the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ. On the wāw (in وثامنهم) there are views beyond counting; it has occupied scholars and men of letters, who have written lengthy works about it; we shall come to mention them, and the gist of what has been said about it, in the Benefits section [Translator's note: in fact the discussion follows in the Rhetoric section]. What reason most readily accepts is that it is the wāw which enters a clause occurring as a naʿt of an indefinite noun, by analogy with the clause occurring as a ḥāl after a definite noun — e.g. "Zayd came, and with him another man" — in order to emphasise the adhesion of the quality to the thing described, meaning that its being so qualified is a settled matter, firmly established in minds. This is what al-Zamakhsharī and Ibn Hishām chose; wait for the details. The clause ثامنهم كلبهم is a naʿt of سبعة. Abū Ḥayyān rejected this view; his words are:
"That the wāw enters a clause occurring as a naʿt, indicating the adhesion of the quality to the thing described and the firmness of its connection with it, is something the grammarians do not know. Rather, they have established that a naʿt that is not a clause is not conjoined to another naʿt unless the meanings differ, so that the conjunction indicates difference; if they do not differ, conjunction is not permissible in these single nouns; and clauses that occur as naʿt are even further from allowing it. They refuted those who held that in Sībawayh's words 'As for what comes for a meaning and is neither a noun nor a verb', the phrase 'and is neither a noun nor a verb' is a naʿt of 'for a meaning' and that the wāw entered the clause, (saying) that 'I passed by a man and he eats' (marartu bi-rajulin wa-yaʾkulu), in the sense of a naʿt, is not of the speech of the Arabs. As for the saying of Allah the Exalted «إلا ولها كتاب معلوم», the clause is circumstantial."
(قُلْ رَبِّي أَعْلَمُ بِعِدَّتِهِمْ ما يَعْلَمُهُمْ إِلَّا قَلِيلٌ): ربي is a mubtadaʾ and أعلم its khabar, and the clause is the maqūl al-qawl; بعدتهم is attached to أعلم; the clause ما يعلمهم is circumstantial; ما is negative; يعلمهم is an imperfect verb and a mafʿūl bihi; إلا is a particle of restriction (ḥaṣr); قليل is the fāʿil of يعلمهم. The comparison (in أعلم) is with respect to quality, because the degrees of certainty differ in strength; the comparison is not with respect to the first two groups, who inclined to casting conjectures at the unseen, to guessing and surmise, rather than to the truth and acquaintance with what actually happened.
(فَلا تُمارِ فِيهِمْ إِلَّا مِراءً ظاهِراً): the fāʾ is the fāʾ al-faṣīḥa, i.e. if you know this — and it is right that you should know it — then do not dispute. لا is prohibitive; تمار is jussive (majzūm) by لا, the sign of its jussive being the dropping of the weak letter; إلا is a particle of restriction; مراء is a mafʿūl muṭlaq (absolute object); ظاهرا is a naʿt.
(وَلا تَسْتَفْتِ فِيهِمْ مِنْهُمْ أَحَداً): the wāw is a conjunction; لا is prohibitive; تستفت is jussive by it, the sign of its jussive also being the dropping of the weak letter; the fāʿil is latent, its implied form being "anta"; فيهم is attached to تستفت; منهم is a ḥāl, because it was originally a naʿt of أحدا; أحدا is the mafʿūl bihi.
