He says: "Al-qubul has seven senses: al-qubul in the eye; al-qubul, the rise of the ground that faces you, as when you say 'I saw a person at that qubul'; al-qubul, when you see the new moon qubulan, small; al-qubul, when a man speaks words he had not prepared, as in 'so-and-so spoke qubulan'; al-qubul, when a man brings his camels to the water, then draws water and pours it over them, so it is said 'he watered them qubulan'; al-qubul, something like wool hung on the necks of children; and al-qubul, the lining of the top of a well."

dervis-irab:27-28.t:
* Vocabulary:
(مُلْتَحَداً): A refuge to which you would incline, seeking shelter, if you were to intend to alter the Qur'an. In al-Miṣbāḥ: "Abū ʿUbayda said: alḥada, ilḥādan, means he disputed and quarrelled; laḥada means he wronged and was unjust; and alḥada in the Sanctuary means he treated its sanctity as lawful and violated it. Multaḥad, with fatḥa, is a noun of place, and it is the refuge." In al-Qāmūs: "iltaḥada ʿani l-dīn has the sense of alḥada; iltaḥada ilā kadhā means he inclined to such-and-such; and iltaḥada ilā fulān means he took refuge with so-and-so."
(وَلا تَعْدُ عَيْناكَ): Do not turn away. One says ʿadāhu when he passes beyond it, and from this their saying ʿadā ṭawrahu (he overstepped his bounds) and "the people came to me ʿadā Zayd (except Zayd)". The proper form of the speech would be to say it in the accusative, that is, "do not pass over them with your two eyes", and it was turned to the nominative only because he meant the owner of the two eyes, so it is a figurative usage; further explanation will come in the section on Rhetoric.
(فُرُطاً): With two ḍammas, meaning going beyond the limit. The explanation of this root was given in detail earlier.

* I'rab:
(وَاتْلُ ما أُوحِيَ إِلَيْكَ مِنْ كِتابِ رَبِّكَ) The wāw is a conjunction. (اتل) is an imperative verb, indeclinable (mabnī) with the dropping of the weak letter, and its agent is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "you". (ما) is a direct object; the clause (أوحي) is a ṣila; (إليك) is attached to (أوحي); and (من كتاب ربك) is a ḥāl from (ما).
(لا مُبَدِّلَ لِكَلِماتِهِ وَلَنْ تَجِدَ مِنْ دُونِهِ مُلْتَحَداً) (لا) is the lā of generic negation, and (مبدل) is its name, indeclinable on the fatḥa. (لكلماته) is the khabar, and the clause is circumstantial. (ولن تجد) is conjoined; (من دونه) is a ḥāl; and (ملتحدا) is a direct object.
(وَاصْبِرْ نَفْسَكَ مَعَ الَّذِينَ يَدْعُونَ رَبَّهُمْ بِالْغَداةِ وَالْعَشِيِّ يُرِيدُونَ وَجْهَهُ) (واصبر) is conjoined; it is an imperative verb, its agent is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "you", and (نفسك) is a direct object. The meaning of ṣabr here is restraining the soul and keeping it steady. In al-Mukhtār: "ṣabr is restraining the soul from impatience, and its pattern is ḍaraba; ṣabarahu means he restrained him." The Exalted said: «واصبر نفسك». And Abū Dhuʾayb said, lamenting his son:
فصبرت عارفة لذلك جسرة ... ترسو إذا نفس الجبان تطلع
(I restrained a soul that knew that, bold, that stays firm when the coward's soul rises up.)
That is, I restrained a soul that recognised that calamity. He gave (عارفة) the sense of "patient", and so made it transitive with the lām; (جسرة) means strong and hard, and it is also reported as (حرة) ("free"), staying calm when the soul of the coward rises from its resting place and flies in scattered fragments. (مع الذين) is an adverb of place attached to (اصبر); the clause (يدعون ربهم) is a ṣila; (ربهم) is a direct object; (بالغداة والعشي) is attached to (يدعون); and the clause (يريدون وجهه) is a ḥāl.
(وَلا تَعْدُ عَيْناكَ عَنْهُمْ تُرِيدُ زِينَةَ الْحَياةِ الدُّنْيا) Conjoined to (واصبر). (لا) is prohibitive; (تعد) is jussive by (لا), its sign of jussive being the dropping of the weak letter; (عيناك) is the agent; (عنهم) is attached to (تعد); the clause (تريد زينة الحياة الدنيا) is a ḥāl; and (الدنيا) is an adjective. The discussion of it will come in detail in the section on Benefits.
(وَلا تُطِعْ مَنْ أَغْفَلْنا قَلْبَهُ عَنْ ذِكْرِنا وَاتَّبَعَ هَواهُ وَكانَ أَمْرُهُ فُرُطاً) The wāw is a conjunction to what precedes; (لا) is prohibitive; (تطع) is jussive by it, and its agent is latent; (من) is a direct object; the clause (أغفلنا) is a ṣila; (قلبه) is a direct object; (عن ذكرنا) is attached to (أغفلنا); (اتبع هواه) is a past verb, a latent agent and a direct object; the wāw is a conjunction; and (كان), its name and its khabar.

* Rhetoric:
Intellectual figurative usage (al-majāz al-ʿaqlī):
In His saying «ولا تعد عيناك» there is an intellectual figure, because the verb ʿadā, "to pass beyond", is attributed to the two eyes, whereas it should have been attributed to him so that the eyes are its object, since ʿadā is transitive by itself, as was said earlier. He inclined to the figure only because it is more eloquent than the literal, as if his two eyes were fixed in gazing upon them, and as if they perceived what they do not perceive and sensed the necessity of looking at these people, of restraining the soul and training it to keep their company.
It is also said that it is a case of taḍmīn (embedding a second meaning), in which ʿadā embeds the meaning of nabā and ʿalā, from their saying nabat ʿaynuhu ʿanhu when it passed over him and did not settle on him. The purpose of this embedding is to give the sum of two meanings, which is stronger than giving a single meaning, that is: "let your two eyes not plunge past them, going beyond them to others." That too is beautiful.

* Benefits:
The rule concerning the elative (ism al-tafḍīl) is that when it is joined with the article (al-), it may not be followed by the genitive-governing (min), so one does not say "so-and-so is the best than so-and-so", and it must agree with what precedes it in singular, dual and plural, masculine and feminine. It is anomalous that it was followed by (min) in the poet's words:
ولست بالأكثر منهم حصى ... وإنما العزة للكاثر
(I am not the more numerous of them in pebbles [number]; honour belongs only to the one who outnumbers.)
When it is stripped of the article and of annexation, it must be singular and masculine in all circumstances and be followed by the genitive-governing (min), even if only implied, as in His saying, the Exalted, «وللآخرة خير وأبقى».
When it is annexed to an indefinite noun, it must be singular and masculine and may not be followed by (min).
When it is annexed to a definite noun, it may not be followed by (min), and two forms are permissible: singular and masculine, like the one annexed to an indefinite noun, or agreement with what precedes it. Both usages occur in the Qur'an. Of the first: «ولتجدنهم أحرص الناس على حياة» (and He did not say "aḥriṣī al-nās"); of the second: «وكذلك جعلنا في كل قرية أكابر مجرميها».
The ruling on (الدنيا): Analogy would require (الدنيا) to come with the article, since it is originally an adjective on the pattern fuʿlā, the masculine being al-adnā, so it ought to agree, as it does in the verse we are dealing with. But they used it as they use nouns, rarely mentioning the thing described with it, so they used it without the article like other nouns. Al-ʿAjjāj said:
يوم ترى النفوس ما أعدت ... من نزل إذا الأمور غبت
في سعي دنيا طالما قد مدت ... حتى انقضى قضاؤها فأدت
(On the day when you see souls with what they prepared as provision, when the matters turn out their results, in the pursuit of a worldly [life] that was long extended, until its decree ran out and it paid.)
And Bashāma ibn Ḥazn al-Nahshalī said, and it is also ascribed to al-Murraqqish the Elder:
وإن دعوت إلى جلى ومكرمة ... يوما سراة كرام الناس فادعينا
(If you ever call the chiefs of noble people to a great matter and a noble deed, then call us.)
It is said that (جلى) is the feminine of ajall on the pattern of al-akbar/al-kubrā, and in this it follows (دنيا) in the course of usage as a noun. It is also said that it is a verbal noun like al-rujʿā and al-bushrā, meaning "return" and "glad tidings". As for the saying of Abū Nuwās al-Ḥasan ibn Hāniʾ, describing wine:
كأن صغرى وكبرى من فواقعها ... حصباء در على أرض من الذهب
(As if the small and large of its bubbles were pebbles of pearl on a ground of gold.)
some have faulted it for using these two indefinitely, whereas this kind of adjective is used only definite. The excuse offered for him is that he used them as nouns, because of how often this form comes without a preceding described noun. It is also possible that he did not intend the elative sense but the sense of the active form, as if he had said "as if a small one and a large one of its bubbles", along the lines of His saying, the Exalted, «وهو أهون عليه». It is also said that the (من) mentioned is redundant and that (كبرى) is annexed to (فواقعها), but against this it is objected that the redundancy of (من) in an affirmative context is not permitted.
Ibn al-Athīr said in al-Mathal al-Sāʾir: "Do you not see that Abū Nuwās was counted among the classes of the scholars, in addition to his precedence among the classes of the poets, yet he erred in a matter in which one like him does not err, saying in the description of wine: كأن صغرى وكبرى … (the verse above)? This was not hidden from Abū Nuwās, for it belongs to the obvious part of Arabic grammar and not to its obscure parts, because it is a matter of transmission, which the transmitter carries on as transmitted without latitude. Abū Nuwās' saying «صغرى وكبرى» is not permissible, since for fuʿlā with an aʿfal counterpart the article may not be dropped; it may be dropped only from fuʿlā that has no aʿfal counterpart, such as ḥublā, unless the fuʿlā of aʿfal is annexed; and here it is bare of annexation and of the article. See how Abū Nuwās fell into such a place, despite its nearness and ease."
Ibn Abī l-Ḥadīd answered this statement in his book al-Falak al-Dāʾir, saying: "It cannot be denied that many of the imams of Arabic criticised this verse, but many of them also defended Abū Nuwās. They said: we have found fuʿlā of aʿfal occurring in more than one place without the article, without annexation and without (min), like dunyā in the rajaz poet's words: «في سعي دنيا طالما قد مدت», and the other's words: «وإن دعوت إلى جلى ومكرمة», and another's «لا تبخلن بدنيا وهي مقبلة», and they say ṭūbā laka. There is also another way to take the verse, which is that the (من) in «من فواقعها» is redundant, following the view of Abū l-Ḥasan al-Akhfash on the redundancy of (من) in the affirmative, for he holds that and argues with His saying, the Exalted: «فيها من برد», that is «فيها برد». This favours taking (صغرى) and (كبرى) in the verse as annexed."
Shaykh Bahāʾ al-Dīn ibn al-Naḥḥās said: "This is astonishing from such an eminent man. As for his citing dunyā and its sisters, all their cases are mentioned in the books of the grammarians, which spares us lengthening by citing them, unlike ṣughrā and kubrā. As for his statement about the redundancy of (من), it is as if he thinks that when (من) is redundant, the genitive is by annexation, or that the annexation remains; this has no basis. The genitive is rather by the preposition, because prepositions do not attach [to anything]. As for a redundant preposition between two terms of a genitive construct, no one held that except in the like of lā abā laka, as an anomaly, and this is not of that; nor does al-Akhfash, in saying that (من) is added in the affirmative, mean what Ibn Abī l-Ḥadīd meant." Similar is the prosodists' saying fāṣila ṣughrā and fāṣila kubrā, meaning "small" and "large", not intending the elative but the noun. Likewise the saying of Abū Tammām describing spring:
دنيا معاش للورى حتى إذا ... حل الربيع فإنما هي منظر
(A world of livelihood for mankind, until, when spring arrives, it is merely a sight to behold.)
Here the nominal sense has so prevailed over it that the original elative sense is no longer perceived in it.
We take the opportunity to cite some verses of the poem from which this verse of Abū Nuwās comes, for their beauty. Its opening is:
ساع بكأس إلى ناس على طرب ... كلاهما عجب في منظر عجب
(A cup-bearer hastens with a cup to people in delight; both are wonderful, in a wonderful sight.)
قامت تريني وستر الليل منسدل ... صبحا تولد بين الماء والعنب
(She stood up, showing me, while the veil of night hung down, a dawn born between water and grape.)
Then: «كأن صغرى وكبرى …» (the verse), and after it:
كأن تركا صفوفا في جوانبها ... تواتر الرمي بالنشاب من كثب
(As if Turks in ranks along its sides were firing arrows in succession from close by.)
في كف ساقية ناهيك ساقية ... في حسن قدّ وفي ظرف وفي أدب
(In the hand of a cup-bearer, and what a cup-bearer, in beauty of form, in refinement and in manners.)

dervis-irab:60-63.t:
* Vocabulary:
(مَجْمَعَ الْبَحْرَيْنِ): the meeting-place of the two seas. It is the place in which Moses was promised he would meet al-Khiḍr. The commentators differ about it: it was said to be the meeting-place of the Sea of the Romans and the Sea of Persia, and other things were said which may be consulted in the longer works.
(حُقُباً): a long time. Al-ḥuqub is eighty years. In al-Qāmūs: al-ḥuqb, with ḍamma on the ḥāʾ and on the qāf, is eighty years or more; also the era (dahr) and the years; its plural is aḥqāb and ḥiqāb. It was also said that it is al-ḥuqb with ḍamma on the ḥāʾ and sukūn on the qāf, with the plural ḥiqāb. In al-Miṣbāḥ: al-ḥuqb is the era, the plural being aḥqāb, like fuql and aqfāl; the ḍamma on the qāf is a dialectal assimilation to the vowel before it. It is said that al-ḥuqb is eighty years. Al-ḥuqba means a period, and the plural is ḥuqab, like sidra. It was also said that al-ḥuqba is like al-ḥuqb.
(سَرَباً): that is, like a sarab, which is a long cleft with no outlet. In the dictionaries: al-sarab (with fatḥa on both letters) is a trench underground, and the channel through which water enters. One says "ṭarīq sarab", meaning a road on which people follow one another continuously.
(غَداءَنا): what is eaten at the beginning of the day.

* I'rab:
(وَإِذْ قالَ مُوسى لِفَتاهُ لا أَبْرَحُ حَتَّى أَبْلُغَ مَجْمَعَ الْبَحْرَيْنِ أَوْ أَمْضِيَ حُقُباً): The wāw is resumptive, and the clause is resumptive, brought to begin the story of the meeting of Moses and al-Khiḍr and the wonders that were interspersed in it, whose details we shall give in the section on benefits. The adverbial noun is attached to an omitted element, its implied form being "mention". The clause قال موسى is in the position of genitive by the annexation of the adverbial noun to it. لفتاه is attached to قال. لا is negative, and أبرح is an imperfect defective verb whose subject is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "I", and the khabar is omitted, its implied form being "travelling". It is possible that it is complete and so does not require a khabar, meaning "I will not depart from the travelling and seeking I am engaged in, and will not leave it". حتى is a particle of limit and genitive. أبلغ is made accusative by an implied أن after حتى, and مجمع البحرين is a direct object. أو is a conjunction, and أمضي is conjoined to أبلغ. حقبا is an adverbial of time attached to أمضي. Abū al-Baqāʾ and others preferred that it (حتى) have the meaning of "until" (ilā), with أبلغ made accusative by an implied أن after it, and I do not think that correct. (فَلَمَّا بَلَغا مَجْمَعَ بَيْنِهِما نَسِيا حُوتَهُما فَاتَّخَذَ سَبِيلَهُ فِي الْبَحْرِ سَرَباً): The fāʾ is a conjunction, and لما is an adverbial noun meaning "when", and the clause بلغا is in the position of genitive by the annexation of the adverbial noun to it. The alif is the agent, and مجمع is a direct object. بينهما is an adverbial noun annexed to مجمع, that is, "between the two seas". The clause نسيا has no grammatical position, because it is the answer to لما. حوتهما is a direct object. فاتخذوا [Translator's note: the source prints "فاتخذوا"; the verse and the following parsing read فاتخذ]: the fāʾ is a conjunction, and اتخذ is a past verb whose agent is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "he", that is, the fish. سبيله is a direct object, and سربا a second direct object. في البحر is attached to an omitted element, a ḥāl. In the speech there is a putting-forward and a putting-back, because the fish's taking its way into the sea was before the forgetting. (فَلَمَّا جاوَزا قالَ لِفَتاهُ آتِنا غَداءَنا): The fāʾ is a conjunction, and لما is a temporal adverbial, and the clause جاوزا is the genitive complement of the adverbial. The object is omitted, that is, "the appointed place", which is the rock. The clause قال لفتاه has no position, and the clause آتنا غداءنا is the content of the saying. غداءنا is a second direct object of آتنا.
(لَقَدْ لَقِينا مِنْ سَفَرِنا هذا نَصَباً): The lām is the answer to an omitted oath, and قد is a particle of confirmation. لقينا is a verb and agent. من سفرنا is attached to لقينا. هذا is an adjective of سفرنا or a substitute for it. نصبا is a direct object of لقينا. (قالَ: أَرَأَيْتَ إِذْ أَوَيْنا إِلَى الصَّخْرَةِ): أرأيت has been discussed at length, and it means "tell me". The two objects of أرأيت are omitted for brevity, that is, "Have you seen what the outcome of our affair was?" This is a style familiar in speech current among people: one says to his companion, when some calamity has befallen him, "Have you seen what befell me?" The adverbial noun is attached to this omitted element, that is, to "befell me". More of the discussion of this "seeing" will come in the section on rhetoric. The clause أوينا is the genitive complement of the adverbial noun. إلى الصخرة is attached to أوينا. (فَإِنِّي نَسِيتُ الْحُوتَ وَما أَنْسانِيهُ إِلَّا الشَّيْطانُ أَنْ أَذْكُرَهُ): The fāʾ gives the reason for the bewilderment that overcame them both at what had befallen them. إن and its noun, and the clause نسيت الحوت is its khabar. The wāw is parenthetical, and the clause is parenthetical between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined. ما is negative. أنسانيه is a past verb; the nūn is for protection, the yāʾ is the first direct object and the hāʾ the second direct object. إلا is a particle of restriction, and الشيطان is the agent of أنسانيه. أن and what is within its scope is a badal ishtimāl (substitute of inclusion) for the hāʾ, that is, "and none made me forget remembering it except Satan." (وَاتَّخَذَ سَبِيلَهُ فِي الْبَحْرِ عَجَباً): The wāw is a conjunction, and اتخذ is a past verb conjoined to نسيت, whose agent is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "he", that is, the fish. سبيله is the first direct object, في البحر is a ḥāl, and عجبا is the second direct object of اتخذ, or an absolute object (mafʿūl muṭlaq) of an omitted verb, with في البحر being the second object. That is, Moses said: "I marvelled a marvel: a fish that is eaten for an era, then becomes alive after part of it has been eaten."

* Rhetoric:
In his saying «أرأيت», the "seeing" here is borrowed for complete knowledge and full witnessing. It is an explicit derivative metaphor (istiʿāra taṣrīḥiyya tabaʿiyya), because it is applied to a verb; the thing likened is omitted and the thing to which it is likened is put in its place. The question in أرأيت is for astonishment, as though he were trying to arouse wonder in the soul of Moses at the miracles he had seen, which do not enter the mind and which the intellect can hardly credit; these may be consulted in the longer commentaries and the transmitted reports, which would take us beyond the scope of this book. We shall content ourselves with narrating the story of the meeting of Moses and al-Khiḍr, relying on the text of the ḥadīth and reasonable logical analysis, leaving the field to those with a gift for storytelling, in the hope that they may weave on the loom of the story-writer Tawfīq al-Ḥakīm.

dervis-irab:64-70.t:
* I'rab:
(قالَ ذلِكَ ما كُنَّا نَبْغِ): ذلك is a mubtadaʾ and ما the khabar. The clause كنا is a ṣila: كان and its noun, and the clause نبغي is its khabar. The clause ذلك etc. is the content of the saying. In the Muṣḥaf the yāʾ of نبغي is dropped, because it is one of the "additional yāʾs" (al-yāʾāt al-zawāʾid). (فَارْتَدَّا عَلى آثارِهِما قَصَصاً)
The fāʾ is a conjunction. ارتدا is a verb and agent. على آثارهما is attached to an omitted element, a ḥāl, that is, "they returned the way they had come". قصصا is an absolute object of an omitted verb, that is, "they follow the tracks (yaquṣṣāni qaṣaṣan), following their traces with real following". You may also make it a ḥāl, that is, "so they went back upon their tracks, tracing them". (فَوَجَدا عَبْداً مِنْ عِبادِنا آتَيْناهُ رَحْمَةً مِنْ عِنْدِنا وَعَلَّمْناهُ مِنْ لَدُنَّا عِلْماً): The fāʾ is a conjunction. وجدا عبدا is a verb, agent and direct object. من عبادنا is an adjective of عبد, and the clause آتيناه is a second adjective. رحمة is a second direct object, and من عندنا is an adjective of رحمة. علمناه is a verb, agent and direct object. من لدنا is a ḥāl, because it was an adjective of علما and was put before it. علما is a second direct object of علمناه. Had it been an absolute object it would have been taʿlīman, because its verb is of the pattern faʿʿala with doubling, and the regular maṣdar of such a verb is taf ʿīl. (قالَ لَهُ مُوسى هَلْ أَتَّبِعُكَ عَلى أَنْ تُعَلِّمَنِ مِمَّا عُلِّمْتَ رُشْداً): قال is a past verb, له is attached to it, and موسى is the agent. هل is a particle of question. اتبعك is an imperfect verb with a latent agent and a direct object. على أن تعلمني: أن and what is within its scope are in the position of genitive after على, and the preposition and its genitive noun are attached to an omitted element, a ḥāl from the kāf in هل اتبعك, that is, "May I follow you, you being a teacher to me?" مما is attached to تعلمني, and the clause علمت is a ṣila. رشدا is a second object of تعلمني, because the yāʾ is the first object. It is also permissible to parse رشدا as mafʿūl li-ajlihi (object of purpose), that is, "for the sake of right guidance", or as a maṣdar in the position of accusative as a ḥāl. (قالَ إِنَّكَ لَنْ تَسْتَطِيعَ مَعِيَ صَبْراً): The clause إنك is the content of the saying. إن and its noun; لن is a particle of negation, accusative and futurity; تستطيع is made accusative by لن. معي is an adverbial of place attached to an omitted element, that is, "in your being with me". صبرا is a direct object. (وَكَيْفَ تَصْبِرُ عَلى ما لَمْ تُحِطْ بِهِ خُبْراً): وكيف: the wāw is a conjunction, and كيف is an interrogative noun in the position of accusative as a ḥāl. تصبر is a nominative imperfect verb, whose agent is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "you". على ما is attached to تصبر, and the clause لم تحط is a ṣila. به is attached to تحط. خبرا is, in meaning, an absolute object of تحط, because لم تحط has the sense of "you did not become informed". Al-Zamakhsharī parsed it as a tamyīz converted from the agent, that is, "your knowledge did not encompass it", and that is not far-fetched. (قالَ سَتَجِدُنِي إِنْ شاءَ اللَّهُ صابِراً وَلا أَعْصِي لَكَ أَمْراً): ستجدني: the sīn is a particle of futurity, and تجدني is a nominative imperfect verb; the nūn is for protection; its agent is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "you"; the yāʾ is an attached pronoun in the position of accusative as the first direct object. The clause إن شاء الله is parenthetical. صابرا is the second direct object of تجدني. He mentioned the mercy [Translator's note: the source says "mercy", presumably meaning the conditioning on Allah's will, which is the point of the sentence] as a precaution against what comes in his saying «حتى إذا لقيا غلاما فقتله»; for his killing of the boy suggests that he is characterised by harshness and severity. The clause ولا أعصي لك أمرا is conjoined to صابرا, so it is in the position of accusative; or it is conjoined to ستجدني and so has no grammatical position. لك is attached to an omitted element, a ḥāl, because it was an adjective of أمرا. Moses restricted it with the will of Allah only because he knew how severe and difficult the matter was, and that zeal might overtake him when he saw something at variance; the details of that will come in their place. (قالَ فَإِنِ اتَّبَعْتَنِي فَلا تَسْئَلْنِي عَنْ شَيْءٍ حَتَّى أُحْدِثَ لَكَ مِنْهُ ذِكْراً): The fāʾ is a conjunction, and إن is conditional. اتبعتني is a past verb, agent and direct object, and it is in the position of jussive as the protasis. The fāʾ is the linking one, and لا is prohibitive. تسألني is an imperfect verb made jussive by لا, and the nūn is for protection and the yāʾ is a direct object. عن شيء is attached to تسألني. حتى is a particle of limit and genitive. أحدث is an imperfect verb made accusative by an implied أن after حتى. لك is attached to أحدث, منه is a ḥāl, and ذكرا is a direct object. It is necessary to posit an omitted adjective after شيء, that is, "a thing whose secret is hidden from you and whose matter is obscure to you".

* Benefits:
1- ʿinda and ladun:
Ladun has the meaning of ʿinda, so it is a noun for the time and place of presence, just as ʿinda is. But ladun is distinguished by six matters: 1- It is bound to the starting-point of limits of time and place, whereas ʿinda is not bound. Hence the two alternate in such as "I came from his side" (min ʿindihi) and "from his presence" (min ladunhi), and in the noble verse; and they may not alternate in such as "I sat beside him" (jalastu ʿindahu), because there is no sense of beginning here. The alternation was left out in the verse only to avoid repetition of the composition. 2- That ladun is mostly used governed in the genitive by min, and its accusative is rare, while ʿinda governed by min is more frequent than ladun governed by min. 3- That it is indeclinable on sukūn, unlike ʿinda, which is always declinable. 4- That it may be annexed to sentences, as in the saying of al-Quṭāmī:
صريع غوان راقهن ورقنه ... لدن شبّ حتى شاب سود الذوائب
(Felled by beauties, whom he pleased and who pleased him, from when he was young until the black locks turned grey.)
5- That it may stand alone before ghudwa, as in his saying:
وما زال مهري مزجر الكلب فيهم ... لدن غدوة حتى دنت لغروب
(My mount did not cease to be a dog-driving place among them, from morning until it drew near to sunset.)
with ghudwa accusative as a tamyīz or by likeness to the direct object, and genitive according to the regular rule. 6- That it occurs only as a complement (faḍla), unlike ʿinda, which may occur as an essential element.
Some have said: ʿinda in the tongue of the Arabs is for what is apparent, and ladun for what is hidden; so the "mercy" meant would be the apparent of His favours, and the "knowledge" the hidden, concealed, known with certainty to be special.
2- The Prophet's ḥadīth about al-Khiḍr:
It is time to cite for you the eloquent ḥadīth that was narrated from the Prophet ﷺ about al-Khiḍr, and the other ḥadīth in which he spoke of the meeting of Moses and al-Khiḍr.
The first ḥadīth: It was narrated on the authority of Abū Umāma, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Shall I not tell you about al-Khiḍr?" They said, "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "One day, while he was walking in the market of the Children of Israel, a man who was a mukātab (a slave contracting to buy his freedom) saw him and said: 'Give charity to me, may Allah bless you.' Al-Khiḍr said: 'I believe in Allah, whatever may come to pass; I have nothing to give you.' The poor man said: 'I ask you by the face of Allah to give me charity, for I have seen generosity in your face and hoped for blessing from you.' Al-Khiḍr said: 'I believe in Allah; I have nothing to give you, unless you take me and sell me.' The poor man said: 'Is this possible?' He said: 'Yes. I say: you have asked me by a great matter; as for me, I shall not disappoint you, by the face of my Lord. Sell me.' He said: so he took him to the market and sold him for four hundred dirhams. He stayed with the buyer for a time, who did not put him to any work. He said: 'You bought me only seeking some good in me, so give me some work to do.' He said: 'I dislike burdening you; you are a very old man, and weak.' He said: 'It will not burden me.' He said: 'Get up, then, and move these stones' (which no fewer than six men could move in a day). The man went out for some need of his and then came back, and he had moved the stones in an hour. He said: 'You have done well and beautifully, and you have managed what I did not see you could manage.' He said: then a journey came up for the man, and he said, 'I like you as a trustworthy man, so be my deputy over my family in a good deputyship.' He said: 'And give me some work.' He said: 'I dislike burdening you.' He said: 'It will not burden me.' He said: 'Then mould bricks for my house until I return to you.' He said: the man went on his journey. He said: the man returned and he had raised the building. He said: 'I ask you by the face of Allah, what is your story? What is your affair?' He said: 'You asked me by the face of Allah, and the face of Allah is what threw me into this servitude.' Then al-Khiḍr said: 'I shall tell you who I am. I am al-Khiḍr, of whom you have heard. A poor man asked me for charity, and I had nothing to give him, so he asked me by the face of Allah, and I put my neck at his disposal, and he sold me. And I tell you that whoever is asked by the face of Allah and turns away the one who asks while he is able, will stand on the Day of Resurrection a skin with no flesh on it, rattling.' The man said to him: 'I believe in Allah. I burdened you, O Prophet of Allah, and I did not know.' He said: 'No harm; you have done well and thoroughly.' The man said: 'May my father and mother be your ransom, O Prophet of Allah: rule over my family and my wealth as you wish, or choose, and I shall set you free.' He said: 'I would like you to set me free so that I may worship my Lord.' So he set him free. Then al-Khiḍr said: 'Praise be to Allah, who bound me in servitude and then delivered me from it.'"

An analytical glance:
In this ḥadīth the Messenger of Allah ﷺ reported an interesting sketch about al-Khiḍr, and the depth of his faith in Allah, his desire for His reward and his fear of His punishment, so that it might serve as the signposts of dawn for every believer in what he holds to be true and right, who cares not what he bears in the cause of establishing in souls what he believes. The sketch also contains his inclination to answer the poor, needy asker even by selling himself. One of them said:
يجود بالنفس إذ ضنّ الجواد بها ... والجود بالنفس أقصى غاية الجود
بثّ النوال ولا تمنعك قلته ... فكلّ ما سدّ فقرا فهو محمود
(He gives his very self when the generous man is stingy with it, and giving oneself is the furthest limit of generosity. / Spread your giving and let its smallness not stop you, for whatever fills a need is praiseworthy.)
Then al-Khiḍr gave precious advice, suitable to be followed in all circumstances of time and place. He warned those who are asked against miserliness, for fear of standing on the Day of Reckoning barefoot and naked, their bodies worn and threadbare, trembling for their wretchedness and foulness, as though the body were a skin like a mere frame that shakes and moves and can be detected only by a faint rattling. I think Abū al-Ṭayyib [al-Mutanabbī] looked at the sky of this meaning when he said, describing his own thinness:
كفى بجسمي نحولا أنني رجل ... لولا مخاطبتي إياك لم ترني
(It is enough of thinness in my body that I am a man who, were it not for my speaking to you, you would not see me.)
And look after that at the highest request that the wise incline towards: «Set me free so that I may worship my Lord.» This serves as a parable that the Prophet ﷺ struck for every person: that he should be generous with his wealth in projects of good; that he should trust in Allah the Provider, who spends and replaces; and that he should adorn himself with the qualities of generosity and giving. How beautiful is the saying of Abū Firās al-Ḥamdānī, which contains all these lofty meanings and portrays chivalry in the fairest portrait:
غيري يغيره الفعال الجافي ... ويحول عن شيم الكريم الوافي
إن الغنيّ هو الغنيّ بنفسه ... ولو انه عاري المناكب حاف
ما كل ما فوق البسيطة كافيا ... وإذا قنعت فكل شيء كاف
وتعاف لي طمع الحريص فتوتي ... ومروءتي وقناعتي وعفافي ومكارمي عدد النجوم ومنزلي ... مأوى الكرام ومنزل الأ
ضياف لا أرتضي ودا إذا هو لم يدم ... عند الجفاء وقلة الانصاف
(Another than I may be changed by harsh deeds and turn from the ways of the perfectly generous. The rich man is the one rich in himself, even if bare-shouldered and barefoot. Not everything on the face of the earth suffices; but if you are content, everything suffices. My chivalry, my manliness, my contentment and my chastity shun the greed of the covetous; my noble deeds are as many as the stars, and my house is the refuge of the noble and the dwelling of guests. I do not accept an affection that does not last through harshness and want of fairness.) [Translator's note: the source's lines are garbled here, two verses being run together and the word "الأضياف" being split across a line; they are translated as they stand.]

The second ḥadīth, on the meeting of Moses and al-Khiḍr:
It is reported in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim: "On the authority of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: Moses, peace be upon him, stood up to preach to the Children of Israel, and was asked: 'Who is the most knowledgeable of people?' He said: 'I am the most knowledgeable.' He said: Allah rebuked him, as he had not referred the knowledge to Him, and Allah revealed to him: 'I have a servant at the meeting-place of the two seas who is more knowledgeable than you.' Moses said: 'O Lord, how can I reach him?' It was said to him: 'Carry a fish in a basket (miktal); wherever you lose the fish, he is there.' So he set out, and his youth set out with him, and he was Yūshaʿ ibn Nūn. Moses, peace be upon him, carried a fish in a basket, and he and his youth set out walking until they came to the rock, and he saw a man covered with a garment. Moses greeted him, and al-Khiḍr said to him: 'How is there greeting of peace in your land?' He said: 'I am Moses.' He said: 'Moses of the Children of Israel?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'You have a knowledge from the knowledge of Allah that Allah taught you which I do not know, and I have a knowledge from the knowledge of Allah that He taught me which you do not know.'"
The explanation of their deeds will come in the following verses. Yūshaʿ ibn Nūn was not mentioned because he was a follower of Moses and so was included in what was said of him. As for the deeds of the two, they are:
1- the splitting of the ship;
2- the killing of the boy;
3- the bringing out of a treasure from a wall.
The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "May Allah have mercy on Moses; I wish he had been patient, so that He might relate to us more of their reports."

Why was he called al-Khiḍr?
Al-Nawawī said: "It is authentic in al-Bukhārī and elsewhere that the Prophet ﷺ said: He was called al-Khiḍr only because he sat on a fleece (farwa), and behold, it was quivering green behind him. The majority of scholars hold that he is alive and exists among us. The fish was a salted fish. Al-miktal is the basket, the zanbīl, and the wicker container. His saying «musajjan» means covered. And «annā bi-arḍika al-salām» has the meaning of 'how?', that is, 'how strange, greeting of peace in this abode of unbelief.'"

Courtesy in seeking knowledge:
Al-Bayḍāwī said: "It does not contradict his prophethood, nor his being the bearer of a law (our master Moses), that he learn from another what was not a condition in the matters of religion; for the messenger ought to be more knowledgeable than those to whom he was sent in what he was sent with, of the principles and branches of religion, not absolutely. He observed in this the utmost humility and courtesy: he counted himself ignorant, asked permission to be his follower, and asked him to guide him and favour him by teaching him part of what Allah had favoured him with."

Is al-Khiḍr alive?
Many have claimed that al-Khiḍr is alive, and this is not correct, for there is no evidence for it from a revealed book or an established sunna that would require us to accept it, and it has not been transmitted from anyone reliable, on whose transmission one relies, that he saw him and that he told him he was al-Khiḍr, the companion of Moses. Such a thing cannot be relied on, depended upon, or believed except by one of two ways: either truthful report or seeing with the eye; without that, believing in his existence is a sort of confusion. The established custom is that a human being does not live such a long life; whoever claims something contrary to custom in an individual of this species is asked for proof of it. All that those who say that al-Khiḍr is alive and will remain alive until the end of the world rely on, up to now, are ḥadīths none of which is authentic according to the people of knowledge, and tales fabricated by storytellers to promote their standing with the common people. For that reason the mujtahid imam Abū Muḥammad ʿAlī ibn Aḥmad ibn Ḥazm al-Ẓāhirī and the Shaykh al-Islām Abū al-ʿAbbās Aḥmad ibn Taymiyya al-Ḥarrānī al-Ḥanbalī denied the authenticity of that. Their saying, given the breadth of their knowledge of the ḥadīth of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and their knowledge of what is sound and weak in it, suffices as proof for us in what we have said; moreover, the Qur'an contradicts what those who say he lives hold, for Allah, majestic is His affair, said in the precise text of His Book «وما جعلنا لبشر من قبلك الخلد», and He said to the worst of His creation, Iblis, «انك من المنظرين», in answer to his saying «انظرني إلى يوم يبعثون», making that a distinction for His enemy Iblis, to try His creation by him and so that His curse on him might be complete, and He did not make that for anyone else, neither as favour nor as punishment. So whoever says otherwise is not right in what he says, and Allah knows best.
As for the word al-Khiḍr, they have vocalised it with kasra on the khāʾ and sukūn on the ḍād, and with fatḥa on the khāʾ with sukūn on the ḍād and with kasra on it; so it has three dialectal forms. This is his epithet; his kunya is Abū al-ʿAbbās; his name is Balyā; he is of the descendants of Noah, and his father was one of the kings.
[Volume Six]
[Continuation of Sūrat al-Kahf]

dervis-irab:32-44.t:
* Vocabulary:
(أَعْنابٍ): plural of ʿinab; a single grape is ʿinaba. In al-Qāmūs and elsewhere: "ʿannaba al-karm: the vine came to have grapes; al-ʿinab is the fruit of the vine, its plural is aʿnāb, and a single grape is ʿinaba."
(وَحَفَفْناهُما): we made the palm trees surround each of them. One says ḥaffahu al-qawm when they circled around him, and ḥafaftuhu bihim when you made them circle around him; the bāʾ adds a second object, like ghashiyahu and ghashaytuhu bihi. In al-Asās: "ḥaffū bihi and iḥtaffū: they circled him, and they are ḥāffūn around him; ḥafaftuhu bi-l-nās: I made them surround him; 'Paradise is surrounded (ḥuffat) by disliked things'; 'وحففناهما بنخل'; I went in to him while he was surrounded by his servants; a howdah surrounded with brocade. Imruʾ al-Qays said:
رفعن حوايا واقتعدن قعائدا ... وحفّفن من حوك العراق المنمّق
(They raised the saddle-cushions and mounted the seats, and were wrapped about with the embroidered weaving of Iraq.)
They sat on both sides (ḥafāfayhi) of him and on both sides of his bed, that is, its two flanks; I rode in her litter; he is a man wrapped in a garment; nothing remained on his head but a fringe (ḥafāf), which is the border around his head; the woman ḥaffat her face and iḥtaffathu: she removed its hair; and ḥaffa the horse, the wind, the bird and the arrow, ḥafīfan, which is the sound of its passing, and the rustling of tree branches."
(ثَمَرٌ): kinds of wealth, from thammara mālahu (with shadda) when he increased it. In al-Miṣbāḥ: "al-thamar with two fatḥas, and al-thamara is like it; the first is masculine and has the plural thimār, like jabal and jibāl, which is then pluralized as thumur, like kitāb and kutub, which is then pluralized as athmār, like ʿunuq and aʿnāq; the second is feminine and its plural is thamarāt, like qaṣaba and qaṣabāt. Al-thamar is the load that the tree brings forth, whether it is eaten or not, so one says the thamar of the arāk, the thamar of the ʿawsaj, the thamar of the dawm, which is al-muql, as one says the thamar of the palm and the thamar of the vine." Al-Azharī said: "Athmara al-shajar: it put forth its fruit the first time it brought it out, so it is muthmir; hence of what has no benefit it is said 'it has no fruit'." In al-Asās: "'وكان له ثمر', that is, wealth; and see the thamar of your wealth and its growth; a māl thamir is one blessed; athmara al-qawm and thamarū thumūran: their wealth increased; thamara mālahu yathmuru: it increased; and so-and-so is fortunate: his wealth bears fruit." What is meant in the verse is that, beside the two described gardens, he had abundant wealth of gold, silver and other things, and he was very well off in every respect.
(حُسْباناً): it is either a maṣdar like ghufrān and buṭlān, for ḥasiba has several maṣdars. You say ḥasabahu (with fatḥa on the sīn) yaḥsubuhu (with ḍamma), ḥasban, ḥisāban, ḥusbānan, ḥisbānan, ḥisba, ḥasāba: he counted it. You say ḥasibahu (with kasra on the sīn) yaḥsibuhu (with kasra and fatḥa), ḥusbānan, maḥsabatan, maḥsibatan: he thought it. You say ḥasuba (with ḍamma on the sīn) yaḥsubu (with ḍamma too), ḥasaban, ḥasābatan:
he was a man of lineage and nobility, so he is ḥasīb. To which of these branches does this maṣdar belong? It is clear from what precedes that it belongs either to ḥasaba yaḥsibu in the sense of counting, and the meaning then is "He sends upon it a measure of punishment that Allah has determined and reckoned, which is its ruin and destruction", and that ḥusbān is the reckoning of what his hands earned; or else it is ḥusbān as the plural of ḥusbāna (with ḍamma on the ḥāʾ), which is the arrow or the thunderbolt. Al-Zajjāj said: "A punishment of ḥusbān, and that ḥusbān is the reckoning of what your hands earned."
(زَلَقاً): an adjective of «صعيدا», that is, smooth, on which the foot does not stay firm. In al-Qāmūs: "al-zalaq with two fatḥas and al-zalq with fatḥa and sukūn: smooth ground on which there is nothing", and it becomes so by the uprooting of its vegetation.
(غَوْراً): the maṣdar of ghāra fī l-arḍ, that is, it went away so that there is no way to it; it is in the sense of the agent, that is, sunk in the earth, unattainable. Abū Naṣr added ghuʾūran: ghārat ʿaynuhu taghūru ghuʾūran, and ghārat al-shams taghūru ghuʾūran also; and al-ghawr is the noun; one says "I fell into the ghawr", meaning the sun; and ghāra al-rajul yaghūru ghawran when he came to al-Ghawr. Al-Liḥyānī added: and aghāra also, and he recited the verse of al-Aʿshā:
نبيّ يرى مالا ترون وذكره ... أغار لعمري في البلاد وأنجدا
(A prophet who sees what you do not see, and his fame, by my life, has gone to the lowlands and to the highlands of the lands.)
This is according to what al-Liḥyānī said. Al-Kisāʾī used to say: it is from al-ighāra, which is speed. Al-Aṣmaʿī used to say: aghāra is not from al-ghawr; it merely means he ran. Al-Liḥyānī said: of a horse it is said "it is a mighwār", that is, intense in running, and the plural is maghāwīr. The first interpretation is the better one, because he said "and anjada", so he meant that he went to al-Ghawr and came to Najd, al-Ghawr being Tihāma. Ghāra fulān ʿalā ahlihi yaghāru ghayratan; a man ʿayūr from a people ghuyur, and a woman ghayrā from women ghayārā. Al-Aṣmaʿī said:
so-and-so is intense in al-ghār for his family, that is, intense in jealousy; and al-Liḥyānī added "al-ghayr". Abū Naṣr said: aghāra fulān ʿalā banī fulān yughīru ighāratan; and al-Liḥyānī said: of a man it is said "he is a mighwār", that is, intense in raiding, and the plural is maghāwīr. Abū Naṣr said:
one says ghārahum yaghīruhum when he supplied them with provisions, and al-ghiyār is the maṣdar. ʿAbd Manāf ibn Ribʿī al-Hudhalī said:
ماذا يضير ابنتي ربع عويلهما ... لا ترقدان ولا بؤسى لمن رقدا
(What harm does the wailing of the two daughters of Ribʿ do? They do not sleep, and no misfortune to those who slept.) He means that their weeping over their father does not avail anything for the seeking of his blood-revenge.
Abū Naṣr said: al-ghārān are the belly and the private part; one says "the man strives for his ghārayn", that is, his belly and his private part. Abū ʿUbayda said: the mouth of a human being and his private part are called al-ghārān. Abū Naṣr said: al-ghār is like a cave in the mountain. Among their proverbs it is said "ʿasā l-ghuwayru abʾusan" (perhaps misfortunes will come from al-Ghuwayr). Its origin is that there was a cave in which people were, and it collapsed upon them, or an enemy came to them in it and killed them there, so it became a proverb for everything from which evil is feared. It is also said that al-Ghuwayr is the name of a water in the region of al-Samāwa; al-Zabbāʾ said it when she saw Qaṣīr, who came to take vengeance for Jadhīma al-Abrash by the way of al-Ghuwayr; and al-Ghuwayr is the diminutive of ghār. The gist of the meaning of the proverb: perhaps misfortune has come from the cave. Let what has preceded suffice us, for the depth (ghawr) of this root cannot be fathomed.
(خاوِيَةٌ عَلى عُرُوشِها): al-ʿurūsh. In al-Miṣbāḥ: "al-ʿarsh is something like a house of palm branches over which thumām is placed, and the plural is ʿurūsh." So it was originally made so that the vine be placed upon it; when it falls, what is upon it falls. This has been explained before.
(الْوَلايَةُ): with fatḥa on the wāw and with kasra: sovereignty, domination and authority.

* I'rab:
(وَاضْرِبْ لَهُمْ مَثَلًا رَجُلَيْنِ) It was mentioned in Sūrat al-Baqara that ḍaraba with al-mathal may take two objects, because it has the sense of "to make". «اضرب» is an imperative verb, its agent a latent pronoun, its implied form being "anta" (you); «لهم» is attached to «اضرب»; «مثلا» is a direct object; as for «رجلين», you may make it a badal (substitute) from «مثلا», so that «لهم» is in the position of the second object and «مثلا» is the first object; or you may make «رجلين» the second object. The account of the two men will come later. (جَعَلْنا لِأَحَدِهِما جَنَّتَيْنِ مِنْ أَعْنابٍ وَحَفَفْناهُما بِنَخْلٍ وَجَعَلْنا بَيْنَهُما زَرْعاً)
The clause «جعلنا» is an adjective of «رجلين»; «لأحدهما» is the second object of «جعلنا»; «جنتين» is the first object; «من أعناب» is an adjective of «جنتين»; «وحففناهما» is conjoined to «جعلنا», and it is a verb, an agent and a direct object; «بنخل» is attached to «حففناهما»; «وجعلنا بينهما زرعا» is conjoined to what precedes; the parsing of its counterpart has already been given. (كِلْتَا الْجَنَّتَيْنِ آتَتْ أُكُلَها وَلَمْ تَظْلِمْ مِنْهُ شَيْئاً) «كلتا» is a mubtadaʾ, its sign of nominative being an implied ḍamma on the alif because it is a maqṣūr noun (ending in alif); the rule of kilā and kiltā will come in the section of Benefits; the clause «آتت أكلها» is the khabar of «كلتا»; its form (lafẓ) was observed, so the predicate came singular. «ولم تظلم» is conjoined to «آتت»; «منه» is a ḥāl because it was an adjective of «شيئا»; «شيئا» is either a direct object, if «تظلم» means "to diminish", or a mafʿūl muṭlaq; the verification of this has been given before. Among the rare sayings of the Arabs: a Bedouin was asked, "Do you eat grapes?" He said, "It did not wrong me (mā ẓalamanī) to eat it", that is, it did not prevent me. Abū ʿUthmān Saʿīd ibn Hārūn al-Ushnandānī said: "From this is the saying of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: «ولم تظلم منه شيئا», that is, 'it did not withhold'." (وَفَجَّرْنا خِلالَهُما نَهَراً) «فجرنا» is a verb and an agent; «خلالهما» is an adverbial attached to «فجرنا»; «نهرا» is a direct object.
(وَكانَ لَهُ ثَمَرٌ فَقالَ لِصاحِبِهِ وَهُوَ يُحاوِرُهُ) The واو is a conjunction; «كان» is a defective past verb; «له» is the fronted khabar of «كان»; «ثمر» is its postponed noun; «فقال» is conjoined to «وكان»; «لصاحبه» is attached to «قال»; the واو is a ḥāl-waw; «هو» is a mubtadaʾ and the clause «يحاوره» its khabar, the clause being circumstantial; what is meant by it is one of the two. (أَنَا أَكْثَرُ مِنْكَ مالًا وَأَعَزُّ نَفَراً) The clause is the reported speech; it will come in the Rhetoric section that he made three statements contrary to the truth. «أنا» is a mubtadaʾ; «أكثر» is the khabar; «منك» is attached to «أكثر»; «مالا» is a tamyīz; «وأعز نفرا» is conjoined to «أكثر مالا». (وَدَخَلَ جَنَّتَهُ وَهُوَ ظالِمٌ لِنَفْسِهِ قالَ ما أَظُنُّ أَنْ تَبِيدَ هذِهِ أَبَداً) «ودخل جنته» is a verb, an agent and a direct object by extension (ʿalā l-ittisāʿ); the واو of «وهو» is a ḥāl-waw; «هو» is a mubtadaʾ and «ظالم» a khabar, the clause being circumstantial; «لنفسه» is attached to «ظالم»; «قال» is a past verb with a latent agent, its implied form being "huwa"; the clause «ما أظن» is the reported speech; «أن» and what follows it fill the place of the two objects of «أظن»; «هذه» is the agent of «تبيد»; «أبدا» is an adverb of time attached to «تبيد». (وَما أَظُنُّ السَّاعَةَ قائِمَةً وَلَئِنْ رُدِدْتُ إِلى رَبِّي لَأَجِدَنَّ خَيْراً مِنْها مُنْقَلَباً) «وما أظن» is conjoined to the first «ما أظن»; «الساعة» is the first direct object and «قائمة» the second direct object. He meant, being a denier of the resurrection: "I do not suppose the Hour to be coming, as you claim", just as his doubt about the perishing of his garden and his wealth arose from long self-delusion and the dominance of greed over him. «ولئن»: the واو is a conjunction, the لام is the preparatory lām for an oath, and «إن» is conditional; «رددت» is a passive past verb in the position of the jussive, the protasis, and the تاء is the deputy agent; «لأجدن»: the لام occurs in the answer of the oath, and the apodosis of the condition is omitted, indicated by the answer of the oath, as is the rule, in the words of the author of al-Khulāṣa:
واحذف لدى اجتماع شرط وقسم ... جواب ما أخرت فهو ملتزم
(When a condition and an oath come together, omit the answer of whichever you put later; that is obligatory.)
«خيرا» is a direct object of «لأجدن»; «منها» is attached to «خيرا»; «منقلبا» is a tamyīz, that is, "a destination", so it is a maṣdar. It is also permissible to parse «خيرا» as a ḥāl and «منقلبا» as an object, that is, "a destination better than the destination of this world". (قالَ لَهُ صاحِبُهُ وَهُوَ يُحاوِرُهُ أَكَفَرْتَ بِالَّذِي خَلَقَكَ مِنْ تُرابٍ ثُمَّ مِنْ نُطْفَةٍ ثُمَّ سَوَّاكَ رَجُلًا) «قال» is a past verb, «له» is attached to it, and «صاحبه» is the agent; the واو is a ḥāl-waw; «هو» is a mubtadaʾ and the clause «يحاوره» its khabar; the hamza is for a rebuking, reproaching question; «كفرت» is a verb and an agent; «بالذي» is attached to «كفرت»; the clause «خلقك» is a ṣila; «من تراب» is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to «خلقك»; «ثم من نطفة» is conjoined; «ثم» is a conjunction; «سواك» is a past verb with a latent agent and the كاف a direct object; «رجلا» is a ḥāl. It is permissible for it to come as a ḥāl, though it is not derived, because it follows «سواك», since it was possible for Him to fashion him as other than a man; this will be discussed in detail in the section of Benefits. It may also be parsed as the second object of «سواك», and some parsed it as a tamyīz. (لكِنَّا هُوَ اللَّهُ رَبِّي وَلا أُشْرِكُ بِرَبِّي أَحَداً) «لكنا»: the original is «لكن أنا»; the vowel of the omitted hamza was cast onto the nūn and the nūn was assimilated into the nūn. The better usage is to drop the alif in connected speech and keep it in pause, because «أنا» is so, the alif in it being redundant, to show the vowel. «أنا» is a mubtadaʾ; «هو», that is, the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-shaʾn), is a second mubtadaʾ; «الله» is a third mubtadaʾ; «ربي» is the khabar; and the yāʾ refers back to the first mubtadaʾ. It is not permissible for it to be the doubled «لكنّ», which governs the accusative, since if so «هو» could not come after it, because it is a nominative pronoun. It is also permissible for the name of Allah to be a badal from «هو». Like this construction is the saying of the poet:
وترمينني بالطرف أي أنت مذنب ... وتقلينني لكن إياك لا أقلى
(You shoot me with the glance, meaning "you are at fault", and you hate me, but you I do not hate.)
and «ولكن» is originally «لكن أنا»; the vowel of the hamza was moved to the nūn, then it was dropped, then the nūn was assimilated into the following nūn, and the final alif was dropped in writing as in pronunciation. Had he treated connection like pause, it would have been kept. The object «إياك» was fronted for the sake of stressing her innocence from being hated and singling her out for that apart from other women. It is clear that his saying «ترمينني بالطرف» is an explicit metaphor (istiʿāra taṣrīḥiyya), because he likened the casting of the glance to the casting of a stone. The واو is resumptive, «لا» is negative, «أشرك» is an imperfect verb whose agent is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "anā" (I); «بربي» is attached to «أشرك»; «أحدا» is a direct object.
(وَلَوْلا إِذْ دَخَلْتَ جَنَّتَكَ قُلْتَ ما شاءَ اللَّهُ لا قُوَّةَ إِلَّا بِاللَّهِ) «ولولا»: the واو is a conjunction and «لولا» is a particle of urging, that is, "why not"; «إذ» is an adverb for past time attached to «قلت»; «ما شاء الله»: «ما» is a relative noun in the position of the nominative, the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ, that is, "This is what Allah willed, of wonders of beauty, awesome blessings and marvellous favours and bounties"; or we parse «ما» as a mubtadaʾ whose khabar is omitted, its implied form being "kāna"; the clause is the reported speech; the clause «شاء الله» is a ṣila and the returning pronoun is omitted as we have implied. It is also permissible that it be conditional, in the position of the accusative by the protasis verb, with the apodosis omitted, that is, "kāna"; the meaning: "whatever Allah wills, comes to be"; and the whole clause is the reported speech. «لا» is the lā of generic negation; «قوة» is its noun, indeclinable on the fatḥa; «إلا» is a particle of restriction; «بالله» is the khabar of «لا». (إِنْ تَرَنِ أَنَا أَقَلَّ مِنْكَ مالًا وَوَلَداً) «إن» is conditional; «ترني» is the protasis, its sign of jussive being the dropping of the weak letter; the nūn is the nūn of protection and the yāʾ is a direct object, and it was dropped in the writing of the muṣḥaf; «أنا» is a pronoun of separation (ḍamīr faṣl); «أقل» is the second object of «ترني». It is permissible to parse «أنا» as emphasis of the yāʾ; «منك» is attached to «أقل»; «مالا» is a tamyīz and «ولدا» is conjoined to it. (فَعَسى رَبِّي أَنْ يُؤْتِيَنِ خَيْراً مِنْ جَنَّتِكَ) The فاء is the connector of the apodosis, because it is joined to a verb of hope, which is rigid. The places where the apodosis must be linked with the فاء were mentioned earlier, gathered in the saying of one of them:
اسمية طلبية وبجامد ... وبما ولن وبقد وبالتنفيس
(A nominal clause, a requestive one, one with a rigid verb, one with mā, lan, qad, and with the particle of futurity.)
«ربي» is the noun of «عسى»; «أن» and what is within its scope is in the position of the accusative, its khabar; «خيرا» is a second object of «يؤتيني»; «من جنتك» is attached to «خيرا». (وَيُرْسِلَ عَلَيْها حُسْباناً مِنَ السَّماءِ فَتُصْبِحَ صَعِيداً زَلَقاً) «ويرسل» is conjoined to «يؤتيني», and the agent is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "huwa"; «عليها» is attached to «يرسل»; «حسبانا» is a direct object; «فتصبح»: the فاء is a conjunction upon what precedes; «تصبح» is an imperfect verb in the subjunctive because it is conjoined to what precedes; the noun of «تصبح» is latent, its implied form being "hiya" (it); «صعيدا» is the khabar of «تصبح»; «زلقا» is an adjective of «صعيد», of the kind of description by a maṣdar. (أَوْ يُصْبِحَ ماؤُها غَوْراً فَلَنْ تَسْتَطِيعَ لَهُ طَلَباً) «أو» is a conjunction; «يصبح» is conjoined to what precedes; «ماؤها» is the noun of «يصبح» and «غورا» its khabar; the فاء is a conjunction; «لن» is a particle of negation, subjunctive and futurity; «يستطيع» is subjunctive by «لن», and the agent is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "anta"; «له» is attached to «طلبا»; «طلبا» is a direct object. (وَأُحِيطَ بِثَمَرِهِ فَأَصْبَحَ يُقَلِّبُ كَفَّيْهِ عَلى ما أَنْفَقَ فِيها) The واو is a conjunction upon an omitted element implied according to what the speech indicates, that is, "so the thunderbolts fell upon his garden, the waters in it sank, and his fruit too was encompassed by destruction"; «أحيط» is a passive past verb and the deputy agent is latent; «بثمره» is attached to «أحيط»; «فأصبح» is conjoined, its noun is latent, its implied form being "huwa", and the clause «يقلب كفيه» is its khabar; «على ما» is attached to «يقلب» because it contains the meaning of "regrets"; the secret of this expression will come in the Rhetoric section. It is also permissible that the preposition and its genitive noun be attached to an omitted element as a ḥāl from the agent of «كفيه», that is, "regretful". (وَهِيَ خاوِيَةٌ عَلى عُرُوشِها وَيَقُولُ: يا لَيْتَنِي لَمْ أُشْرِكْ بِرَبِّي أَحَداً) The واو is a ḥāl-waw; «هي» is a mubtadaʾ and «خاوية» a khabar; «على عروشها» is a second khabar, and its parsing has already been given; «ويقول» is conjoined to «يقلب», or the واو is a ḥāl-waw and the clause «يقول» is a ḥāl from the agent of «يقلب»; the clause «يا ليتني لم أشرك» is the reported speech; «لم» is a particle of negation, inversion and jussive; «بربي» is attached to «أشرك»; «أحدا» is a direct object. His saying «يا ليتني» has been discussed several times: that «يا» is either for alerting or for vocative, with the one addressed omitted. (وَلَمْ تَكُنْ لَهُ فِئَةٌ يَنْصُرُونَهُ مِنْ دُونِ اللَّهِ وَما كانَ مُنْتَصِراً) The واو is a conjunction; «لم» is a particle of negation, inversion and jussive; «تكن» is a defective imperfect verb in the jussive; «له» is its fronted khabar and «فئة» its postponed noun; the clause «ينصرونه» is an adjective of «فئة»; the adjective was made masculine and plural because «فئة» contains the idea of a group, and a group includes males and females; «من دون الله» is a ḥāl; the واو is a conjunction; «ما» is negative; «كان» and its latent noun, and «منتصرا» is its khabar. (هُنالِكَ الْوَلايَةُ لِلَّهِ الْحَقِّ هُوَ خَيْرٌ ثَواباً وَخَيْرٌ عُقْباً) «هنالك» is a demonstrative noun in the position of the accusative as an adverb of place, attached to an omitted element which is a fronted khabar; «الولاية» is a postponed mubtadaʾ; «لله» is attached to what is in the meaning of the demonstrative noun, or to what it is attached to; «الحق» is an adjective of «لله». It is also permissible that the demonstrative be attached to the sense of "being established" in «لله», with «الولاية» a mubtadaʾ and «لله» its khabar, that is, "established for Allah"; and it is permissible that it be attached to «الولاية» itself, since it is a maṣdar in the sense of "help". «هو» is a mubtadaʾ; «خير» is a khabar; «ثوابا» is a tamyīz; «وخير عقبا» is conjoined to «خير ثوابا»; «عقبا» is in the sense of "outcome".

* Rhetoric:
This verse is full of numerous kinds of rhetorical arts, and here is the detail:

1- Completion (al-tatmīm), precaution (al-iḥtirās) and metonymy (al-kināya):
Al-tatmīm, or al-tamām, has already been discussed fully in Sūrat al-Baqara at His saying, the Exalted, «أيود أحدكم أن تكون له جنة من نخيل وأعناب». It is here in the description of the two gardens. His saying, the Exalted, «واضرب لهم مثلا رجلين جعلنا لأحدهما جنتين» could imply that the two gardens were merely a gathering of dense trees whose branches shade the ground, as the linguistic meaning of "janna" requires, or that the benefit from them was slight, like tamarisk and arāk trees and the like, so that his grief over them would be less than if the two gardens were of palms and vines, from whose fruit he benefited. So He completed that with His saying «وجعلنا بينهما زرعا», lest it be imagined that the benefit was limited to palms and vines, and so that each of the two gardens would combine staples and fruits, with continuous cultivation in a beautiful form and an elegant arrangement. Then He completed that with His saying «وفجرنا خلالهما نهرا», to indicate the permanence of the benefit from them, for water is the secret of life and the first agent of growth in plants. So this man had fulfilled all pleasures and attained every kind of blessing. Then He completed that with His saying «كلتا الجنتين آتت آكلها», to bring to mind the complete picture of the benefit from the resources, and He took precaution with His saying «ولم تظلم منه شيئا» against ... [source text garbled here; the page footer «اب القرآن وبيانه، ج 5، ص: 605» appears in the middle of the sentence] ... any deficiency in the produce it gave, and so that it be a metonymy for the completeness of the two gardens and their growth always and forever, and that they were not in the way of trees whose fruit is complete in some years and not others, or whose fruit comes deficient year after year; rather their yield was overflowing at every time. So the description of the two gardens fulfilled all these three arts. [Translator's note: in the source this sentence is interrupted by the page footer «إعراب القرآن وبيانه، ج 5، ص: 605» and a gap; the repeated passage below supplies the continuation.]
2- Scrambled laff and nashr (al-laff wa-l-nashr al-mushawwash):
That is in His saying, the Exalted: «فقال لصاحبه وهو يحاوره» and the rest of the verse. The sum of what this disbeliever said is three heinous statements: 1- "I am greater than you in wealth and mightier in manpower"; 2- when he entered his garden, arrogant, boastful, wronging himself, he said, intoxicated with delusion, «ما أظن أن تبيد هذه أبدا»; 3- and the third:
he began with the Hereafter because it is the most important, saying «أكفرت بالذي خلقك», and secondly advised him with the second statement because it comes next in rank, so he said: «ولولا إذا دخلت جنتك» etc., and thirdly rebuked him about the first, saying «فعسى ربي أن يؤتيني خيرا من جنتك». So it is a scrambled laff and nashr, as has been mentioned before.
3- Return to completion and metonymy:
Then he returned to completion, depicting the destruction of the two gardens and the fruit together, saying «وأحيط بثمره», then described his state, saying «فأصبح يقلب كفيه على ما أنفق فيها». The turning over of the two palms is a metonymy for regret and grief, because the regretful person turns his palms back to front, as some have also expressed it with "biting the fingertips" and "falling in the hand".
[Translator's note: the source now repeats, verbatim, the passage from «ثمة نقص في الأكل الذي آتته» to the end of section 3 ending «والسقوط في اليد». It reads: "...any deficiency in the produce it gave, and so that it be a metonymy for the completeness of the two gardens and their growth always and forever, and that they were not in the way of trees whose fruit is complete and which give it in some years and not others, or which bring deficient fruit year after year; rather their yield is overflowing at every time. So the description of the two gardens fulfilled all these three arts." Then it repeats section «2- اللف والنشر المشوش» and section «3- عودة إلى التتميم والكناية» word for word, translated above.]
The story of the two brothers:
It is that one of the two men for whom the parable was struck, whose story has been related in various ways, and the gist of it is that there were two brothers of the Children of Israel, one a disbeliever named Qaṭrūs and the other a believer named Yahūdhā. They inherited from their father eight thousand dinars and divided it between them. The disbeliever bought land for a thousand. The believer said: "O Allah, my brother has bought land for a thousand dinars, and I buy from You land in Paradise for a thousand", and he gave it as charity. Then his brother built a house for a thousand dinars, and the believer said: "O Allah, I buy from You a house in Paradise", and gave it as charity. Then his brother married a woman for a thousand, and he said:
"O Allah, I have made a thousand a dowry for the houris." Then his brother bought servants and goods for a thousand, and he said: "O Allah, I have bought the eternal youths for a thousand", and gave it as charity. Then need befell him, so he sat for his brother on his road, and he passed by him with his entourage; he approached him but he drove him away and rebuked him for giving his wealth in charity. Other versions have also been said. We included the story contrary to our condition in this book because of its charm and so that it may be a beacon for creative writers.

4- Exaggeration (al-mubālagha):
In His saying, the Exalted, «أنا أكثر منك مالا وأعز نفرا» there is an art called al-mubālagha and "excess in description" (al-ifrāṭ fī l-ṣifa), as Ibn al-Muʿtazz called it; the first name is Qudāma's. It is that the speaker mentions a state at which, if he stopped there, it would suffice, but he does not stop there until he adds to the meaning of his speech what is more eloquent for what he intends. Exaggeration has come in the Noble Book in several kinds, and we mention what occurs of them in it:
First: exaggeration in the form-shifted adjective (al-ṣifa al-maʿdūla), which has come in six patterns:
a- fuʿlān, like raḥmān, shifted from rāḥim for exaggeration; it is used only of Allah. The Arabs never applied it to anyone in pre-Islamic or Islamic times except Musaylima the Liar: they called him by it in annexation, saying "raḥmān of al-Yamāma". A poet of Banū Ḥanīfa recited, praising Musaylima with it:
سموت بالمجد يا ابن الأكرمين أبا ... وأنت غيث الورى لا زلت رحمانا
(You have risen in glory, O son of the noblest of fathers, and you are the rain of mankind; may you never cease to be a raḥmān.)
b- faʿʿāl, shifted from fāʿil for exaggeration, as in His saying, the Exalted, «وإني لغفار لمن تاب».
c- faʿūl, shifted from fāʿil for exaggeration, like ghafūr and shakūr.
d- faʿīl, shifted from fāʿil for exaggeration, like ʿalīm and ḥakīm.
These four forms occur in the Qur'an, and there are two other forms: mifʿal as in miṭʿan, and mifʿāl as in miṭʿām and mibṭār.
Second: expressing the speech as a report about the greatest, for exaggeration, while reporting of Him is figurative; from this in the Qur'an is His saying, the Exalted, «وجاء ربك والملك صفا صفا», where He made the coming of His mighty signs a coming of His own, for exaggeration.
Third: bringing the possible out of the condition into the impossible, so that the conditioned thing be impossible to occur; this type was mentioned at His saying, the Exalted, «ولا يدخلون الجنة حتى يلج الجمل في سم الخياط». [Translator's note: the source prints «بلج» for «يلج».]
Fourth: what was figurative and became literal through an indicator, as in His saying, the Exalted, «يكاد سنا برقه يذهب بالأبصار»; for the association of this clause with «يكاد» turns it to the literal, so it is changed from impossibility to reality and possibility. [Translator's note: the source prints «فإن قتران», evidently for «فإن اقتران».]
Fifth: a kind that came in the form of the superlative (ism al-tafḍīl), which is pure literalness without an indicator, as in His saying, the Exalted, «أنا أكثر منك مالا وأعز نفرا», which is what we are dealing with.
Sixth: what is exaggerated in its description by way of simile, as in His saying, the Exalted, «إنها ترمي بشرر كالقصر كأنه جمالة صفر». [Translator's note: the source prints «نرمي», for «ترمي».]

Exaggeration in poetry:
This is what has come of exaggeration and its kinds in the Noble Book. As for it in poetry, it has arts that branch out and kinds whose measures and standards differ, as people's opinions about it differ. Some commend it and see it as the utmost in excellence, among them al-Nābigha of Banū Dhubyān, who is the one who said: "The best poet is the one whose lie is judged excellent, and whose bad verse is laughed at." The author of al-ʿUmda cited as an example of this what passed between al-Nābigha and Ḥassān ibn Thābit, and his demanding exaggeration from Ḥassān and accusing him of falling short in his saying:
لنا الجفنات الغرّ يلمعن بالضحى ... وأسيافنا يقطرن من نجدة دما
(Ours are the white bowls that gleam in the forenoon, and our swords drip blood from valour.)
It is famous and widespread in the books of literature. The author of al-ʿUmda cited among the verses of exaggeration about which opinions differed the saying of Imruʾ al-Qays:
كأن المدام وصوب الغمام ... وريح الخزامى ونشر القطر يعملّ به برد أنيابها ... إذا غرد الطائر المستحرّ
(As if wine, the downpour of the clouds, the scent of lavender and the fragrance of perfume were being poured over the coolness of her teeth when the bird sings at the dawn.)
So he described her mouth thus at the pre-dawn hour, when mouths change after sleep; so how do you imagine it at the beginning of sleep, at the beginning of the night? And Imruʾ al-Qays said:
تنورتها من أذرعات وأهلها ... بيثرب أدنى دارها نظر عال
(I made out her fire from Adhriʿāt, while her people are in Yathrib, the nearest of her dwelling being a lofty look away.)
And between the two places is a distance of days.
He also said, describing her fire:
نظرت إليها والنجوم كأنها ... مصابيح رهبان تشبّ لقفّال
(I looked at it while the stars were like the lamps of monks kindled for returning travellers.)
He says: I looked at the fire of this woman, kindled for returners, while the stars were like the lamps of monks. Returners from raids and forays return only at the break of dawn; so if they see it from a distance of days at dawn, its light having died and all its kindler having tired, how was it at the beginning of the night? And he likened the stars to monks' lamps because their light weakens at dawn, as the light of lamps kindled all night weakens, and perhaps they doze at that time.

Another definition of exaggeration:
A group held that exaggeration is excess in describing something that is customarily possible and near to occurring. We will cite some marvellous exaggeration that captivates minds. Among it is what Aḥmad ibn Ḥamdūn related. He said: al-Fatḥ ibn Khāqān was intimate with me and let me in on private matters of his. Once he said to me: "O Abū ʿAbd Allāh, when I entered my house last night, one of my slave-girls met me, and I could not stop myself from kissing her, and I found between her lips an air that if a hung-over man slept in it he would wake sober." That was reckoned as witty and charming from al-Fatḥ ibn Khāqān, and one of them borrowed it, saying:
سقى الله ليلا طاب إذ زار طيفه ... فأنحلته حتى الصباح عناقا
بطيب نسيم منه يستجلب الكرى ... ولو رقد المخمور فيه أفاقا
(May Allah water a night that was sweet when his phantom visited; I wore it out with embracing until morning, with a sweet breeze that draws sleep, in which even a hung-over man, were he to sleep, would awake sober.)
Abū Tammām took a wondrous path in exaggeration, and said, composing excellent love poetry:
تلقّاه طيفي في الكرى فتجنّبا ... وقبلت يوما ظله فتغضّبا
وخبر أني قد مررت ببابه ... لأخلس منه نظرة فتحجّبا
ولو مرت الريح الصبا عند أذنه ... بذكري لسب الريح أو لتعتّبا
ولم تجرمني خطرة بضميره ... فتظهر إلا كنت فيه مسببا
وما زاده عندي قبيح فعاله ... ولا الصدّ والإعراض إلا تحببا
(My phantom met him in sleep and he shunned it; one day I kissed his shadow and he grew angry. He was told that I passed by his door to steal a glance from him, so he veiled himself. Had the east wind passed by his ear with a mention of me, he would have cursed the wind or reproached it. No thought crossed his mind and appeared but I was its cause. His ugly deeds only added to my love for him, and so did his turning away and avoidance.)
And he also said:
قد قصرنا دونك الأبصار خوفا أن تذوبا
كلما زدناك لحظا ... زدتنا حسنا وطيبا
مرضت ألحاظ عينيك فأمرضت القلوبا
(We have restrained eyes from you for fear that you melt away; whenever we added a glance at you, you added to us beauty and sweetness. The glances of your eyes fell ill, so they made hearts ill.)

* Benefits:
1- Kilā and kiltā:
Kilā and kiltā are two words that are parsed as a dual if they are annexed to a pronoun; if they are annexed to an overt noun, they are parsed as a maqṣūr noun, that is, with implied vowels on the alif in every case. They are two nouns that must be annexed; their form is singular and their meaning dual. Therefore it is permissible to predicate of them with what carries a singular pronoun, regarding their form, and a dual pronoun, regarding their meaning. Both were combined in the saying of the poet:
كلاهما حين جدّ الجري بينهما ... قد أقلعا وكلا أنفيهما رابي
(Both of them, when the running between them became serious, had desisted, and both their noses were swollen.)
However, regarding the form is more frequent, and the noble Qur'an came with it. The Exalted said:
«كلتا الجنتين آتت أكلها». Ibn Hishām said in Mughnī al-labīb: "I was asked long ago about the saying of one who says 'Zayd and ʿAmr kilāhumā qāʾim' or 'kilāhumā qāʾimān'. I wrote: if 'kilāhumā' is taken as emphasis, 'qāʾimān' is said because it is a predicate of Zayd and ʿAmr; if it is taken as a mubtadaʾ, both forms are allowed, and the preferred one is the singular. Regarding the form is obligatory in cases like:
kilāhumā muḥibb li-ṣāḥibihi, because its meaning is 'each one of them'; and his saying:
كلانا غني عن أخيه حياته ... ونحن إذا متنا أشدّ تغانيا
(Each of us is, in his lifetime, independent of his brother, and when we die we shall be even more independent of each other.)
Among the verses in which kiltā is mentioned is the saying of Ḥassān ibn Thābit:
إن التي ناولتني فرددتها ... قتلت، قتلت، فهاتها لم تقتل
كلتاهما حلب العصير فعاطني ... بزجاجة أرخاهما للمفصل
(The one you handed me and I returned, was "killed", was "killed" [mixed with water]; so bring it unkilled. Both are the milking of the juice, so hand me a bottle of the one more loosening to the tongue.)
He predicated of «التي» with the singular, so he made it singular; then he said «كلتاهما» and made it dual. [Objection:] And what is the meaning of 'kiltāhumā ḥalab al-ʿaṣīr' when he mentioned only one wine, and he predicated of 'kiltāhumā' with 'arkhāhumā'? The correct is predicating of them with a singular, since they criticized as a solecism anyone who said 'kilā l-rajulayn qāmā' and 'kiltā l-marʾatayn ḥaḍaratā' in the eloquent dialect; and this is shown by His saying, the Exalted, «كلتا الجنتين آتت أكلها». Moreover, the report is authentic that «المفصل» is with kasra on the mīm and fatḥa on the ṣād, whereas one says only «مفصل» with fatḥa on the mīm and kasra on the ṣād. [Translator's note: translated as written; the source's vowel description appears inverted.]
Al-Ḥarīrī and others answered these objections by saying: As for his saying:
ان التي ناولتني فرددتها قتلت he addressed it to the cupbearer who had handed him a mixed cup, because it is said "qutilat al-khamra" when it is mixed; so he wanted to let him know that he had noticed what he did; then he invoked against him with his saying "qutilta". And his saying "arkhāhumā li-l-mufaṣṣal" means the tongue, which is called mufaṣṣal because truth and falsehood are distinguished (yufṣal) with it.
Abū Bakr Muḥammad ibn al-Qāsim al-Anbārī said: A group gathered over drink, and the singer sang them the two verses above. One of them said: "My wife is divorced if I do not ask the judge ʿUbayd Allāh ibn al-Ḥasan tonight about the reason for this poetry, why he said 'inna llatī' in the singular, then said 'kiltāhumā' in the dual." They feared for their friend, left what they were doing, and went on, passing through the tribes, until they reached Banū Shaqra while ʿUbayd Allāh was praying. When he finished his prayer, they explained to him and asked him for the answer to that. He said to them: "'Alladhī' he meant by it the wine mixed with water, then he said afterwards 'kiltāhumā ḥalab al-ʿaṣīr', meaning the wine milked from the grape and the water milked from the clouds, alluded to by the muʿṣirāt in His saying, the Exalted: «وأنزلنا من المعصرات ماء ثجاجا»."

2- The fixed ḥāl (al-ḥāl al-thābita):
The rule for the ḥāl is that it be transitory, because it is taken from al-taḥawwul, which is moving about. It occurs as fixed in places referred to in the longer works. Among them is that its governing element indicates the renewal of the essence of its owner and its coming to be, or the renewal of a quality of it, as in «ثم سوّاك رجلا», since it was possible for Him to fashion him as other than a man; and their saying "Allah created the giraffe, its forelegs longer than its hind legs": "yadayhā" is a badal baʿḍ min kull (partial substitute) from "al-zarāfa", "aṭwal" is a permanent ḥāl from "yadayhā", and "min rijlayhā" is attached to "aṭwal" because it is a superlative, and the governing element of the ḥāl is "khalaqa", which indicates the renewal of the created.
